# Duet v1 architecture specification

Author: Software Architect. Date: 2026-09-21. Status: proposed. Revision 23.

## How to read this document

Every section states a decision and the reason for it. Nothing here is an option.

Sources of record:

- `roadmap/duet-v1/research/gpui-kit-audit.md`, cited as **audit N**.
- `roadmap/duet-v1/research/ardour-concepts.md`, cited as **Ardour N**.
- `roadmap/duet-v1/research/crate-survey.md`, cited as **survey**.
- `roadmap/duet-v1/research/linux-macos-platform.md`, cited as **platform N**.
- `roadmap/duet-v1/research/critic-premise-review.md`, cited as **critic N.N**.

**A claim this specification supersedes carries a dated correction note IN the file that states
it** (critic C19-W22, N22I-5). The rule binds `research/`, `product-requirements.md` and
`design-contract.md`, because each one is a source of record and a superseded line that stands with
no note is a second answer a reader can find and follow. Revision 22 bound `research/` alone, and
design contract 5.3 then offered four loudness targets where PR Q7 and B75 give two plus Custom, so
a chunk K5 implementer who read the contract would have built a four-item control. **The note at
contract 5.3 is OWED and this paragraph is the record of it**: `design-contract.md` and
`product-requirements.md` sit outside the write scope of this revision, so the Architect cannot
write the note into the file in this changeset and will not claim that it did. Until the note
lands, B75 decides the preset set and a chunk K5 implementer reads B75. **PR R-14 is the second
owed note** (critic C23I-N8): B126 records that this plan meets the free-space half of that story
and defers the per-drop time list, and `product-requirements.md` carries no note of the deferral. Revision 21 wrote four such notes, each one
dated 2026-09-21 and each one naming the ADR or the section that decides: the storage format
(ADR 0002), the allocator guard (ADR 0004, section 5.7), `arc-swap` (ADR 0004, section 5.8), and the
global image cache (ADR 0006, section 10.5). Two earlier revisions closed the same finding with a
sentence inside THIS document, which no reader of `research/` ever meets.
- `roadmap/duet-v1/product-requirements.md`, cited as **PR section.item**.
- `roadmap/duet-v1/design-contract.md`, cited as **contract N.N**.
- `CLAUDE.md`, the root `Cargo.toml` lint policy, `clippy.toml`, `deny.toml`.

Decision records live in `roadmap/duet-v1/adr/`. Six decisions carry one.

### The seven document rules

Four revisions failed on one defect class. A fix landed in the section a review named, and the same
fact stayed wrong in two other sections. Revision 5 removes the class by construction: a fact has
one home, and every other place cites it.

**DR1. A decision is edited in place.** A revision rewrites the sentence it changes. It never adds a
lettered successor beside a sentence it contradicts.

**DR2. A type is defined exactly once.** At most one Rust block declares it, and section 1.5 names
its crate and the section. Every other mention is the bare name, with no field list and no derive
list. `cargo xtask check-placement` reads section 1.5 and fails on a type the table omits.

**DR3. A number is stated exactly once.** Section 1.6 is the one table of budgets and bounds, and
each row carries an id of the form B1. Every other place writes the id. Section 1.6 also declares
every workspace constant, so a literal appears in no other Rust block.

Four forms are exempt, and each one is a fact rather than a budget this design chooses. A **version
pin** (`cpal` 0.18.2, `gpui-kit` 0.6.4) names an artifact. A **platform or format constant** (a
supported sample rate, a divisor in a factorization) is arithmetic. A **type size in bytes** is a
compiler fact that VR5 reads. A **recorded count from a guard run**, which section 1.9 prints, is a
measurement of this document and changes whenever the document changes. Nothing else is exempt.

**DR4. A rule is stated exactly once.** Each rule carries an id. DR is a document rule, PL a
placement rule, VR a vocabulary rule, TH a thread rule, SM a plan seam rule, PG a placement-guard
rule, and CG a conversion-guard rule. Section 1.7 indexes the ids and states nothing. Every other
place cites the id.

**DR5. Every guard rule has exactly one probe, and the two counts are equal.** A guard rule with no
probe is an unverified rule, and revision 6 failed on exactly that class: each machine implemented a
narrower rule than its own sentence claimed. Section 1.9 holds the one-to-one table, rule id `PG<n>`
against probe id `PP<n>` and rule id `CG<n>` against probe id `CP<n>`, together with the recorded
result of each probe against this document. **A rule that no probe covers is deleted from the guard,
not left in the text.** A lettered id, such as `PG10b`, is a rule in its own right and carries its
own probe.

**Every rule also states the class it does not cover.** A probe proves that a rule fires; it does
not prove that the rule covers the class its own sentence names, and revision 7 failed on that
distinction five times (critic Q2, Q3, Q13, Q14, Q15). A rule sentence therefore ends with what the
rule declines to decide, and a counter prints how often it declines. `COPY UNDECIDED`, `UNKNOWN`,
and `UNJUSTIFIED` are those counters for the derive claim.

**DR6. A decision record cites a section; it never carries a second copy of one.** An ADR states the
decision and the reason, and every number, type, and rule inside it is a citation: a B id, a type
name, or a section number. It never restates a rule in its own words, because both guards read one
file and the ADRs went eight revisions with no guard and collected nine statements the architecture
had replaced (critic R12, C12).

**DR7. Every block or table a guard rule reads is a registered block.** A registered block carries
four things: a `####` heading of its own, a marker line
`<!-- GUARD BLOCK id=<id> rows>=<n> -->` on the line before its opening fence or its table header, a
stated minimum row count inside that marker, and a matching row in the guard's own registry. The
guard **exits 2** when the heading is absent, when the marker is absent, when the marker's id or
minimum differs from the registry, when the fence or the table header does not follow the marker at
once, or when the parsed row count is below the minimum. Revision 12 read each block with a lazy
regular expression that skipped a deleted block and parsed the next fence, so deleting the
audio-owned block under a kept heading raised the coverage counter from 22 to 88 and the run exited
0 (critic CR-14, WR-16). **A count is the only check that separates a damaged block from an absent
one**, and a marker is the only check that separates a block from the next block.

**Every registered block also carries a membership rule, and every row of it names a referent.** A
`rows>=` minimum refuses a DELETED row and accepts an ADDED one, and three blocks grant coverage by
row, so one added word took a type out of four rules: a Critic probe added `ProbeUnplaced` to the
candidate drop list and a red document went green (critic WR-18). A row must therefore name an
entity that exists elsewhere in this document or in the external table. Section 1.9 states the one
membership kind of each block in its own registered block, PG27 runs it, and the run prints
`MEMBER BLOCKS`, `MEMBER ROWS`, and `MEMBER BAD`. **A marker is also unique across the whole
document, and a marker id the register does not hold is a failure**, because `read_block` anchors
inside one heading region and a Critic probe hid a second marker and an unregistered marker outside
every region (critic C-13, C-14).

PG27 holds the whole contract, section 1.9 registers every block, and the run prints the register
size on `BLOCKS`. **No conversion-guard rule reads a document
block**, because the conversion guard takes its whole input from `cargo metadata`; the registry is
therefore a placement-guard and roster-compile register, and CG rules carry no row.

Appendix C maps every Critic finding from every review to the one section that now holds its
mechanism. **No sentence of this document states how many reviews there have been**, because the
section list of Appendix C and the closure blocks it registers are the fact and a sentence would age
(critic N21I-3).

---

## 1. Bounded contexts and crates

### 1.1 Changes to the working hypothesis

The orchestrator's hypothesis named twelve crates. Five decisions change it, and each one answers a
premise-review finding.

1. **Add `duet-command`**: commands, events, snapshots, and the `BundleDocument` trait, as plain
   data with serde. Without it the application would depend on the transport adapter (critic 8.1).
2. **Add `duet-dsp`**: buffers, filters, gain, pan, meter laws, the peak format, and the monitor
   voice. The engine and the analysis crate need the same primitives, and a shared crate stops a
   back edge (critic 8.5).
3. **Fold the mixer in.** The runtime is a module of `duet-engine` and the document lives in
   `duet-session`. `duet-mix` does not exist, because a mixer is a processor chain and a crate that
   re-exports its dependency protects no invariant (critic 8.4).
4. **Replace `duet-master` with `duet-export`**, and split `duet-interchange` out of `duet-midi`.
   The offline graph is the invariant that earns a boundary, and `quick-xml` and `midly` must not
   reach `duet-score` (critic 8.4, Ardour 10).
5. **Narrow `duet-project` to the bundle, the store, the history, and the watch.** It declares no
   document, because a hub crate defeats the bounded contexts and serializes the build
   (critic 8.2).

`crates/duet` stays the only binary. It opens a window, or serves the Model Context Protocol, or
applies one verb (PR 11 Q2).

### 1.2 The crate table

Each crate names the one invariant it protects (critic 8.6). Every crate goes under `crates/`. Every
crate declares `[lints] workspace = true` and fills `description` in `[package]`, because the denied
`cargo` lint group contains `clippy::cargo_common_metadata`.

**The dependency column lists third-party crates only.** Section 1.3 is the source of truth for
every internal edge, and a member manifest is built from both.

**Part of the column is derived, and the honest fraction is stated.** Guard rule PG12 reads every
derive name and every path segment inside the declarations that section 1.5 places in a crate, maps
each one to its crate through the name map below, and fails on a row that omits a crate its own
declarations prove it uses. **The column holds 70 crate-and-dependency pairs, and the run prints how
many of them PG12 proves on its own `DEP PROVEN` counter** (section 1.9). Every other pair is a
decision that no declaration can show, because a crate reaches most of its dependencies from a
function body and not from a field type. Revision 12 wrote the proved count and the unproved count
as two hand numbers beside a rule that prints neither (critic WR-14). Revision 7 wrote "the column is
derived" and "three rows carry a crate that no declaration proves", and both sentences were false
(critic N2, Q12). `cargo machete` is the backstop for an entry a crate does not use, and the
compiler is the backstop for one it needs and the row omits.

**PG12 had never read one declaration of the application crate, and revision 21 found it by reading
the rule rather than by running it.** Section 1.5 spells the crate `crates/duet` and this table
spells it `duet`, and `dependency_audit` compared the two spellings without normalising, so every
declaration of the largest crate fell out of the rule. `HeldDuration(ArrayVec<NoteValue, 6>)` is the
live instance it hid: the row carried no `arrayvec` entry and nothing said so. The rule normalises
the name now and the row carries the entry.

#### The third-party name map

Each line maps a name that a declaration may carry to the crate that supplies it. The guard reads
this block, so the map is data and not prose. A name outside the map proves nothing about a
dependency, and PG12 states that limit at its own site.

<!-- GUARD BLOCK id=name-map rows>=23 -->
```text
Serialize        serde
Deserialize      serde
DeserializeOwned serde
serde            serde
serde_json       serde_json
SmallVec         smallvec
ArrayVec         arrayvec
basedrop         basedrop
Owned            basedrop
Shared           basedrop
Collector        basedrop
triple_buffer    triple_buffer
rtrb             rtrb
ArrayQueue       crossbeam-queue
thiserror        thiserror
Output           triple_buffer
Input            triple_buffer
Producer         rtrb
Consumer         rtrb
Sender           async-channel
CoreReceiver     async-channel
OneshotSender    futures
OneshotReceiver  futures
```

**Three of those unproved decisions are worth naming, because a reader would otherwise look for the
declaration.** `duet-command` implements `BundleDocument` for four documents and the canonical form
is JSON (section 3.6), so it writes JSON bytes through `serde_json`. `duet-engrave` reads the
Bravura SMuFL `metadata.json` in its own metrics reader (section 10.5), so it needs `serde` and
`serde_json`. `duet-time` returns a `SmallVec` from `split_tuplet` (section 2.4), which is a
signature and not a field. **`duet-core` carries no `serde` entry**: no declaration and no stated
use needs one, and `cargo machete` would reject the entry at the chunk that added it (critic Q12).

The invariant of `duet-command` reads "every value that crosses the transport is plain data", not
"every item in the crate is plain data". The crate also declares the `BundleDocument` trait of
section 1.8, which is not a value. Section 3.5 gives the compile-time assertion that holds VR2.

**Two placements in that table are decisions, not edits.** `rustfft` and `realfft` belong to
`duet-dsp`, because the calibration cross-correlation lives in `duet_dsp::align` and pYIN reaches
the transforms through `duet_dsp::fft`. `duet-engine` therefore depends on no analysis crate, and
`crates/duet` depends on `duet-dsp` so that `LaneView` can paint a `Pyramid` the core hands it.

#### Audio file crate per path

| Path | Crate | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| WAV read and write below the container limit | `hound` | It is the simplest correct WAV reader and writer, and the survey confirms it is maintained. |
| RF64 read and write | `bwavfile` | `hound` has no RF64 support and fails above the container limit (survey). |
| FLAC encode | `flacenc` | The only maintained pure-Rust FLAC encoder (survey). |
| Decode of an imported audio file | `symphonia` | It decodes MP3, AAC, FLAC, and OGG, which a user may drag into a project. |

`duet-engine` depends on `duet-media`, not on those four crates. `duet-analysis` depends on
`duet-dsp` only, because it takes a `SampleSource`. `duet-export` depends on `duet-media` for the
encoder.

**The RF64 promotion rule for a take.** The disk writer opens a take as WAV through `hound`. It
counts written bytes. At the promotion threshold B67 it closes the WAV, reopens the take as RF64
through `bwavfile`, and copies the written frames. A take that starts above the limit opens as RF64
at once. `ManifestEntry::container` records which one.

### 1.3 The dependency graph

Each edge reads "A depends on B". This list is the whole internal graph.

duet-interchange     -> duet-time, duet-score, duet-command
duet-analysis        -> duet-time, duet-dsp, duet-session, duet-command
duet-media           -> duet-time, duet-dsp, duet-session
duet-engine          -> duet-time, duet-dsp, duet-session, duet-command, duet-media
duet-midi            -> duet-time, duet-command
duet-project         -> duet-time, duet-session, duet-command, duet-media

A topological order exists: `duet-time`, `duet-dsp`, `duet-score`, `duet-session`, `duet-command`,
`duet-engrave`, `duet-interchange`, `duet-analysis`, `duet-media`, `duet-engine`, `duet-midi`,
`duet-project`, `duet-export`, `duet-core`, `duet-agent`, `duet`. The graph is acyclic, and the
sixteen names above are exactly the sixteen rows of section 1.2.

**Every crate a declaration names is a direct edge of this list, and PG20 proves it.** Revision 9
stated that the list was the whole internal graph and no rule read a declaration against it, so
sixteen field references crossed an edge the list did not carry and five of them were Cargo cycles
(critic S2). Five edges enter the list in revision 10, and each one answers a declared field.

| Edge | The field that needs it |
|---|---|
| `duet-session` -> `duet-score` | `Track` names one `PartId` and one `StaffId` (section 6.5), and `BusRole::Part` and `SessionCommand::TrackAdd` name the same two |
| `duet-interchange` -> `duet-command` | `MusicXmlImport` and `SmfImport` each carry `Vec<ImportWarning>` (section 3.7) |
| `duet-analysis` -> `duet-session` | `PitchTrack` names the `SourceHash` it measured (section 15.8) |
| `duet-analysis` -> `duet-command` | `LoudnessReport` crosses the transport inside `VerbData`, so VR3 declares it in `duet-command` and the measurement crate consumes it |
| `duet-project` -> `duet-media` | `ProjectError::Media` wraps a `MediaError` (section 15.12) |

**Four references moved instead of gaining an edge, because the edge would close a loop.**

| Type | Was in | Is in | Why the edge is impossible |
|---|---|---|---|
| `InverseCost` | `duet-core` | `duet-score` | `duet-core` depends on `duet-score`, and `Applied` holds the cost |
| `TransportCommand` | `duet-engine` | `duet-command` | `duet-engine` depends on `duet-command`, and `DomainEvent` carries the command |
| `LoudnessReport` | `duet-analysis` | `duet-command` | VR3: `Verb` reaches it through `VerbData`, and a `duet-command` edge to `duet-analysis` would drag `ebur128` into nine crates |
| The four upper arms of `GatewayError` | `duet-engine`, `duet-project`, `duet-interchange`, `duet-export` | `duet-command`, as `UpstreamFailure` | All four crates depend on `duet-command`, so the arm was blocker V1 reopened (section 15.5) |

**`duet-backend-coreaudio` and `duet-backend-alsa` are not in this plan.** Revision 8 carried both
in this list, in no 1.2 row, in no 1.5 row, and in no chunk (critic C7). Section 5.4 states the
condition that would start them: the drift measurement at B70 shows that cpal's two-callback shape
costs more than a native duplex backend saves. Until that measurement exists they are later work,
and this graph names only crates this plan builds.

#### The placement rules

**PL1. A type crosses a crate edge only when the list above carries that edge.**

**PL2. A type is declared in the lowest crate that every consumer reaches.**

**PL3. A name maps to one type in one crate.** No type is re-exported under a second name.
`duet-score` re-exports `Tempo`, `Meter`, and `NoteValue` from `duet-time` under their own names.
`MeterPoint` is a tempo-map entry in `duet-time`; `MeterTap` is where a strip meter reads, in
`duet-session`. Two types with one name would collide inside `duet-engine`.

Five placements follow from PL1 and PL2 and are stated once here.

| Type | Declared in | Consumers, and the edge each one uses |
|---|---|---|
| `MidiRecord`, `NoteEntry` | `duet-command` | `duet-midi` writes them; `duet-engine` reads the audio ring; `duet-core` drains the note queue. `crates/duet` never sees one (section 8.3). |
| The calibration cross-correlation | `duet-dsp`, module `align` | `duet-engine` calls it through its `duet-dsp` edge. `duet-analysis` reaches the transforms through `duet_dsp::fft`. |
| `Calibration`, `DeviceKey` | `duet-session` | They are project state. `duet-engine`, `duet-command`, `duet-project`, and `duet-core` all carry a `duet-session` edge. |
| `Finite` | `duet-time` | `duet-score`, `duet-session`, `duet-command`, and `duet-dsp` all carry a `duet-time` edge. |
| `InverseCost` | `duet-score` | `Applied` holds one, and `duet-core` reaches it through its `duet-score` edge. `duet-core` cannot declare it, because `duet-score` would then need a back edge (critic S2). |
| `TransportCommand` | `duet-command` | `DomainEvent` carries it, and `duet-engine` reads it through its `duet-command` edge. |
| `LoudnessReport`, `UpstreamFailure`, `FailureSurface`, `FailureCode` | `duet-command` | Every one of them crosses the transport, so VR3 puts it in `duet-command` or lower. `duet-analysis` and the four upper crates each convert at their own boundary. |
| `SampleSource`, `Pyramid`, `PyramidHeader`, `PeakBin` | `duet-dsp` | `duet-media` implements the source; `duet-engine` writes a pyramid; `duet-analysis` reads one; `crates/duet` paints one. |

#### Six rules that fall out of the graph

1. `duet-score` declares `ScoreCommand`, `ScoreEvent`, `Applied`, `InverseCost`, and
   `Score::apply`. `duet-command` wraps those types inside `Verb`. Nothing below `duet-command`
   names `Verb`.
2. `duet-session` declares `SessionCommand` and `SessionEvent` the same way.
3. `duet-project` depends on `duet-session` directly. `ManifestEntry` holds `SourceHash` and
   `AudioContainer`, and no re-export stands in for the edge.
4. `duet-engine` depends on `duet-session`. `duet-session` names no engine type. It does name two
   `duet-score` identifiers, because a `Track` belongs to a part and follows a staff.
5. `duet-core` does not depend on `duet-engrave`. The agent never engraves.
6. `crates/duet` depends on no crate that opens a file. It has no `duet-media` edge and no
   `duet-project` edge. Every byte it paints arrives through `duet-core`.

#### Framework types

A **framework type** belongs to `gpui-kit`, to `gpui-pre`, or to tokio. Only `crates/duet` and
`duet-agent` may name one, because no other crate carries an edge to either framework (section 1.2).
`cargo xtask check-placement` reads this block, so the list is data and not prose.

<!-- GUARD BLOCK id=framework-types rows>=7 -->
```text
Pixels Px Bounds Point Size Rems Entity WeakEntity App Window Context AsyncApp Task Global
Render RenderOnce IntoElement Element ElementId Subscription FocusHandle Root WindowExt
AppMenuBar Menu MenuItem Button ButtonGroup Separator Badge Sheet Alert Progress Notification
VirtualList VirtualListScrollHandle Slider RenderImage PathBuilder Path Canvas Scene SharedString
Theme DropdownMenu PopupMenu
AnyView AnyElement Hsla
Runtime Handle CancellationToken UnixStream TcpStream AsyncRead AsyncWrite
```

A struct or an enum that section 1.5 places in any other crate row fails the guard when one of its
field types is a name in that block. A variant payload type counts as a field. That is the shape of
blocker P1: a GPUI type inside a `duet-command` struct, not a GPUI type inside the ownership table
(critic S5).

`duet-engine` names no `gpui-kit` type. The audit records `Priority::RealtimeAudio` and
`spawn_realtime` (audit 10). This design rejects both, because a dependency on `gpui-kit` would stop
the headless host from running the engine. The engine starts its own threads with
`std::thread::Builder`.

**The cost of `duet-command` as a hub is stated, not hidden.** Nine crates depend on it, and it
depends on `duet-score` and `duet-session`. A change to a note field recompiles the engine, the MIDI
crate, and the project crate. That cost buys one vocabulary, which is the product requirement. The
mitigation is that `duet-command` holds no logic.

### 1.4 Pure crates

Eight crates are pure. A pure crate opens no file, opens no device, starts no thread, and names no
GPUI type. `cargo test -p <crate>` covers it with no fixture directory and no hardware.

`duet-time`, `duet-dsp`, `duet-score`, `duet-session`, `duet-command`, `duet-engrave`,
`duet-interchange`, `duet-analysis`.

Those eight hold the whole time kernel, the whole score model, the whole layout engine, every score
file format, every signal block, and every measurement. `duet-media` is not pure, because it opens
files. `duet-engine` is not pure either, and the dummy backend makes it deterministic.

### 1.5 Who owns each type

This table is the one register of types. A type that this document declares and that the table omits
fails `cargo xtask check-placement`. The guard also fails a type that two Rust blocks declare, which
is what holds DR2.

**A module-private type that no section of this document declares is outside this register, and the
chunk that writes it declares it.** The candidate set comes from the fenced Rust blocks of this
document, so a helper that lives inside one module and that only a chunk body names is invisible to
the guard and needs no row here. Ten such names exist in the chunk set of section 13, and this
paragraph is the site that states the class: `Column`, `Beams`, and `LyricPlacement` in line A,
`PoolClass` and `VoiceState` in line D, `Candidate` in line E, `WavSink`, `Rf64Sink`, and
`DecodedAudio` in line N, and `ReadContext` in line X. Each chunk body names its own module types
and states their shapes. A chunk that needs a type this document DOES declare reports the
discrepancy instead of writing a second shape (SM0), and a type a second crate reads is not module
private and takes a row above.

#### The placement guard

`cargo xtask check-placement <document>` reads this document and fails on a placement defect. The
prototype is `roadmap/duet-v1/tools/placement_check.py`, and chunk M0 ports it to
`tools/xtask/src/check_placement.rs`.

**The guard is not in `scripts/dod.sh`.** It runs as the `plan-lint` job of
`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, on a change under `roadmap/` (section 14). Revision 5 put it in the gate,
which made every commit in the repository depend on one roadmap markdown file (critic S11).

**Every rule carries exactly one probe, and the run prints the pair count on `PROBE ROWS`**
(DR5). **This paragraph states no rule count.** Revision 13 wrote "twenty-eight rules" above a list
of thirty-two, because the sentence counted the rules of revision 10 plus three and stopped before
PG27, PG28, and PG29 (critic C-9). A count of this document is a measurement, so section 1.9 prints
it and no prose repeats it (DR3 exemption 4). **The compiler reads the
lint table, and the lint table is a second file.** The tenth Critic review compiled the declarations
on the pinned toolchain and found 81 that trip a denied nursery lint, one enum that does not build
at all, and three stated type sizes that are not facts, while every guard counter stayed at zero
(critic C-1, C-2, C-4). Revision 11 added three rules that close that gap, and revision 12 adds **PG26**, which reads the
section 5.7 thread contract against every declaration the audio thread owns. **PG30** reads every
`B` citation in this document against the `Used by` column of section 1.6, in both directions
(critic C-1). **PG23** reads a
`PartialEq` derive against the field set. **PG24** computes every declaration's size and every enum
arm's size. **PG25** builds the whole roster as a scratch Cargo workspace under the repository's own
`[workspace.lints]` table and runs the real lint invocation over it. A lettered id such as PG4b is a
rule in its own right and carries its own probe (DR5). The rule list and the probe list are one
table, which section 1.9 holds and section 14 runs.

**PG1. It takes the document path from `argv`.** With no argument it prints usage and exits 2.

**PG2. A path that does not open is a failure, not a pass.** The guard is **fail-closed** and exits
2 (critic S11).

**PG3. It fails when the candidate count is zero.** An empty candidate set is a broken parse.

**PG4. It fails on a type that a Rust block declares and that the table above omits.** The
candidate set drops the names below before the rule runs. The list is a fenced block of this
section, so the guard carries no hidden set; revision 9 held fifty-two names inside the machine,
which no section stated and no probe covered (critic C2). A name here is a standard-library type, a
derive name, a trait name, or a marker, and the guard exits 1 when the block is absent. **A name the drop list carries is invisible to this rule**, because the candidate set drops
it before the rule runs; `Duration` is the one name section 1.5 places that the list also carries,
and the compiler is the backstop for a second declaration of it (critic 4). **The primitive trait
sets are a second such block**, and section 1.9 holds it; revision 10 kept a table
of seventeen primitive names inside the machine while this site claimed the guard carries no hidden
set, which made the claim false (critic K-4). The guard exits 1 when either block is absent, and the
run prints `DROP LIST` and `PRIMITIVES` side by side.

**PG4b. It fails on a name that the table above places and that no Rust block declares.** PG4 and

**PG5. It fails on a type that two Rust blocks declare**, which is the mechanism of DR2.

**PG6. It fails on a framework name that the table above claims for a crate other than
`crates/duet` or `duet-agent`.** This is the ownership-table half of the framework check.

**PG7. It fails on a framework type inside a non-application declaration, whether the name is bare
or path qualified.** Take every struct and enum that the table above places outside `crates/duet`
and `duet-agent`. The guard reads every field type and every variant payload type of each one, **on
the declaration text before `strip_paths` runs**, and it matches the **last segment** of a path
against the framework block of section 1.3. `gpui_kit::Px` and `Px` are therefore one failure.
Revision 6 ran the check after `strip_paths`, which deleted the name it was looking for
(critic N8). **The rule reads a field type and a variant payload type, and nothing else.** A type
alias, a method signature, a `where` clause, and a `const` all pass it. The backstop is the
compiler: neither `duet-command` nor `duet-session` carries an edge to `gpui-kit`, so a framework
name in any of those positions fails to build (critic Q14).

**PG8. An enum arm is masked only inside the enum that declares it.** The guard removes the leading
identifier of each top-level arm from that enum's body before it extracts used types. It keeps no
global variant set, so a struct named `Reverb`, `Track`, or `Peak` is still a candidate (critic S6).

**PG9. Every type whose fields are all `Copy` either derives `Copy` or carries an
`#[expect(missing_copy_implementations, ...)]`.** The guard computes Copy-ness transitively over the
document's own declarations, from a fixed set of `Copy` primitives.
`missing_copy_implementations` is a workspace lint at `warn`, and `-D warnings` makes it an error,
so a type that trips it does not build (critic S1). VR5 states the rule this check enforces.

**PG10. A type that derives `Copy` and holds a field this document proves is not `Copy` is a
failure.** PG9 checks the missing direction; PG10 checks the impossible one. Revision 6 derived
`Copy` on `MidiRecord` and `NoteEntry` over a `Box<str>` newtype, which `rustc` refuses, and the
guard reported zero (critic N1).

**PG10b. A type that derives `Copy` and holds a field whose Copy-ness this document does not decide
is a failure.** PG10 needs proof that a field is not `Copy`; an undeclared type gives no proof in
either direction, so the derive rests on a shape no section states. Revision 7 declared `Calibration`
`Copy` over `DeviceKey`, which no block declared, and the guard reported nothing (critic Q1, Q2).
**PG10b asks every field, and no suffix answers for one.** A name a `Copy` derive touches is
declared in a Rust block of this document, or it carries a verdict in the external table of section
1.9. Nothing else passes. Revision 8 let a suffix answer, and the answer for `CommitId` was a `u64`
(critic R1).

**PG11. It parses the section 1.3 edge list and checks every edge claim.** A sentence that joins two
crate names with `uses`, `reads`, `holds`, `carries`, `calls`, `paints`, `drains`, `writes`, or
`depends` must resolve to an edge the list carries. Revision 7 read eight verbs and not `depends`,
which is the verb sections 1.2 and 1.3 use for an edge (critic Q13). **The rule reads a verb from
that closed list and no other**, so a claim phrased another way is outside it; the compiler is the
backstop, because a missing edge does not build. **A subject the edge list does not name carries the empty edge
set**, so a claim about `duet-time`, which is the root and has no edge, fails (critic S14).

**PG12. A section 1.2 dependency row names every crate that its own declarations prove it uses.**
The guard reads the name map of section 1.2, scans every declaration the table above places in a
crate, and fails on a row that omits a mapped crate (critic N2). **It reads the dependency cell as a
list of code spans**, so a word in the cell's prose proves nothing and cannot stand in for a
dependency; revision 7 read every word and the `duet-midi` cell yielded `and`, `two`, and `section`
as dependency names (critic Q15).

**PG13. Every type the audio thread publishes is declared and is `Copy`.** The guard reads the
high-rate table of section 5.8, takes each row whose source is the audio thread, extracts the type
inside `triple_buffer::Output<...>`, and fails when no Rust block declares that type or when the
declaration does not derive `Copy`. TH9 states the rule this check enforces (critic N6).

**PG14. Every undecidable field of every declaration is counted and printed with its type and its
field.** The count covers a declaration that derives `Copy` and one that does not. Revision 7
counted the PG9 direction alone, so the blind spot of PG10, which is the rule that closes the
revision-6 Critical, was itself invisible: the guard printed `UNKNOWN: 23` while twenty-five
`Copy`-deriving declarations held an undecidable field (critic Q2, N13). The run now prints two
numbers. `COPY UNDECIDED` is the one that must be zero, and PG10b enforces it. `UNKNOWN` is the
remainder, and PG17 holds it to a list this document carries.

**PG19. A declaration that derives a closure trait reaches no field type that lacks it.** The nine
closure traits are `Copy`, `Default`, `Serialize`, `Deserialize`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`, `Ord`,
and `PartialOrd`. The guard parses every field type expression, resolves each name against the
document's own declarations and the trait column of the section 1.9 external table, and evaluates an
array, a slice, a tuple, and a generic application structurally. The rule reads a **derive** and
never a hand-written impl: a derive demands the trait of every field and an impl supplies it, which
is why `Finite` carries five hand impls over an `f64` (section 2.6a). **Three classes sit outside
the rule, and each one names its backstop.** A `trait` declaration has no field to read. A
framework type inside an application declaration carries no verdict, because PG7
exempts the application rows and section 1.9 holds the one justified unknown. A `Default` derive
over an array longer than thirty-two reads as the element's `Default`, and the standard library
stops at thirty-two; the guard declines that case and the compiler is the backstop, whatever the
document holds at the time (critic K-7). **A shared reference field is a fourth class, and the rule
is loud there rather than silent**: `&T` is always `Copy`, and the guard reds a `Copy` derive over
one, which is a false red inside the stated preference and not a miss (critic K-6). The compiler is the backstop for all three. Revision 9 had ten `Default` derives over
`Finite`, which has none, and three `Serialize` derives over a type with none, and no rule looked
(critic S1, S4).

**PG20. Every field type of every declaration sits in a crate that the section 1.3 graph reaches
from the declaring crate.** The crate itself, or a transitive dependency, passes; anything else is a
failure. The rule reads the graph and not the member manifest, so a type reached only through a
transitive edge passes the guard; section 1.3 states the stronger rule that every crate a
declaration names is a direct edge, and `cargo machete` and the compiler are the backstop for that
half. Revision 9 carried sixteen references across an absent edge, and five of them were Cargo
cycles (critic S2). **The parser reads a `dyn Trait` and an `impl Trait` argument from revision 11
onward**: it drops the leading keyword, splits a `+` bound list at top level, drops a lifetime
bound, and gives every remaining path its own name. Revision 10 returned nothing for a trait-object
argument, so a `Box<dyn AudioProcess>` field in `duet-command` passed in silence, which is the exact
Cargo-cycle shape the rule exists to catch (critic W-4). **Four forms the parser still declines**,
and each one is outside the document: a function pointer such as `fn(Ticks) -> Span`, a closure
trait with a parenthesized argument list such as `Fn(Ticks)`, a qualified path such as
`<Score as Document>::Id`, and an associated type of a generic parameter. The compiler is the
backstop for all four.

**PG21. The `#[expect(missing_copy_implementations)]` sites and the Appendix B.1 table are one
set.** Both directions: a site B.1 omits is a failure, and a B.1 row no declaration carries is a
failure. B.1 is the list the Orchestrator adjudicates before dispatch, so a row that names nothing
is a decision nobody needs and a site that is not on it is a suppression nobody approved. Revision 9
held eight sites and listed three (critic W7).

**PG22. Every `Eq`, `Hash`, and `Ord` derive is named in the VR1 derive-use table of section 3.5.**
**The rule runs in one direction only, and this is the site that says so.** It fails on a derive the
table omits; it does not fail on a table row that no declaration uses, exactly as PG15 and PG17 are
one-directional. The printed row count lets a reader compare the two and see a stale row. Revision 9
had eight types deriving one of the three with no stated use, and VR1 had no rule and no probe
(critic W16). **The rule reads `Hash` and `Ord` alone from revision 11 onward**, because
VR1 no longer treats `Eq` as a choice and PG23 holds that half.

**PG23. A declaration that derives `PartialEq`, derives no `Eq`, writes no hand `impl Eq`, and
whose every field type supplies `Eq` is a failure.** That is the exact shape
`clippy::derive_partial_eq_without_eq` refuses, and the root `Cargo.toml` sets `clippy::nursery` to
`deny` and relaxes two nursery lints, neither of which is this one. The guard resolves each field
type through the same machinery PG19 uses: the document's own declarations, the hand impls, and the
`Traits` column of the section 1.9 external table. **A field the guard cannot decide makes the
declaration undecided, never a failure**, and the run prints `EQ UNDECIDED` beside `EQ MISSING`. The
rule skips a trait and an empty body. **No declaration writes a placeholder body from revision 12
onward**, so no declaration leaves this rule by that door; revision 11 had 44 of them and PG25
answered each one with a substitute that supplied eight closure traits it never earned (critic
WR-1). PG3 fails on a comment where a field belongs. An application-row declaration that names a
framework type is outside the rule for the reason PG19 states. Revision 10 removed `Eq` from six more types to satisfy PG22, which moved the design
further from the policy while every counter stayed at zero (critic C-1).

**PG24. The guard computes the size and the alignment of every declaration and of every enum arm,
and it fails an enum whose largest arm passes three times the next largest.** That is the rustc lint
`variant_size_differences`, which `[workspace.lints.rust]` sets to `warn` and which
`.cargo/config.toml` turns into an error. The model lays out a struct by field alignment, lays out
an enum arm as a struct and rounds it up to the enum's payload alignment, reads an array length from
a section 1.6 constant, and reads every external size from the section 1.9 block. **It reads every primitive size and every primitive trait set from a section 1.9 block, so it
carries no hidden table** (critic K-4). **It models no niche.** An expression that carries an `Option`, a fat pointer, or a third-party container therefore
carries a recorded row or counts as undecided, and the run prints `SIZE UNDECIDED`. The rule compares the arms that carry a payload, each one padded to the enum's payload alignment,
and it applies the filter rustc applies first: **rustc lints a direct tag only.** rustc puts the tag
in a spare bit pattern of the largest arm when that arm has one and returns before its own
comparison, so an enum whose largest arm offers a spare pattern is outside the rule. `SlotState` is
the one site in this plan, because `EqualizerState` is `f64` all the way down and a float offers no
spare pattern. **Every size this document states is a
value this rule printed and PG25 measured**, because revision 10 stated six sizes by hand and three
were wrong (critic C-2, C-4).

**PG26. A type the audio thread owns names no heap-owning type outside a deferring wrapper.**
Section 5.7 holds the fenced block of audio-owned declarations, and the rule is transitive over this
document's own declarations. It refuses a field that names `Box`, `Vec`, `String`, `Arc`, `Rc`,
`BTreeMap`, `BTreeSet`, `HashMap`, `HashSet`, `VecDeque`, `Cow`, `PathBuf`, or any external name
whose section 1.9 row carries the word "heap". TH1 forbids an allocation and a free on that thread,
and no rule read a thread contract before revision 12: revision 11 boxed one enum arm to satisfy
`variant_size_differences` and put one allocation in migration rule 2 and one free in migration
rule 3, both inside `GraphRunner::run` (critic CR-2).

**The rule has exactly one escape, and it is a type.** A field whose outermost head is an external
name whose section 1.9 `Why` cell carries the word "defers" is legal, and the walk stops there:
`basedrop::Owned` and `basedrop::Shared` each move the free of everything below them to the
collector thread (TH5). A bare `rtrb`, `triple_buffer`, `crossbeam_queue`, `async_channel`, or
`std::thread` handle inside an audio-owned declaration is therefore a failure, whatever a block or a
paragraph says about who allocated it. Revision 13 exempted `ChainState.reader` and
`ChainState.writer` by hand, and a Critic probe put a `Vec<u8>` behind that exemption and got a
green run with `HEAP IN AUDIO: 0` (critic CR-16). **An exemption line answers the allocation half
and never the free half**, and the section 5.7 exemption site states it. The guard is fail-closed
when either block is absent, and the run prints `AUDIO DEFERRED`.

**PG25. The roster compiles.** The guard writes a scratch Cargo workspace outside the repository:
one crate per crate row of the table above, with the section 1.3 edges as path dependencies, every
declaration in its own crate, the section 1.6 constants a declaration names, the external crates of
the section 1.9 pin block, and the repository's own `[workspace.lints]` table,
`.cargo/config.toml`, `clippy.toml`, `rust-toolchain.toml`, and `Cargo.lock`. It then runs
`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`. A cycle in section 1.3 and a missing edge
each fail at `cargo`, because a crate imports a name from a direct edge and from nothing else. The
prototype is `roadmap/duet-v1/tools/roster_compile.sh`, and chunk M0 ports it to
`tools/xtask/src/check_roster.rs`.

**The stated profile, which is the only thing PG25 relaxes.** Seven lints, each with its reason.
`missing_docs` and `clippy::missing_docs_in_private_items`, because the roster carries declarations
and not documentation. `clippy::must_use_candidate`, `clippy::missing_const_for_fn`,
`clippy::new_without_default`, `clippy::missing_panics_doc`, and `clippy::missing_errors_doc`.
**The reason is substitution 1 and not the absence of a body**: the roster compiles every complete
`impl` block this document spells out, the run prints that count on `ROSTER IMPLS`, and with the
profile removed those four lints fire on `Finite::new`, `Finite::get`, and `Finite::from_finite_const`,
whose `#[must_use]` attributes and whose `# Panics` section live in the doc comment that
substitution 1 removes. Revision 11 stated a reason the compiler contradicts (critic WR-3). **Nothing else is
relaxed**, and the workspace lint table is otherwise a byte copy of the repository's own.

**The stated substitutions, because a roster is not a crate.** This paragraph states no count, for the reason the substitution block states none: only the run can produce one, and it prints `ROSTER SUBS`. Section 1.9 holds the block,
PG25 reads it, and the guard refuses to run when its own list and that block differ, so the count
here and the count in the script are one number (critic WR-3). **Substitution 2 of revision 11 is
gone**: no declaration writes a placeholder body any more, so no declaration is taken out of PG19,
PG23, PG24, or PG25 by a substitute that supplies eight closure traits it never earned (critic
WR-1). PG3 fails on a comment where a field belongs.

**PG25 carries a denominator floor.** Substitution S7 drops a declaration that section 1.5 does not
place, so the roster's item count is PG4's output and it can never sit below the number of names the
section 1.5 table places. The run prints `FLOOR` beside `ROSTER ITEMS` and refuses a smaller count.
A Critic run deleted the `RenderJob` declaration and the roster exited 0 with one item fewer, while
the placement guard on the same copy printed `UNDECLARED: 1`; the pair covered it and neither guard
was non-vacuous on its own (critic C-3).

**PG25 also measures every size.** The workspace carries a `roster-sizes` binary that prints
`size_of` and `align_of` for every declaration the roster spells out and for every whole expression
in the section 1.9 size block. **A recorded row the compiler contradicts is a failure**, so no size
in this document can go stale and every `#[expect]` reason that states a size rests on a measured
fact.

**What PG25 does not cover, stated at the site.** It reads a declaration and never a function body,
so a defect that needs a body is outside it. It builds the application row as a library, so that row
carries two crate-level `#[expect]` attributes for the two reachability lints that section 15.16
states cannot fire on a `pub(crate)` type in a binary. It runs outside `scripts/dod.sh`, in the
`plan-lint` job, for the reason the guard-placement paragraph above states.

**PG18. Every external type a declaration names carries a verdict in the external table of section
1.9.** There is no drop list. Revision 8 skipped a fixed set of eight tokens, and `AtomicU32` was
one of them, so a `Copy` derive over the reset counter this design puts on the audio path passed in
silence (critic R2). The verdicts are `Copy`, `not Copy`, `transparent`, and `undecided`.

**PG17. Every undecidable field type is named in the justified-unknown table of section 1.9.** The
guard reads that table and fails on an undecidable field whose type the table omits. A new field of
an undeclared type therefore stops the guard until an author either declares the type or adds a row
with a reason. Section 1.9 carries the list and the reason for each class (critic Q1).

**PG15. The `Declared in` cell of a crate row names every section that declares one of that crate's
types.** The guard tracks the section heading above each Rust block and fails on a declaring section
the cell omits. The check runs in one direction only: a section in the cell that declares nothing is
not a failure, because a section may hold a signature rather than a declaration (critic N14).

**PG16. Every test that section 14 selects has a row that names the chunk which writes it.** The
guard collects every `test(<name>)` term and every `--test <name>` target inside section 14, and
fails on a name with no row in the selected-test table of that section, or on a row whose chunk id
appears in no phase of section 13.3 (critic N3).

**The guard prints one counter line per claim family, and section 1.9 records every line of the
baseline run.** PG4, PG4b, and PG5 to PG8 support the placement claim, PG9, PG10, and PG10b the
`Copy` claim, PG19 the derive-closure claim, PG20 and PG20b the reachability claim, PG11 the edge
claim, PG12 the dependency claim, PG13 the snapshot claim, PG15 the register claim, PG17 the
unknown-list claim, PG18 the external claim, PG21 the suppression claim, PG22 the vocabulary claim,
PG23 the `Eq` claim, PG24 the size claim, PG26 the audio-allocation claim on `AUDIO OWNED`,
`AUDIO EXEMPT`, and `HEAP IN AUDIO`, PG27 the block-contract claim on `BLOCKS`, PG28 the
shared-limit claim on `LIMIT ROWS` and `LIMIT BAD`, and PG29 the probe-table claim on `PROBE ROWS`
and `PROBE BAD`. PG14 prints `COPY UNDECIDED` and `UNKNOWN`. PG25 prints its own block, because it
runs `cargo`. Revision 12 stated a family count of sixteen and named fifteen, and PG26 appeared in
neither (critic concern 2).

**PG20b. Every constant a declaration names sits in a crate the section 1.3 graph reaches.** An
array length and a const generic argument are values and not types, so PG20 cannot see one. The rule
reads every `pub const` of section 1.6 with the crate comment above it, finds each one inside a
declaration's field expressions, and fails when the declaring crate does not reach the constant's
crate. It states its own limit: **a constant inside a function body is invisible to it**, because
this document writes few bodies, and PG28 holds that half from the section 1.6 shared-limit block
(critic CR-12).

**PG27. Every block and every table the guard reads is a registered block.** DR7 states the
contract, section 1.9 holds the register, and the run prints the register size on `BLOCKS`. The
rule exits 2 on an absent heading, an absent
marker, a marker that disagrees with the register, a fence or table header that does not follow the
marker at once, a row count below the stated minimum, a parsed token that is not the shape the block
declares, or a register and a rule-to-block map that are not one set. It states its own limit: **it proves that a block is present, whole, and well
formed, and it decides no cell of it.**

**PG26e. The audio-owned root set is CLOSED under reachability, and the closure is the third
source PG26d does not have.** The audio thread holds one value, `GraphState`. Everything that value
reaches through a declared field is on the audio thread by construction, so every declared type the
rule reaches from `GraphState` is an audio-owned root or a row of the `audio-reachable-leaf` block.
Both directions run: a reachable name that is neither is a failure, and a leaf row `GraphState` does
not reach is a failure, so the exception block cannot grow a row that covers nothing.

**Why the rule exists.** PG26d compares the `audio-owned` block with the `**Audio-owned**` markers.
Those are two hand-written copies of ONE judgement, in one document, by one author, in one
changeset, so holding them consistent tests self-consistency and not truth. The Critic moved
`Transport` out of the block and `ChannelConfig` in, moved the marker line with them, and the run
stayed green with a `Vec<u8>` planted on the swapped-out type: four lines defeated all three TH1
rules (critic C16-W1). PG26e reads NEITHER source. It reads the declaration bodies, which the same
edit does not touch, so the same coordinated edit at a reachable root is red.

**The rule's own limit, stated here.** It covers the REACHABLE part of the root set, and **every
count of that split is a counter the run prints and never a hand number** (critic C22I-W2):
`AUDIO OWNED` is the root set, `ASSERTED ROOTS` is the part this rule does not derive, and the
difference is the part it does. Revision 22 stated four counts here and at the PG26f site that its
own run refuted, and a limit statement is the honesty mechanism of this document. The asserted part
is the `audio-asserted` block, row for row: each of those roots reaches the audio thread as a
function argument or as a published value and not as a field of `GraphState`, so a coordinated
four-line edit at one of them is still green, and PG26f is the third source that raises the cost of
that edit. The block names every one, `SlotMeterSnapshot` and `CpalBridge` included.

**PG31. Every section 13.4 link runs forward, and two chunks of one line never share a phase.**
SM8 states the rule. The guard parses each 13.4 row's first cell into a predecessor set and a
successor set around the word `before`, reads the section 13.3 phase table, and fails on a link
whose predecessor is in the same phase as its successor or in a later one. It fails on a link that
names a chunk no phase holds. It then reads each chunk's line from the `line-map` block and fails on two
chunks of one line in one phase, which is SM6. **The map is DATA and never a derivation from the
id** (critic C17-W9, C19-W11): revision 17 derived the line from the first letter of the chunk id,
which is wrong for every trunk chunk, and revision 19 left the derivation sentence standing three
sections away from the fix.

Revision 16 put three pairs in one phase across a crate edge section 1.3 states and carried no link
row for any of them (critic C16-12). The phase table then asserted a parallelism the build could
not deliver, and nothing read the two tables against each other.

**The rule's own limit, stated here.** It reads the links the document WRITES. A crate edge that
binds and that section 13.4 does not carry is invisible to it, exactly as PG17 is one-directional
for the unknown table. SM8 states when an edge binds, and the table is the record.

**PG26f. The eleven roots the closure does not reach have a THIRD source.** The
`audio-asserted` block names each one with the reason it is on the audio thread, and the rule holds
that block and the root set to one set outside the reachable part. Both directions run.

**Why it exists.** The sixteenth Critic defeated PG26d with a four-line coordinated edit, and the
seventeenth Critic showed the same edit is still green under PG26e on the eleven roots the closure
does not reach, `Transport` among them (critic C16-W1, C17-W8). The root set is now the reachable
set plus the asserted set, and the three sources must agree, so the edit costs six lines in three
blocks. **The rule's own limit, stated here**: the asserted block is an assertion, exactly as the
other two are, and no derivation exists for an argument type because this document does not write
`GraphRunner::run`'s body. What the rule adds is a third place to edit and a checkable reason per
row.

**PG31b. Two chunks in one phase whose crates carry a section 1.3 edge are visible.** The rule
reads no link row. It pairs the line chunks of each phase, asks the edge list whether one crate
depends on the other, and refuses a pair that is neither a 13.4 link nor a row of the
`phase-pair-exempt` block. C16-12 was three such pairs with no link row for any of them, and PG31
reads rows, so a new pair in that state stayed invisible (critic C17-W9).

**Every exemption row must NAME both chunks of its own pair** (critic N18-1). A reason is prose, and
prose that no rule reads is a reason that can drift off the pair it excuses, which one of the 24
rows had already done. The rule therefore parses each row's own reason and fails when the two chunk
ids of the pair are not both in it. Revision 18 ran this check inside the prototype and stated it in
no rule, and its failures printed under another rule's counter, so the specification an implementer
ports carried neither the check nor the counter.

**The rule's own limit, stated here**: it decides that an edge EXISTS and never that it binds at
build time; SM8 states when an edge binds and the exemption block is the reviewed record of every
pair where it does not.

**PG32. Every finding of every review has one closure row, the count is generated, and the review
file is identified.** Appendix C carries one registered block per review. The rule has eight parts.

- **CL0. The review format is REQUIRED, and this is the one place that states it** (critic C19-3).
  A review states one finding per `## CRITICAL <n>.` heading, one per `## WARNING <n>.` heading, and
  one per `## CONCERN <n>.` heading, each numbered from one inside its own family, and it states
  **one count sentence of exactly this shape**, near its verdict:

  ```text
  **Counts: <n> Criticals, <n> Warnings, <n> Concerns.**
  ```

  **No other shape counts as a finding.** A `### CRITICAL 11`, a `**W1.**`, and a Concerns TABLE are
  each invisible to the parser, and revision 19's own review used two of the three: its Warnings
  were `**Wn.**` and its Concerns were a table, so a parse of it would have generated a fraction of
  its findings and this appendix would have recorded a complete closure over that fraction. **The
  Critic brief repeats this block verbatim**, so the reviewer is told the format before the review
  is written and never after it is refused.
- **CL1.** `tools/review_ids.py` reads the CL0 headings and prints the id list. It removes every
  fenced block first, because a review of a review quotes headings and one quoted heading made a
  seven-Critical review generate eight ids; the only way to green was then a row for a finding no
  review made (critic C18-W6). An empty WARNING or CONCERN family is allowed, and a review with no
  heading of any family is a refused run.
- **CL1b. The count sentence is a SECOND SOURCE, and a disagreement is a refused run** (critic
  C19-2). The heading scan is one reading of the review by one parser, and CL1 alone therefore
  trusts that reading the way revision 18 trusted the review file. The reviewer writes the count
  sentence in prose that the parser does not build, so a heading the parser cannot see makes the two
  disagree and the run refuses with both numbers. **A review of revision 20 or later must carry the
  sentence**, and an earlier review is printed as `COUNT SENTENCE: absent`. The cut-off is the
  review's own stated revision and never a flag a runner passes, because a flag that removes a check
  is the defect C16-2 already cost this plan one revision.
- **CL1c. The SECOND SOURCE comes from outside the Architect's write scope, and CL1b does not**
  (critic C21-W1). CL1b reads a second SENTENCE of the file CL1 reads, under one hand, and the
  twenty-first Critic defeated the whole closure record with seven coordinated edits: it deleted one
  `## WARNING 6` section of a stored review, retyped that review's own count line, dropped the
  matching closure row, retyped the document count sentence, retyped the digest sentence, lowered
  the `rows>=` marker, and edited one line of the `placement_check.py` register. Every gate stayed
  green. **A count of edits is not the property the rule needs.** The Architect owns the document,
  the path `reviews/critic-spec-<n>.md`, and both guard registers, so no rule that reads only those
  files can ever answer.

  The Critic stores every review with `.claude/plan-coordination/db.sh append`, which mints a
  `<simpleflake>-<suffix>` key. That keyspace is append-only, the store sits outside the repository,
  and the Critic is the writer, so the Architect cannot rewrite a stored review. **The closure
  section records that key beside the digest**, in the sentence
  ``The review file this block records is stored at plan-store key `<key>` (closure-<id>).``, and
  `closure_check.py` reads the stored copy back with `db.sh get` and compares its content digest
  with the file's. A section with no key sentence, a store that does not answer, a key that holds
  nothing, and a digest that differs are each a failure.

  **A rewrite was never the attack, and revision 22's rule could not see the one that was** (critic
  C22I-W5). The store refuses a rewrite and it does not refuse an APPEND, so a coordinated edit
  needed no rewrite: it appended a doctored review under a NEW key and retyped one sentence of the
  closure section, and both acts sat inside the Architect's own write scope. Two halves close it.
  **The suffix comes from the review FILE NAME and not from the sentence**: a review named
  `critic-spec-<rev>.md` may be stored only under `review-<rev>`, `run_all_gates.py` derives that
  file name from `reviews/`, and CL5 binds the file to its digest, so a key outside that suffix is
  refused whatever the document says. **The guard reads EVERY stored copy of that suffix, not the
  one key the document names**, and it fails when any copy differs from the file, so a second
  append under the right suffix is a second copy that disagrees. The run prints `STORE COPIES` so
  the denominator is readable.

  **There is no way to skip the store half** (critic C22I-W4). Revision 22 shipped a `--no-store`
  flag that printed `STORE: skipped` and exited 0, so a run in which every closure block skipped its
  second source was, by exit code, identical to a run in which every one matched; the CL1b site
  above condemns exactly that shape in its own words. The flag is gone, and a run that reaches the
  end with the store half unrun is a failure that says so.

  **`check-closure` runs at review time and in no job, and section 14 states why** (escalation
  M0-2). A hosted runner carries no store under `~/.claude/plan-dbs/`, and the three ways to give it
  one each break this rule: a restore needs a secret no chunk owns, a copy inside the repository
  puts the second source back inside the Architect's write scope, and a pass on an absent store is
  the vacuous green the paragraph above refuses. Chunk M0 measured both states and removed the nine
  job lines that revision 23 promised. **The party that runs the guard is the party that holds the
  store**: the Architect runs it before a plan revision, and the Engineering Critic re-runs it over
  the same store when it verifies a closure. Revision 23 wrote that the job runs it "against the
  store the workflow restores", and no chunk owned that restore.
- **CL1d. Every run of the guard is recorded in the store, and a closure section of revision 24 or
  later cites the run that verified it** (critic C1-10). CL1c moved the guard out of every job, and
  revision 24 left the verdict as a claim in prose with no party able to reproduce it, which is the
  state CL1b refuses one rule above. The party that runs the guard appends one row with
  `.claude/plan-coordination/db.sh append roadmap/duet-v1 closure-run "<body>"`, which mints the key
  `<simpleflake>-closure-run`. The body opens with `COMMAND: `, `EXIT: ` and `TREE: `, one per line,
  and then holds the whole stdout of the run. **The closure section records the key** in the
  sentence ``The `check-closure` run that verified this block is recorded at plan-store key `<key>`.``,
  which carries its own head and never collides with the CL1c review-key sentence. The guard reads
  the key back with `db.sh get`. **A section of revision 24 or later with no run-key sentence, a key
  whose suffix is not `closure-run`, a store that does not answer, and a body whose `EXIT: ` line
  states anything but `0` are each a failure.** A section below revision 24 prints
  `RUN KEY: absent`, which is the forward cut-off CL1b already uses for the count sentence, and the
  guard states the cut-off in its own source rather than in a flag a runner passes.

  **The order is append first, then record, and the rule states why that is not circular.** A run
  cannot record the key of itself. The run a section cites is the run the Critic made over the
  FROZEN document of the revision the section closes, exactly as the stored review is appended
  before the section that names it. So the `EXIT: 0` the guard demands is the verdict on the
  document the closure was verified against, and the next revision's Critic appends its own row.

  **A PREFIX scan cannot enumerate this family** (critic C2-2). The suffix sits at the END of the
  minted key, and `scan` matches a key prefix, so `db.sh scan roadmap/duet-v1 closure-run` prints
  nothing however many rows exist. The enumeration that works is
  ``.claude/plan-coordination/db.sh keys roadmap/duet-v1 | grep -- '-closure-run"'``, which prints
  one record per key with its byte size and no value. Section 14 states the same command.

  **The rule's own limit, stated here.** The guard reads the exit code of a recorded run and it
  cannot prove that the run is the one the author meant. The `TREE: ` line names the commit, and a
  reader compares it; no rule does. That is a smaller gap than the one CL1d closes, and the record
  is the thing a later party can check at all.

  **One append per review, and the cost of a second one is stated** (critic C23I-N4). The keyspace is
  append-only and `plan-db` offers no command that removes a key, so a second append under one
  suffix makes that closure gate red for ever. The party that appends is the Critic, the rule that
  binds it is one append per review file, and a retried or interrupted Critic run that appended
  twice is repaired by a NEW review file name and a new block, never by a removal.

  **The rule's own limit, stated here.** The seven reviews before revision 22 were appended to the
  store BY THE ARCHITECT during revision 22, because the keys the earlier Critic runs printed were
  never recorded in this plan. For those seven the stored copy is a CHECKSUM and not a second party.
  **From revision 22 on the stored copy is the one the Critic appended and the key is the one the
  Critic printed**, so the two writers differ and the rule is what it claims to be. The suffix half
  declines a review whose file name is not `critic-spec-<rev>.md`, which is a probe's throwaway
  file and never a review of this plan.

  **The repository root is an explicit ARGUMENT and never an environment variable.** A frozen copy
  of this plan sits outside the repository, so the guard cannot derive the path to
  `.claude/plan-coordination/db.sh` from its own location; `run_all_gates.py` passes its own
  `<repo-root>` argument through, and a guard that guessed would be a guard that guessed wrong.
  N19-3 refused a second environment seam for the same reason.
- **CL2.** The generated list and the block are one set in both directions.
- **CL3.** The document holds the count sentence the guard builds from the generated counts,
  character for character.
- **CL4.** Every row carries a finding, a state from CLOSED, PARTIAL and OPEN, and, when it says
  CLOSED, a section that a heading of this document holds. Revision 18 checked emptiness alone, so a
  row could be emptied of everything it says, or name a section number the document does not hold,
  and stay green (critic C18-W1).
- **CL5.** The document states the review file's own md5 beside the block, and the digest of the file
  this run was handed matches it.

**CL5 is the rule that makes the other four mean something** (critic C18-1). Revision 18 proved
`rows == generated(input)` and never `input == the review`: the Critic handed the guard a truncated
copy of one review and it reported a complete closure over 20 of 26 findings, at production
defaults, in one command. The denominator was taken on trust from the one party the appendix exists
to check. Each closure section already recorded the md5 of the frozen DOCUMENT its review read, and
CL5 is that discipline applied to the review.

**Who runs this guard, and when.** The Architect runs it as the last step of every closure, once
per review block, before the document is frozen for the next review, and pastes the three lines into
the revision report. It is not in `scripts/dod.sh`, for the reason rung one gives for
`check-placement`: it reads a roadmap markdown file, and its value falls to zero once the plan is
built while its cost stays on every commit forever.

**It is ALSO a gate, in the `plan-lint` job, and revision 19 said the opposite** (critic C19-4).
Revision 19 wrote that the change "needs a write scope this document does not own, because
`roadmap/duet-v1/reviews/` holds no file today and no chunk creates one". **Both halves were
false.** `roadmap/duet-v1/reviews/` is a tracked plan record and it already holds one file per
review; every review this appendix records was read from it, and CL5 computes the md5 of a file in
that directory on every run. A rule whose input is a tracked file needs no new write scope, so the
decision the sentence routed away was a decision this document could make and had already made in
practice. Chunk M0's write scope therefore holds `tools/xtask/src/check_closure.rs`, and the
`plan-lint` job of `.github/workflows/ci.yml` holds one `cargo xtask check-closure` line per closure
block. `plan-lint` runs only on a change under `roadmap/`, so the cost stays off every commit
exactly as `check-placement`'s does.

**The review-time run and the gate run are the same command over the same files**, so the Architect
still runs it at closure and learns the answer before the Critic does. The gate is the backstop that
stops a closure row from drifting once the plan is built.

**The rule's own limit, stated here**: it decides that a row EXISTS, that it is well formed, and
that it records the review the digest names. It never decides that the closure the row claims is
true; a reviewer decides that, and CL4 makes the row name a real section so the check is one
lookup. PG27 holds the block's shape inside this document, and `closure_check.py` holds it against
the review file.

**PG40. A chunk writes only into the crate its own line owns.** Section 13.0 SM4 and SM5 both rest
on the Writes columns, and no rule held a chunk's write scope to the crate its line owns, so a chunk
could take a path inside a crate another line is building in the same phase and every guard stayed
green (N19-4, recorded as debt for three revisions). The `line-map` block is the data that debt row
named. The rule takes the line of each chunk id, takes that line's crate from the block, and fails
on a `crates/<name>/` path in the chunk's row whose `<name>` is not that crate.

**The rule's own limits, stated here.** The M chunks are outside it, because SM1 makes a manifest
chunk create the skeleton of every crate whose first chunk runs in its phase, so a manifest row names
several crates by design and the line map gives it none. It reads a path that opens `crates/`, so a
chunk that writes `tools/`, `scripts/` or a workflow file is outside it and SM4 holds those. It reads
the ROW and never the file system, exactly as PG35 does. **A chunk id whose line prefix the
`line-map` block does not carry is a FAILURE and not a skip**, and the run prints `LINE CHUNK FLOOR`
beside `LINE CHUNKS` (critic C22I-W3). Revision 22 skipped an unmapped id in silence and printed no
floor, so one added chunk row with a new prefix could write into any crate and the run stayed green;
N21-3 had already forced a floor on PG37 for exactly that reason.

**PG41. Every cross-thread carrier has two declared ends, and every declared end has one row.** TH13
is the rule and the `carrier-table` block of section 5.8 is the data. The guard reads every row: the
Sender cell and the Receiver cell must each name one `` `Type.field` `` path that a Rust block of
this document declares, the Carrier cell must name one of the five primitives section 5.8 decides
and, for every primitive but `triple_buffer`, one B id of section 1.6, the Threads cell must name a
sender thread, an arrow, and a receiver thread, each of which is a row of the section 5.7 thread
table, and the overflow cell must not be empty. It then reads every declared field whose type
expression names a channel end, a ring end, a queue or a publication end, and fails on one that no
row names. **It also decides the DIRECTION of every end it reads** (critic C23I-W1): `Sender`,
`SyncSender`, `Producer`, `Input` and `OneshotSender` are write ends, `Receiver`, `CoreReceiver`,
`Consumer`, `Output` and `OneshotReceiver` are read ends, and an `ArrayQueue` behind an `Arc` is one
value both ends share. A Sender cell that names a read end, and a cell that names a field which
holds no carrier at all, are each red; revision 23's first form of this rule read the two cells and
never held either one against the declared end set, so the Critic turned both shapes green.

**Why the rule exists** (critic C22I-1, C22I-2, C22I-3, C22I-7, C22I-8). All eight Criticals of the
twenty-second inner review were one class: a stated duty whose carrier no declaration holds. The
class spanned the engine, the core, the MIDI path, the view seam and the plan graph, and it was
invisible to all sixty-three rules of revision 22. This plan held a rule for a type with no place, a
place with no type, a derive with no use, a citation with no site and a chunk with no crate, and no
rule for a message with no channel. The review's own words are that a rule which reads every
"sends", "receives", "publishes", "reports", "waits for" and "carries" claim against the declared
field set would have caught seven of the eight on its first run.

**The rule's own limits, stated here.** It reads the ENDS and never the bodies, so a row proves that
two fields exist and never that a statement pushes a value; only a chunk's test proves that. It
reads the declared field SET and never the prose, so a duty this document states in a sentence and
omits from the table is caught by the reverse half alone, which fires when that duty needs a field.
It declines an owned handoff that is no channel: a `basedrop::Shared<T>` moved into a callback
closure and the `Arc<ResetGenerations>` of the audio-exempt block are each an owned value, and the
third table of section 5.8 decides them. **It also declines a SHARED COUNTER** (critic C23I-N2):
`MidiSink::dropped`, `HotplugSink::resync` and `DuetCore::entry_dropped` are each an atomic behind
an `Arc` that two threads read and write, which carries a fact and not a message, so no row can name
a sender and a receiver for one; the third table of section 5.8 decides them beside the owned
handoffs. The run prints `CARRIERS` and `CARRIER FIELDS`, so both
denominators are readable.

**PG31b also carries a CEILING now** (N19-1). The found pair set and the allow list are the same 24
pairs, so the rule fires on nothing this document holds; PG27b's floor already refuses a DELETION
from the exemption block, and the ceiling refuses an ADDITION, so a twenty-fifth pair cannot be
waved through by typing one more row and must be reviewed with the ceiling raised in the same
changeset. **The ceiling bounds the SIZE of the allow list and never the truth of a row**, and the
reason rule beside it is what holds a row to its own pair.

**PG33 also refuses an AMBIGUOUS site now** (N19-6). The register is about a suppression's site and a
site is a function, so a B.1 row that shares a name with an unrelated function was green. A name this
document declares more than once resolves to no one site, and the rule fails on it; a unique name
resolves to exactly the declaration the row means, which is the whole of that hole.

**PG38. No table row of this document has a cell count that differs from its own header.** A
GitHub-flavoured renderer keeps the first `n` cells of a ragged row and DROPS the rest, so one
unescaped `|` inside a backtick span truncates the row a reader sees while the source still holds
the text. Revision 21 carried two, and neither was visible to any rule (critic C21-5). Chunk M0's
section 13.1 row parsed to seven cells under a five-column header, which dropped `scripts/bootstrap.sh`,
`deny.toml`, `.cargo/config.toml`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `clippy.toml`, `.gitignore`,
`.claude/skills/gpui-kit/SKILL.md`, `crates/duet/Cargo.toml`, `Info.plist`, `assets/fonts/` and
`NOTICE` from the write scope, together with the Completion command; those are the SM4 policy set,
and SM4 is the rule that keeps a policy edit out of an implementation chunk. The C20-W6 closure row
parsed to six cells under four. Section 13.1 is not a registered block, so DR7 gives it no marker,
and `closure_check.py` read `row[3]`, found a token that looked like a section number, and passed
CL4 on the truncated cell.

**The rule covers every markdown table of this document**, outside every fenced block, and not the
section 13 tables and the closure blocks alone. **The rule's own limit, stated here**: it decides a
row's cell COUNT and never a cell's content, so a row with the right number of cells and the wrong
text is outside it and CL4 and the membership rules are what read content.

**PG39. Section 1.7 and the live rule set are one set.** DR4 makes section 1.7 the one index of rule

guard families and declines DR, PL, VR, TH and SM, because no machine holds those ids and only a
reader can.

**PG33. The Appendix B.1 suppression-reason table and the section 2.3 list are one set.** Appendix

**PG28. Every shared limit is reachable from every crate that enforces it.** The rule reads the

It states two limits of its own. **The enforcer list is a hand list**, because an enforcement lives

**PG29. The section 1.9 probe table and the implemented rule set are one set.** DR5 claims the two

unchecked**, because only a run can produce it; chunk M0 ports each cell to one test, and the

**PG35. The per-phase `Cargo.lock` writer sequence is derived from the chunk tables.** Section 13.3

stated here**: it counts a chunk that DECLARES the file in its own write scope, so a chunk that
writes a member manifest and omits `Cargo.lock` from its cell is an SM5 defect this rule cannot see.

**PG36. The Appendix B.3 and B.5 owner columns and the section 13.1 pin lists are one set.**

**PG30. Every `B` citation of this document and the section 1.6 `Used by` column are one set.**

limits, and there are THREE (critic N18-4). **It reads this document alone**, so a citation inside
an ADR is outside it. **It skips the budget block itself**, because one budget row that derives from
another is a derivation and not a use. **It skips every closure section**, which is C.20, C.21,
C.22, and C.23, because a closure row quotes the finding it records and a quoted `B` id is evidence
of a past defect and not a use site. Revision 18 implemented that third skip and stated two limits,
so one of the rule's three exemptions lived in the prototype alone.

**What the guard does not cover, stated at the site.** The candidate set comes from fenced Rust
blocks, so a type named only in prose is not checked; a new type must appear in a Rust block or in
the table above. **Every count belongs to section 1.9 and to no other place.** Revision 8 wrote
three coverage numbers here by hand, and all three were a revision out of date and flattered the

implementation, so a dependency a crate needs only inside a function body is outside its reach;
`cargo machete` and the compiler are the backstop, and this guard is the early warning.

**One test in `tools/xtask` holds each rule, and section 1.9's table is the count (DR5).** PG25 is the one rule
whose test builds a workspace rather than a document fixture, and section 1.9 states that limit at
its own site. Section 1.9 pairs each rule
with its probe and records the result. **Each test builds its own fixture document as an inline
string in a temporary directory, and no guard test opens any file under `roadmap/`.** The fixture is

runs `cargo nextest run --workspace`, and `tools/xtask` is a workspace member, so a test that read
this document would put the gate back on a roadmap markdown file, which is the coupling that moving
the guard to `plan-lint` removed (critic N4, S11).
