A gate remains a `SlotKind` a user may insert, and B45 leaves the free slots for it. The 8 part buses each carry an equalizer and a compressor, which is 16 each, or 128. The 4 reverb buses cost 12 and the 2 delay buses cost 6. The master chain of contract 5.2 draws five stages and three of them automate a slot: an equalizer, a compressor, and a limiter, which is 12 plus 4 plus 3, or 19. Its Gain stage is the strip trim that the fixed four already count, and its Dither stage automates nothing at all, because it changes no live sample (section 7.4). The sum is 1413, and 2048 leaves the user the free slots B45 allows. `ConfigError::ParamBudgetExceeded` and `MixError::ParamBudgetExceeded` refuse the parameter that would pass it. `duet-session`, `duet-engine`, and `crates/duet` each enforce it, so the constant sits in the one crate all three reach (critic CR-12) | 1.6, 3.5, 5.5, 6.1, 7.1, 7.2, 10.2, 15.4, 15.10, C.10 |

#### Every workspace constant

Every workspace constant is declared here, so no other Rust block carries a literal.

<!-- GUARD BLOCK id=constants rows>=122 -->
```rust
/// Build a non-zero constant with no panic primitive (house form 5, 12.3).
/// # Panics
/// It panics when `value` is zero, so a bad constant fails the build.
const fn non_zero(value: i64) -> NonZeroI64 {
    assert!(value != 0, "a non-zero constant must not be zero");
    match NonZeroI64::new(value) {
        Some(checked) => checked,
        None => NonZeroI64::MIN,
    }
}

// duet-time
/// Ticks per quarter note in the beat domain (B40).
pub const TICKS_PER_QUARTER: NonZeroI64 = non_zero(1_920);
/// Ticks per second in the audio domain (B41).
pub const SUPERCLOCK_HZ: NonZeroI64 = non_zero(282_240_000);

// duet-time
/// Strips one project may hold, and the meter array length (B86).
pub const MAX_STRIPS: usize = 48;
/// Automatable parameters one project holds (B90).
pub const MAX_PARAMS: usize = 2_048;
/// Pre-fader and post-fader slots per chain (B45).
pub const MAX_SLOTS: usize = 8;
/// Aux sends per chain (B46).
pub const MAX_SENDS: usize = 8;
/// Per-slot meter cells one `SlotMeterSnapshot` carries. It is arithmetic
/// over three constants and never a literal, so a change to any one of them
/// moves it and DR3 holds (B133, section 7.3).
pub const MAX_SLOT_METERS: usize = MAX_STRIPS * 2 * MAX_SLOTS;

// duet-score
/// The current schema number of the canonical document (B42).
pub const SCHEMA: SchemaVersion = SchemaVersion::new(1);

// duet-session

**The `non_zero` body above is the repair of the defect chunk T1 found, and it is mandated character
for character.** Revision 23 wrote a fallback arm that substitutes `NonZeroI64::MIN`, which is
`i64::MIN`, so a zero constant SHIPPED where `Finite::from_finite_const` asserts and a zero fails
the build. Both constants this block builds are positive divisors everywhere in `duet-time`, so a
negative value for either would invert the whole timeline. The two compile-time helpers of the
workspace answered a bad input in opposite ways, and one of the two answers was wrong. **The repair
is the assertion `Finite::from_finite_const` already carries**, which is house form 5 of section
12.3: in a `const` item the assertion runs at compile time, so a zero fails the build and no binary
carries the panic. The `None` arm stays, because a `match` over an `Option` must be total, and the
assertion above it makes that arm unreachable. `clippy::missing_assert_message` is denied, so the
assertion carries its message. Plan store `fluid:next_steps_from_T1`, item FU-3 (chunk T1,
2026-09-22); ADR 0008 records the decision.

**`duet-time::units::non_zero_u32` takes the identical shape, and chunk M91 lands both.** Chunk T1
added that second helper for `SampleRate::SUPPORTED`, and it carries the same wrong arm. Its body is
`assert!(value != 0, "a non-zero constant must not be zero");` followed by the same `match` over
`NonZeroU32::new`, with `None => NonZeroU32::MIN`. It takes no row of this block, because this block
states every workspace CONSTANT and `non_zero_u32` builds none of the eleven `duet-command` values.

**Each helper carries a `# Panics` section in the crate, and REVIEW is what holds that rule**
(critic C1-13). House form 5 of section 12.3 requires the section unconditionally. Revision 24 named

**The block above holds the SUMMARY and step 15 of chunk M91 holds the full text** (critic C1-14).
The `constants` block sits exactly at its `rows>=122` floor, so no line may be added to it; the

A test in `duet-time` asserts that both non-zero constants hold their literal values, so a wrong

### 1.8 The `BundleDocument` trait

`duet-command` declares it. `duet-project` consumes it and declares no document (critic N22).

```rust
/// A document the bundle stores as one or more canonical text files.
pub trait BundleDocument: Sized {
    /// The paths this document owns, relative to the bundle root, in a
    /// fixed order. The order is the order of `to_bytes` and `from_bytes`.
    fn paths() -> &'static [&'static str];

    /// Serialize into one byte block per path, in `paths` order.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `CommandError::Serialize` when a value has no canonical form,
    /// which today means only a non-finite float that escaped `Finite`.
    fn to_bytes(&self) -> Result<Vec<Vec<u8>>, CommandError>;

    /// Parse from one byte block per path, in `paths` order.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `CommandError::Parse` for malformed text, and
    /// `CommandError::Schema` for a version this build cannot migrate.
    fn from_bytes(blocks: &[Vec<u8>]) -> Result<Self, CommandError>;

    /// Unknown keys the reader kept in an `extra` bag (section 3.6).
    fn warnings(&self) -> &[ImportWarning];

    /// Whether git tracks this document's paths.
    ///
    /// `Score`, `Session`, and `MixState` return true; `ViewState` returns
    /// false, because `state/view.json` holds the viewport and a scroll must
    /// not churn a commit (section 4.2). The save path reads this method
    /// rather than matching a path against section 4.2 at four call sites
    /// (critic Q21).
    fn tracked() -> bool;
}
```

`duet-command` implements it for `Score`, `Session`, `MixState`, and `ViewState`, which the orphan
rule allows because the trait is local.

### 1.9 Every guard rule and its one probe

DR5 makes this table the contract of both guards. The left half is the rule, the right half is the
one probe that turns that rule red. The two counts are equal by construction: a rule enters the
guard with its probe, and a rule whose probe cannot be written is deleted.

**How a probe runs, and what runs it.** Three revisions recorded a probe result that no run had
produced, and the revision-12 review found two of them inside one cell (critic CR-3, CR-13). A
recorded result is a measurement, so revision 13 gives every probe a machine.

**Five harnesses run, not three, and each row states the working directory** (critic C19-W7,
C20-N6). Revision 19 named three harnesses while five existed, so a reader who followed this table
never ran PP32 at all. **Every command below runs from `roadmap/duet-v1/` with
`PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` set**, which is the second half of the same finding: `conversion_check.py`
resolves the repository through `cargo metadata` and fails closed from any other directory, and a
run that writes `__pycache__` mutates the tree it is verifying (critic C20-N7).

| `tools/probe_roster.sh <document> <scratch> <repo>` | PP25 in all four shapes, the mixed-impl shape, the six planted gate defects below, and the recorded-text compare through `probe_roster_text.py` | A toolchain and a scratch directory outside the repository |
| `tools/probe_closure.py <document> <repo>` | PP32 in all fifteen shapes, over a throwaway review and a throwaway block it writes itself, and one throwaway suffix in the plan store | The document and the repository root that holds `.claude/plan-coordination/db.sh` |

Each harness plants the defect, runs the guard, and prints the exit code and the lines the probe's

#### The guard family speaks two words, and each one names an exit code

**`FAIL:` marks exit 2 and nothing else.** Exit 2 is the fail-closed state: the guard could not
decide. Exit 1 is a finding: the guard decided, and the input breaks a rule. Exit 0 is a clean run.
The six guards are `check-conversions`, `check-manifests`, `check-placement`, `check-plan-graph`,
`check-closure`, and `check-roster`.

**At exit 1 a guard prints `FINDING: ` when the finding carries no rule tag, and the rule tag when
the rule has a name.** `check-manifests` and `check-plan-graph` print `FINDING: `.
`check-placement`, `check-closure`, and `check-conversions` print an indented rule tag such as
``  UNPLACED:   `` or ``  CLOSURE:    ``, and this section records more than sixty of those lines
by their exact text. **A blanket `FINDING: ` prefix over every exit-1 line was refused**, because
the tag names the rule that fired and a bare prefix would delete that name from every recorded
line at no gain.

**The dividing line is the SUBJECT of the failure, and one sentence states it.** Exit 1 is a breach
of a rule the guard measures about the DOCUMENT it judges. Exit 2 is a failure of the guard's OWN
input: its register, its parse, or the transform table it applies before it measures anything. A
guard whose own input is broken has measured nothing, so it may not report a breach it never made.

**Two counts, measured and not estimated** (critic C1-11). `tools/xtask/src/` holds 49 `"FAIL:`
string sites: 5 in `check_closure.rs`, 8 in `check_conversions.rs`, 3 in `check_manifests.rs`, 11 in
`check_placement.rs`, 4 in `check_plan_graph.rs`, 17 in `check_roster.rs`, and 1 in `main.rs`. **Five
of the 49 reach exit 1 and the other 44 are fail-closed.** Revision 24 wrote "a fail-closed state on
five paths and a finding on four", which inverted the denominator and miscounted the numerator; the
five exit-1 sites are `check_plan_graph.rs` `collect_chunks`, which carries both the duplicate id
and the empty directory, `check_placement.rs` `run` at the empty candidate set, and the three
verdict paths of `check_roster.rs` `report`.

**Chunk M90 repairs the four sites that broke the rule** (escalation M0-4).

| Site | Today | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `check_plan_graph`, two files state one chunk id | `FAIL:` at exit 1 | `FINDING: duplicate chunk id <id> in <file> and <file>` at **exit 1** | Rule 1 of the guard is that every id is unique. Two files that state one id BREAK that rule, the guard names both files, and an author repairs it. A decidable breach is exit 1 |
| `check_plan_graph`, the directory holds no chunk file | `FAIL: no chunk file found` at exit 1 | `FAIL: no chunk file found; the guard is fail-closed.` at **exit 2** | It is a zero denominator. Rule CG1b part 1 of section 2.3 already states the same answer for a member set, and for the same reason: an empty read is a broken read and never a clean verdict |
| `check_placement`, the candidate set is empty | `FAIL:` at exit 1 | `FAIL: the candidate set is empty, so the parse is broken.` at **exit 2** | The line says the PARSE is broken. A guard whose parse produced nothing has measured nothing about the document, so exit 1 would report a breach the run never made |
| `check_roster`, three verdict paths | `FAIL:` at exit 1 | `FINDING: ` at **exit 1**, with the same text after the word | The roster below the section 1.5 denominator, a mixed impl block, and an impl count that differs from the `impl-sites` block are each a breach of a rule this guard measures about the document |

**The two roster SUBSTITUTION sites keep exit 2, and the sentence above is why** (critic C1-17).
`check_roster.rs` refuses a run when the section 1.9 substitution block and the `SUBSTITUTIONS` list
the guard compiles disagree, and when a substitution line states a number. Both breaches are
decidable, and neither one is about the document the guard judges. **The substitution block is the
guard's own transform table**: the guard applies it to turn the section 15 declarations into a
compilable workspace. A disagreement means the workspace the guard is about to write is not the
workspace this document describes, so every counter downstream of it is unattributable, and a stated
number inside that block is the one input DR3 says only a run may produce. Those are failures of the
guard's input, so they take the same answer as the empty candidate set and the empty plan directory.
**They stay at exit 2 and chunk M90 does not move them**; this paragraph is the site that states the
reason, which revision 24 left unexamined.

#### `check-roster --generate-only` splits PG25 at the compiler edge

**The rule stays ONE subcommand and one rule id, and a flag names the half that runs.** PG25 has no
probe group today, because every shape of it compiles the whole `gpui` dependency tree: one measured
run reached 4.0 GB and several minutes cold. The generator half of the rule reads the document,
writes the scratch workspace, and counts, in about one second. Chunk M90 gives `check-roster` a
`--generate-only` flag with this contract (escalation M0-5).

```
cargo xtask check-roster <document> <scratch> <repo> [--generate-only]
```

1. **With the flag the guard writes the scratch workspace and runs NO cargo command.** It prints
   every `ROSTER ...` counter line it prints today, then one further line,
   `ROSTER COMPILE:   skipped (--generate-only)`, and it exits 0, 1, or 2 on the parse rules and the
   count rules alone.
2. **Without the flag the guard does everything it does today**, the compile and the lint included,
   and it prints `ROSTER CLIPPY:   clean` or `ROSTER CLIPPY:   FAIL` as it does now. The two forms
   are therefore never confusable by exit code alone, because the skipped form always prints the
   line that names itself.
3. **A gate never takes the flag, and a PROBE holds that rule** (critic C1-8). The `plan-lint` job
   of `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs the full command, and section 14 records that.
   `tools/xtask/tests/probes.rs` takes the flag and holds the cheap shapes: the roster below the
   section 1.5 denominator, the mixed impl block, and the impl count that differs from the
   `impl-sites` block. **One further probe reads EVERY file under `.github/workflows/` and fails
   when a `check-roster` line in any of them carries `--generate-only`** (critic C2-7). It reads the
   directory at test time rather than one path through `include_str!`, because the heading of the
   rule is "every job" and a second workflow that runs the roster is unguarded from the day it is
   written, and this plan itself adds `soak.yml` and `audio-smoke.yml`. The directory holds `ci.yml`
   alone today, so the wider denominator costs one directory read and changes no result now. **The probe is fail-closed
   on its own input**: a directory that does not open, and a directory that holds no file, are each
   a failure, because a denominator of zero is the vacuous green CG1b refuses. A committed positive
   control passes a two-line fixture that carries the flag and asserts that the helper returns
   false. Chunk M90 writes both files, so the rule and its red run land in one commit.

   **The rule's own limit, stated here.** The probe reads one LINE at a time. A folded YAML scalar,
   a shell variable that holds the flag, and an `env:` entry each defeat it, and no rule catches
   those; review holds them. Widening the denominator from one file to every file closes the case
   that a new workflow creates, which is the case this plan can create by itself.
4. **A second subcommand was refused.** PG25 is one rule, and DR5 gives one rule one probe. A second
   subcommand would give one rule two names, repeat the argument triple, and let the two drift.

**The flag DOES remove a rule clause, and this is the honest statement of what it removes** (critic
C1-8). The PG25 row of the table above defines the rule as three clauses: a roster that the real
lint table refuses, a roster below the section 1.5 denominator, and a roster below the `impl-sites`
floor. **The compiler is the only oracle for clause one**, so the skipped form decides clauses two
and three and decides nothing about clause one. Revision 24 wrote that the flag "removes no rule the
skipped form can reach", which is true of the two clauses it keeps and false of the rule.

**The difference from `--no-store` is real, and it is these three properties and not that claim.**
Revision 22 shipped a `--no-store` flag on the closure guard that printed `STORE: skipped` and
exited 0, so a skipped run and a matching run had one exit code between them. Here the skipped run
prints `ROSTER COMPILE:   skipped (--generate-only)`, a line no full run prints; the full form is
the only form any job runs; and **a probe now refuses a `--generate-only` on a `check-roster` line
of ANY file under `.github/workflows/`**, so the rule that keeps the flag out of a job has a red run
of its own. Revision 24
left that rule as prose, which is exactly how `--no-store` reached a job in the first place.

**The prototypes under `roadmap/duet-v1/tools/` keep their historical text, and this document states
the divergence.** The Rust ports in `tools/xtask` are the rules of record from chunk M0 onward, and
PG29 reads the prototypes for rule IDS alone and never for message text. The precedent is R3-W1 of
the chunk M0 report: `roster_compile.sh` defines exit 1 for a class where the port returns 2, the
port is right, and the record now says so. A second stated divergence is cheaper than fourteen
Python edits that no rule reads.

**One scratch directory, one cargo target, and the target does not outlive the run.** A `target`
for the roster workspace holds the whole `gpui` dependency tree, which is several gigabytes. One
authoring session made nine of them, filled the volume, and stopped every shell on the machine, so
the rule is now in the scripts and not in a reader's memory. The owner of the target is the process
that CREATES it, and a script traps only the target it created (critic C21-W4).
`roster_compile.sh` sets `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` to `<scratch>/target` and traps `EXIT`, `INT`, and
`TERM` to delete it. A caller that exports **`ROSTER_TARGET_DIR`** takes that ownership instead:
`probe_roster.sh` exports one path for its whole run, so its eleven shapes share one build rather
than paying for eleven, and it traps that path only when it created it itself. **Revision 21 trapped
it whatever the source of the value was**, so a caller that exported a shared target had it deleted
by a script it invoked, against the ownership rule this paragraph states; the twenty-first Critic
lost its shared target to that trap.

**`ROSTER_TARGET_DIR` is the ONE environment variable a documented command sets, and both scripts
validate it.** An absolute path outside the repository is accepted. A relative path and a path
inside the repository are each exit 2 with a named line, which is the rule both scripts already
applied to the scratch directory and applied to nothing else, although this value reaches an
`rm -rf`. **Neither script ever makes a second workspace**, and the fixed scratch directory of this
plan is `<session scratchpad>/roster-scratch`.

**The recorded run is the run against this revision, and ONE script proves it** (critic C20-1,
C20-2). `roadmap/duet-v1/tools/run_all_gates.py` runs every guard and every harness above in a
fixed order, over one tree. It records the modification time of every file under
`roadmap/duet-v1/` before it starts and reads them again when it ends, and **a file that changed
during the run makes the whole run exit 2**, so a transcript it prints belongs to one tree and
never to two. It sets `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` for every child it starts and it excludes
`__pycache__` from that compare, because a bytecode write is not an edit to the plan (critic
C20-N7).

**It DERIVES its closure gate list from `reviews/` and never types it** (critic C21-W3). Revision 21
held the list as a literal tuple, so one new review file in the tree got no closure gate and the run
still printed `GATES BAD: 0`; the twenty-first Critic copied a review to `critic-spec-r22.md` and
the harness was green over it. The script reads `reviews/critic-spec-r<n>.md`, maps each file to the
block `closure-<stem>`, and exits 2 on a review at or above the earliest registered revision with no
block and on a registered block with no review file. The reviews of revisions 2 to 15 carry a section
of Appendix C and no registered block by design, so the forward half opens at the earliest
REGISTERED revision and the reverse half is absolute.

**It refuses a document outside the plan directory** (critic N21-6), because the tree compare covers
`roadmap/duet-v1/` and a document argument that points elsewhere makes the run a measurement of one
tree against another. **It flushes stdout after every gate** (critic N21-5), so a redirected run
prints as it goes and a reader can tell a slow gate from a hang.

```
cd roadmap/duet-v1
PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 ROSTER_TARGET_DIR=<one shared target outside the repository> \
    python3 tools/run_all_gates.py architecture.md <scratch outside the repository> <repository root>
```

`ROSTER_TARGET_DIR` is optional and the paragraph above states what it changes: with it the two
roster runs share one build of the `gpui` tree, and without it each one makes its own. The caller
that exports it owns it and deletes it.

the document that claimed them green. Both failures are one failure: **a recorded result must come
from a run of the FINAL tree, after the last edit.** A habit cannot hold that rule and a script can.

an addition raises the floor in the same changeset and a deletion is always red (critic C20-W10,
C20-N5).

#### Every registered block and its membership rule

PG27 reads this block. Each line names one registered block and the one membership kind the guard
runs over every row of it. **A block with no row here, a row over an id the register does not hold,
and a kind the guard does not implement are each exit 2**, so the register and this block are one
set exactly as the register and the rule-to-block map are (DR7, critic WR-18).

Each kind names the universe a row's referent must sit in. `crate-name` reads the section 1.2
crates. `pin-name` and `map-crate` each read the third-party crates the section 1.2 dependency
cells name, the first from the head of a row and the second from its second token.
`not-declared` refuses a name this document declares. **It cannot ask that a token name anything**
(concern N15-9), so a row that names nothing passes; a Critic probe replaced `Mutex` in `lock-names`
with such a token and the block was green. The rule that reads that block survives it, because
PG26c also reads the word "lock" in the section 1.9 `Why` cell, and one edited source does not
disarm a two-source rule. `ownership-row` reads the crate cell.
`drop-name` refuses a name this document declares that no external block maps, which is the shape
that turned a red document green (critic WR-18). `const-crate` reads the crate comment of a
constant. `limit-row` reads the constant and every enforcing crate, which is the C-4 disposition.
`rule-id` reads the implemented rule set. `block-id` reads the register. `verdict-name` refuses a
name section 1.5 places, which the external table's own site already states and nothing held.
`external-name` asks that another block name the same name. `expr-head` reads the head of a type
expression. `declared-name` asks for a Rust block. `primitive-name` pairs the two primitive blocks.
`unknown-name` asks for a framework name or a declared name. `field-path` asks that the holder be
an audio-owned name and the field a field it declares. `cited-elsewhere` asks that another line of
this document name the same site. `site-crate` and `site-path` read an expectation site.
`chunk-id` reads the section 13.2 chunk ids. `mechanism-name` reads the types a mechanism cell
names. `carrier-end` reads the two `Type.field` ends of a carrier row and asks that a Rust block of
this document declare the type and that the type declare the field, which is the shape `field-path`
already uses for the audio-exempt block (TH13, PG41). `sub-id` reads the id shape alone, and **that limit is stated here**: the referent of a
substitution row is the roster compile's own list, which PG25 holds to this block in both
directions and refuses to run on a difference.

#### Every external type, and its verdict

PG18 reads this table. **There is no drop list.** Revision 8 carried a fixed set of tokens that the
audit skipped, and `AtomicU32` was one of them, so a `Copy` derive over the counter this design puts
on the audio path passed in silence (critic R2). Every name a declaration reaches that section 1.5
does not place has a row here, and PG18 fails on one that does not.

**A framework name has a row here when a rule outside PG7 needs its verdict, and `Path` is the one
such name today** (critic C16-W3). PG7 exempts a framework type inside an application declaration,
so the framework block alone answers PG7. The derive-closure rule PG19 asks a different question,
and `PathCache` stores an `Arc<Path<Pixels>>` by value, so `Path` needs a `Copy` verdict as well as
an exemption. Revision 16 stated that the two blocks never share a name, and the same revision put
`Path` in both.

A verdict is one of four. **Copy** and **not Copy** decide the type. **transparent** means the
Copy-ness is the payload's, and the payload is a separate token in the same field that the guard
asks on its own. **undecided** carries a reason and counts toward `UNKNOWN`; the table uses none
today.

<!-- GUARD BLOCK id=external-verdicts rows>=34 -->
| External type | Verdict | Traits | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `NonZeroI64`, `NonZeroU8`, `NonZeroU16`, `NonZeroU32`, `NonZeroU64` | `Copy` | `Copy!` `Serialize!` `Deserialize!` `PartialEq!` `Eq!` `Hash!` `PartialOrd!` `Ord!` | A `NonZero` integer is `Copy` and totally ordered. It has no `Default`, because zero is the one value it refuses |
| `Instant` | `Copy` | `Copy!` `PartialEq!` `Eq!` `Hash!` `PartialOrd!` `Ord!` | A monotonic reading has no serde form and no zero |
| `SystemTime` | `Copy` | `Copy!` `Serialize!` `Deserialize!` `PartialEq!` `Eq!` `Hash!` `PartialOrd!` `Ord!` | A wall-clock reading has no zero |
| `PhantomData` | `Copy` | `Copy!` `Default!` `Serialize!` `Deserialize!` `PartialEq!` `Eq!` `Hash!` `PartialOrd!` `Ord!` | It holds nothing, so every trait is unconditional |
| `Box`, `Arc`, `Rc` | `not Copy` | `Default` `Serialize` `Deserialize` `PartialEq` `Eq` `Hash` `PartialOrd` `Ord` | Each one owns a heap allocation and forwards every listed trait to its payload. `Box<str>` and `Box<[T]>` each supply `Default`, which a compiler run proves, and the unsized payload carries the verdict (critic K-5) |
| `Vec`, `VecDeque`, `BTreeMap`, `BTreeSet` | `not Copy` | `Default!` `Serialize` `Deserialize` `PartialEq` `Eq` `Hash` `PartialOrd` `Ord` | Each one owns a heap allocation and each one **grows**, so each one may call the allocator after it is built. An empty container is the default, whatever the payload is |
| `HashMap`, `HashSet` | `not Copy` | `Default!` `Serialize` `Deserialize` `PartialEq` `Eq` | A hash container owns a heap allocation and it **grows**. It implements no `Hash` and no order, because it has no stable iteration order |
| `String`, `PathBuf` | `not Copy` | `Default!` `Serialize!` `Deserialize!` `PartialEq!` `Eq!` `Hash!` `PartialOrd!` `Ord!` | Each one owns a heap allocation and each one **grows**. Neither one takes a type argument |
| `Cow` | `not Copy` | `Default` `Serialize` `Deserialize` `PartialEq` `Eq` `Hash` `PartialOrd` `Ord` | A borrowed or owned form of its payload, which **grows** when `to_mut` promotes it. `Cow` does supply `Default` when its payload does (critic K-5) |
| `SmallVec` | `not Copy` | `Default!` `Serialize` `Deserialize` `PartialEq` `Eq` `Hash` `PartialOrd` `Ord` | `smallvec` implements no `Copy` for its vector type, and a `SmallVec` **grows**: past its inline capacity it spills to a heap allocation. It supplies `Serialize` and `Deserialize` behind a crate feature, and B.5 names it. The row is its own, because `ArrayVec` is fixed and the two verdicts differ on the allocation half of TH1 (critic WR-22) |
| `ArrayVec` | `not Copy` | `Default!` `Serialize` `Deserialize` `PartialEq` `Eq` `Hash` `PartialOrd` `Ord` | `arrayvec` implements no `Copy` for its vector type. An `ArrayVec` is FIXED: it holds its elements inline and it never calls the allocator, which is why the audio path uses it. It supplies `Serialize` and `Deserialize` behind a crate feature, and B.5 names it |
| `Mutex`, `RwLock` | `not Copy` | `Default` `Serialize` `Deserialize` | A lock is not duplicable, and it supplies no comparison |
| `AtomicBool`, `AtomicU32`, `AtomicU64`, `AtomicUsize`, `AtomicI32` | `not Copy` | `Default!` `Serialize!` `Deserialize!` | An atomic cell is not duplicable and supplies no comparison. This is the row revision 8 dropped |
| `Value` | `not Copy` | `Default!` `Serialize!` `Deserialize!` `PartialEq!` `Eq!` `Hash!` | `serde_json::Value` owns a heap allocation. `serde_json::Number` compares totally and hashes, so `Value` supplies `Eq` and `Hash`; it supplies no order. A compiler run proves all three (critic K-5) |
| `Owned` | `not Copy` | none | `basedrop::Owned` owns its value, and it **defers** the free of that value to the collector thread (TH5). It supplies none of the nine, and no declaration derives one over it. PG26 reads the word "defers" here, so the set of deferring wrappers is data and not a set inside the machine (critic CR-16) |
| `Shared` | `not Copy` | `Clone` | `basedrop::Shared` is the reference-counted form of `Owned`, and it **defers** the release of the last reference to the same collector. It is the second wrapper PG26 accepts around a heap handle inside an audio-owned declaration |
| `ArrayQueue` | `not Copy` | none | `crossbeam_queue::ArrayQueue` is a bounded multi-producer queue with `force_push`, which evicts the oldest element. It owns a **heap** allocation that its constructor made, and it supplies none of the nine. Every field that holds one spells it behind an `Arc`, because both ends share one queue (section 5.8) |
| `Output` | `not Copy` | none | `triple_buffer::Output` is the read end of a published value. It owns a **heap** allocation it shares with the writer, and it supplies none of the nine. **It only ever hands out a shared reference**, so it **reads** and a container below it cannot grow on the reader's thread; PG26b stops there and PG26 and PG26c do not (section 5.6, critic C20-3) |
| `Input` | `not Copy` | none | `triple_buffer::Input` is the write end of the same value. It owns the same **heap** allocation and supplies none of the nine. The `carrier-table` block of section 5.8 is the one place every write end is decided, and this cell states no count of them (critic C23I-W15) |
| `Producer`, `Consumer` | `not Copy` | `PartialEq` `Eq` | The two ends of an `rtrb` ring. Each one owns a **heap** allocation that `configure` made, and each supplies none of the nine. **Each end is `Send` and neither is `Sync`** (critic C23I-W4), so one thread owns one end and a ring that crosses two callbacks needs one value per callback |
| `Sender` | `not Copy` | `Clone` | `async_channel::Sender` owns a **heap** allocation and supplies none of the nine closure traits |
| `Collector` | `not Copy` | none | `basedrop::Collector` is the drop queue itself. `Collector::new` makes a **heap** allocation, `handle` mints a `Handle` for every `Owned` and `Shared` constructor, and `collect` drains the queue to empty. It is `Send` and not `Sync`, so one thread owns it; `GraphConfigurator` is that thread's state (section 5.5, TH5). It supplies none of the nine, `Debug` included, which is why `GraphConfigurator` writes `Debug` by hand |
| `JoinHandle` | `not Copy` | none | `std::thread::JoinHandle` owns a **heap** allocation and supplies none of the nine |
| `Receiver` | `not Copy` | none | `std::sync::mpsc::Receiver` is the read end of a channel. It owns a **heap** allocation, it is `Send` and not `Sync`, so one thread owns it, and `recv_timeout` gives it the deadline the engine handoff thread needs (section 5.8). It supplies none of the nine |

| `Result` | `transparent` | `Copy` `Serialize` `Deserialize` `PartialEq` `Eq` `Hash` `PartialOrd` `Ord` | Copy follows both payloads, and a result has no default |

#### Where every external name comes from

The roster compile of PG25 reads this block. Each line maps one external name to the path a crate
imports it from. A name the block omits is a name the roster compile cannot resolve, and the build
stops. A name that a `#[derive(...)]` list alone carries is imported only when its path names a
third-party crate, because the standard-library prelude already supplies every derive macro it
declares. The block is data, exactly as the framework block and the candidate drop list are, so the
script carries no hidden set (critic C2, K-4).

**A row may state an ALIAS, and one row does** (critic C22I-1, C22I-2). The whole text after the
name is the import, so `CoreReceiver  async_channel::Receiver as CoreReceiver` emits
`use async_channel::Receiver as CoreReceiver;` and the roster compile builds a crate that names both
read ends. The reason is PL3: `Receiver` already names `std::sync::mpsc::Receiver`, which the engine
handoff thread owns for the B109 deadline, and `duet-core` owns the read end of two
`async_channel` channels at B28 and B138. One name cannot mean two types, so the second end takes a
name of its own.
