**An identifier newtype carries `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord`, and `Hash`, and the string
form carries them too.** A `BTreeMap` needs `Ord`, a `HashMap` needs `Hash` and `Eq`, and an
identity with neither cannot be looked up. `MidiPortId` wraps a `Box<str>` and derives all five
(section 8.1), and `CommitId` wraps a `CommitDigest` and derives the same (section 15.5). The rule
points down, never up: the vocabulary above an identifier asks it for nothing (ADR 0005
decision 2a). **A name is not an identifier by its suffix**: `TransactionName` is a display string
and it carries none of the three.

**Every other type in `duet-command`, `duet-score`, and `duet-session` derives `Debug`, `Clone`,
`PartialEq`, `Serialize`, and `Deserialize`, adds `Eq` when every field supplies `Eq`, and adds
`Copy` when every field is `Copy`.** `Verb` therefore asks no payload for `Hash` or for `Ord`, and a
new payload type can never break the enum above it. Revision 4 derived `Hash` on `Verb` over ten
payload types that carried none, and the crate did not compile (critic R0). An `Eq` derive is the
opposite shape: it is added only after every field already supplies the trait, and the PG25 roster
compile proves that for all 212 sites on every run.

**VR2. Every type that crosses the transport is plain data.** No variant holds a GPUI type, a tokio
type, a file handle, or a trait object (critic 4.3).

**VR3. Every type that `Verb` reaches is declared in `duet-command` or lower** (PL2).

**VR4. No vocabulary type holds a bare float.** Every float field is a `Finite`, which carries the
canonical invariants of section 2.6a. `ExportSpec` and `Normalization` held raw `f32` fields in
revision 4 (critic R0).

**VR5. A public type of a library crate whose fields are all `Copy` derives `Copy` when the type is
at most 32 bytes.** A type that must not be `Copy` carries a single-site
`#[expect(missing_copy_implementations, reason = "...")]`, and Appendix B.1 lists every such site.
Three reasons justify the refusal, and the reason text names which one applies: the type **will
grow** past the size bound, it is an **identity a caller must not duplicate in silence**, or it is
**already larger than the size bound**, so a `Copy` derive would hide a copy of its stated size at
every call site. The third reason is why the size bound exists at all. The size bound is the only
place where a byte count decides a derive, and DR3 exempts it.

`missing_copy_implementations` is a rustc lint set to `warn` in `[workspace.lints.rust]`, and
`.cargo/config.toml` adds `-D warnings`, so a type that trips it does not build.

**The rule binds a library crate, because the lint reads reachability.** The lint fires on a type
that is publicly reachable from a library root. Every type of `crates/duet` is `pub(crate)` inside a
binary (section 15.16), so nothing there is reachable from outside the crate and the lint cannot
fire. `unfulfilled_lint_expectations` is a rustc lint at `warn`, and `-D warnings` then turns an
expectation that cannot be fulfilled into a **build error**, which is the same mechanism this rule
relies on in the other direction. **Inside `crates/duet` a type therefore derives `Copy` or does
not, Appendix B.1 lists nothing from that crate, and an expectation there is a defect.** Revision 9
carried three of them, and a compiler run proves each one does not build (critic S3).

**A type with a hand-written `Drop` impl is outside this rule, and the mechanism is the same one.**
A `Drop` impl makes `Copy` impossible in the language, so `missing_copy_implementations` never
fires, and an expectation there is an unfulfilled expectation and therefore a build error. The rule
is stated here because this plan carries three such handles and a future one may be all-`Copy`:
`HotplugSubscription`, `MidiInputHandle`, and `MidiOutputHandle`. Section 1.9's Drop block names
them, PG9 asks no derive of a name there, PG21 fails on an expectation at one, and the PG25 roster
compile emits the `Drop` impl through substitution S8 so the roster sees the same shape. Revision 12
put `HotplugSubscription` in Appendix B.1 with a reason that named its own `Drop` (critic WR-12).

**No size in this section is written at all.** Every cell cites a B row or the PG24 table row for
the named type, and PG21 fails on a bare byte count inside this table, inside an `#[expect]` reason,
inside an Appendix B.1 reason, and inside any `///` or `//!` doc comment of any Rust block
(critic WR-2, WR-15). Revision 12 closed the first three and left the fourth open, and the
`MeterSnapshot` doc comment stated a size that the `latched` array had already made stale. Revision 10 stated six sizes and three were wrong.
Revision 11 replaced them with measured values and then let one go stale: it stated `MeterSnapshot`
at 1592 bytes under a heading that said no size there is hand written, and the compiler measured
1600. A number no rule reads is a number that rots, so revision 12 writes none.

**A type that must be `Copy` and is larger than the size bound states its size and its reason.**
The size bound decides the *optional* case; it never overrides a rule that requires the derive.
Two types are in that class, and both are required by TH9 or by the audio path.

| Type | Section | Measured size | Why `Copy` is required past the bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MeterSnapshot` | 5.9 | The size the PG24 table prints for `MeterSnapshot`, at B86 | TH9: the audio thread is the writer of this `triple_buffer`, so the published value must own no heap. A fixed array is the only shape that satisfies it |
| `ParamSnapshot` | 15.10 | The size the PG24 table prints for `ParamSnapshot`, at B90 | The audio thread addresses a parameter by index every cycle. The core is the writer and the dropper, and one write is a memory copy off the audio thread (critic C5) |

The answer for the ordinary cases:

| Type | Section | Measured size | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ExportSpec` | 7.4 | The size the PG24 table prints | Derives `Copy`; it sits on the bound |
| `Spanner` | 3.3 | Not all `Copy`: property 4 of section 3.6 gives it an `extra` bag | Derives no `Copy`, and needs no expectation, because a `BTreeMap` field takes it out of the rule |
| `ConfigError` | 15.10 | The size the PG24 table prints | Derives `Copy`. Revision 10 called it 40 bytes and refused the derive as "already larger than the size bound". The measured value is below the bound, so the refusal was false and the suppression was unsanctioned (critic C-4) |
| `Source` | 6.1 | The size the PG24 table prints | `#[expect]`; a source is an identity a caller must not duplicate in silence |
| `ManifestEntry` | 4.3 | The size the PG24 table prints | `#[expect]`; it is one line of a file, and it grows when the manifest gains a column |
| `Transport` | 5.9 | The size the PG24 table prints | `#[expect]`; the live transport is an identity the audio thread owns. Revision 10 called it 120 bytes and named two `Option<Span>` fields at 40 each, and the PG24 table prints 32 for that expression (critic C-4) |
| `SlotState` | 5.5 | B51 | Derives no `Copy` and carries two expectations. Every arm is inline, because audio-owned state holds no heap and revision 11's box put one allocation and one free inside the cycle (critic CR-2). Appendix B.1 carries both rows |

PG9 computes Copy-ness over the document's own declarations and fails on a type that takes neither
answer, PG10 fails on a type that takes the derive and cannot, and **PG21 holds the expectation
sites and the Appendix B.1 table to one set in both directions**, so neither list can go stale
(critic W7).

**`variant_size_differences` binds every enum in this workspace, not only `Verb`.** It is a rustc
lint at `warn` in `[workspace.lints.rust]`, and `.cargo/config.toml` adds `-D warnings`, which is
the same mechanism VR5 relies on for `missing_copy_implementations`. It refuses an enum whose
largest arm passes three times the second largest. ADR 0005 decision 3 already boxes a large `Verb`
payload for it. Revision 11 finds three sites in the whole roster and closes each one: `SlotState`
carries a single-site expectation for its equalizer arm (section 5.5), and `MarkKind` (section 3.3)
and `AnalysisError`
(section 15.8) each carry a single-site expectation that Appendix B.1 lists, because each one
compares a pointer or a four-byte value against a one-byte arm and no shape satisfies the ratio.
**`SlotState` is INLINE in every arm and it boxes nothing** (critic C19-W13). Revision 11 first
boxed the equalizer arm, and revision 13 removed the box because `SlotState` is an audio-owned
declaration and PG26 refuses a `Box` inside one; a `Box` there is a heap allocation the audio thread
would free. The prose that said "boxes its equalizer arm" survived six revisions beside a
declaration that does the opposite, so an implementer who followed it would write code PG26 refuses.
PG24 reads the rule from the roster and PG25 proves it with the compiler.

**VR6. A public function that returns a value and has no side effect carries `#[must_use]`.** Every
accessor of section 2, every `cost`, every `domain`, and every `clamped` carries it. A function that
mutates, that starts work, or that returns `()` does not. The rule exists because
`clippy::let_underscore_must_use` is denied: a caller that drops a computed value must say so.

**There is no identifier template, and there was one until revision 9.** ID1 gave a name that ends
in `Id`, `Name`, or `Text` a shape by inference. `CommitId` names a git object, ID1 told the chunk to
write a `u64`, and the placement guard read the same suffix and certified the answer, so the rule
that decides a shape defeated the rule that checks one (critic R1). **Section 15 declares every name
that section 1.5 places**, PG4b proves the two sets are identical on every run, and PG10b asks every
field of every `Copy` derive with no suffix seed at all.

One compile-time block holds VR2. There is no `assert_eq_hash`, because VR1 removed the property it
asserted.

```rust
/// Fail the build if a vocabulary type stops being plain data.
const fn assert_plain_data<T: Serialize + DeserializeOwned + Send + 'static>() {}

const _: () = {
    assert_plain_data::<Verb>();
    assert_plain_data::<VerbOutcome>();
    assert_plain_data::<VerbData>();
    assert_plain_data::<DomainEvent>();
    assert_plain_data::<Snapshot>();
    assert_plain_data::<EditCommand>();
    assert_plain_data::<ViewState>();
    assert_plain_data::<ExportSpec>();
};
```

**One name for one type.** `Verb` is the vocabulary that crosses the transport. `EditCommand` is the
undoable unit that the undo stack of section 4.9 holds.

```rust
/// One undoable edit. The undo stack holds these, never a `Verb`.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum EditCommand {
    Score(ScoreCommand),
    Session(SessionCommand),
}
```

### 3.6 Storage format decision

**Decision: the canonical format is the storage format from version one. MusicXML is an import and
export format only.**

MusicXML cannot hold most of the model. Takes, playlists, regions, record modes, part assignments,
mixer state, automation curves, pitch tracks, and history have no MusicXML representation
(critic 3.1). A hybrid is already a canonical format plus an interchange format.

The format holds four properties (critic 3.3).

1. **A version field, in every canonical document.** `score/meta.json` carries `"schema": SCHEMA`,
   `session/session.json` carries `SESSION_SCHEMA`, `mix/strips.json` carries `MIX_SCHEMA`, and
   `state/view.json` carries `VIEW_SCHEMA`. **`Session` and `MixState` each hold
   `schema: SchemaVersion` as their first field**, so the refusal of property 4 has a value to read;
   revision 7 refused a version that two of the three documents did not carry (critic Q8). A reader
   migrates an older document through a chain of steps, and `SchemaVersion` derives `Ord` so that
   "older" and "newer" are decidable.
2. **Deterministic output.** The same score produces the same bytes. Field order is the struct
   order, map keys sort, and floats print with a fixed format. A save with no change produces no
   git diff.
3. **One record per line.** Large collections are JSON Lines, sorted by a stable key.
4. **A place for unknown fields, in the score files alone.** Every record of `score/meta.json`,
   `score/notes.jsonl`, and `score/spanners.jsonl` that `duet-score` declares carries
   `#[serde(flatten)] extra: BTreeMap<String, serde_json::Value>`, so `duet-score` depends on
   `serde_json` and `duet-session` does not (section 1.2). **The eight records are `Part`, `Staff`,
   `Voice`, `Measure`, `ScoreMark`, `Note`, `Rest`, and `Spanner`**, and revision 9 gave the bag to
   one of the eight while the property named all of them (critic W8). `Spanner` therefore derives no
   `Copy`, and `Rest` carries `#[serde(flatten)]` rather than a nested key that every save would put
   in the git diff. **The tempo map is the one exclusion.** `TempoPoint` and `MeterPoint` are
   `duet-time` types, `duet-time` carries no `serde_json` edge, and an unknown field on a tempo
   entry would be a tempo this build cannot honour, so the reader refuses it rather than keeping it.
   **The session, mix, and view documents carry no `extra` bag**, and a version they cannot read is
   refused with `CommandError::Schema`.
   The split is a decision, not an omission (critic N2). **The refusal reads the document's own
   `SchemaVersion` and compares it with the constant this build carries**: a greater value is
   `CommandError::Schema`, and a smaller value runs the migration chain of property 1. Two reasons
   hold the split. The score files are
   the ones a foreign tool and a terminal agent hand-edit (section 3.8 path 1), and an unknown
   notation field that survives a round trip costs nothing. A silently kept unknown routing field,
   send level, or record mode would produce audio the user did not ask for, and a stated refusal is
   the safer answer there.

| File | Content | Shape | Sort key |
|---|---|---|---|
| `score/meta.json` | Schema, parts, staves, voices, measures, marks, tempo map | One JSON object | Struct order |
| `score/notes.jsonl` | One note or rest per line | JSON Lines | `(staff, voice, onset, pitch, id)` |
| `score/spanners.jsonl` | One slur, hairpin, or octave shift per line | JSON Lines | `(from, kind, id)` |

Every field of both sort keys derives `Ord` under VR1. The trailing identifier breaks a tie, so each
key is total and the output is unique.

**`LayoutOptions` reaches no file.** It is a `duet-engrave` type, and `duet-engrave` depends on
`duet-score`, so `score/meta.json` cannot hold it without a back edge that Cargo refuses (PL1).
`crates/duet` builds a `LayoutOptions` from the `ZoomStep` of `ModeView` on each engrave call, and
`state/view.json` persists the `ZoomStep`.

Two edge rules keep the output valid JSON.

1. **A non-finite `f64` is rejected at the edge.** `serde_json` writes `null` for a NaN or an
   infinity, which fails the round trip. Every `f64` field is a `Finite`, on the way out and on the
   way back in (section 2.6a).
2. **Every unknown key is reported, not only kept.** The reader returns each key it placed in an
   `extra` bag as an `ImportWarning`, and the command-line interface prints it. A misspelt field
   from a hand edit is visible at once.

```rust
/// Read a canonical document and migrate it to the current schema.
///
/// # Errors
/// Returns `ScoreError::Schema` for an unknown version, and
/// `ScoreError::Parse` for malformed text.
pub fn read(meta: &str, notes: &str, spanners: &str) -> Result<Score, ScoreError>;

/// Write a canonical document with a deterministic byte order.
///
/// # Errors
/// Returns `ScoreError::Serialize` when a field cannot be written.
pub fn write(score: &Score) -> Result<CanonicalDocument, ScoreError>;
```

### 3.7 MusicXML is a narrow in-house reader and writer

`deny.toml` sets `unknown-git = "deny"` and `CLAUDE.md` forbids a git dependency, so a fork cannot be
a dependency. A vendored fork under `crates/` would inherit the full lint policy on code that no
Duet engineer wrote (critic 3.2).

**Decision: write a narrow reader and writer in `duet-interchange` over `quick-xml`.** It covers the
subset that Duet models: parts, staves, measures, notes, rests, key and time signatures, ties, slurs,
dynamics, and lyrics. On import it keeps every unmodelled element in a lossless bucket, keyed by the
parent element path, so an export round trip returns them.

```rust
/// Read a MusicXML document into a score.
///
/// # Errors
/// Returns `InterchangeError` for malformed XML or an unsupported version.
pub fn read_musicxml(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<MusicXmlImport, InterchangeError>;

/// The result of a MusicXML import.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct MusicXmlImport {
    pub score: Score,
    pub unmapped: UnmappedElements,
    pub warnings: Vec<ImportWarning>,
}

/// Write a score as MusicXML, and return the unmapped elements to their place.
///
/// # Errors
/// Returns `InterchangeError::Serialize` when a value has no MusicXML form.
pub fn write_musicxml(score: &Score, unmapped: &UnmappedElements) -> Result<Vec<u8>, InterchangeError>;
```

PR 11 Q9 records that Duet does not print and does not write PDF. MusicXML export is the print path,
and the export surface says so.

ADR: `adr/0002-storage-format.md`.

### 3.8 How a terminal agent edits the score without the application

Three paths exist. All three end at `Score::apply` or at the canonical reader. PR 11 Q2 makes the
`duet` command-line interface the one interface an agent learns.

1. **A text edit of the canonical files.** The agent edits `score/notes.jsonl` and commits. No Duet
   process runs.
2. **The command-line interface with no window.** `duet --project <path> score set-pitch --note 42
   --pitch C4` opens the bundle, takes the writer lock, applies the verb, saves, and exits.
3. **The same interface over the socket.** When a window is open, the same command finds the socket
   and forwards the verb. The result is identical.

#### The writer lock protocol

The protocol is four steps and two checks (critic, the writer lock).

1. **The window process binds its socket first, then writes the lock.** `state/duet.lock` is created
   with `create_new` and holds the process identifier, the start time of that process, and the
   socket path. A lock therefore never names a socket that does not exist.
2. **A second writer that finds the lock reads it and tries the socket**, under B15. When the socket
   answers, the second writer forwards its verbs and never writes a file.
3. **When the socket does not answer, the second writer checks liveness.** It reads `/proc/<pid>/stat`
   on Linux and calls `sysctl` with `KERN_PROC_PID` on macOS, both read-only and both in the
   platform module of `duet-project`. A live process with a dead socket is a start in progress, so
   the second writer waits.
4. **The retry rule is B25.** After the last attempt with a live process, the command exits with
   `GatewayError::ProjectBusy` and a message that names the process identifier. With a dead process,
   the second writer removes the lock and takes it.

The recorded start time defends against a reused process identifier. A live process whose start time
differs from the record is a different process, so the lock is stale.

**The window start path against a stale lock.** A window that finds an existing lock runs steps 2 to
4. When the recorded process is dead, it removes the lock, takes it, and opens normally. When the
recorded process is alive and its socket answers, the new window shows one dialog. It reads `This
project is already open.` and it offers a `Bring to front` action and a `Cancel` action. It opens no
bundle and writes nothing.

**What the running application does when its own lock disappears.** `duet-project` watches
`state/duet.lock`. When the file is gone, or its content no longer matches this process, the core
takes three steps in order.

1. It stops every write at once. The save path, the disk writer, and every job thread refuse with
   `ProjectError::LockLost`.
2. It stops the transport, and it flushes and hashes any open take into `media/incoming/`, which
   needs no lock because the name is a fresh identifier.
3. It emits `CoreEvent::LockLost`. The window shows a blocking dialog with two actions:
   `Re-take the lock`, which runs the four-step protocol again, and `Close without saving`.

The first step is what stops two writers from editing one bundle.

### 3.9 How the running application reconciles an external edit

1. `duet-project` watches the bundle with `notify` 8.2.0 and `notify-debouncer-full` 0.7.0, under
   the debounce window B26. The 9.0 release candidate is rejected; the pair must match, and the gate
   does not run a release candidate.
2. The project writer records the content hash of every file it writes in a `WriterLedger`. The
   watcher drops an event whose current hash matches the ledger, which stops a watch storm from our
   own saves.
3. A surviving batch reaches `duet-core` as `CoreInput::FilesChanged(Vec<PathBuf>)`.
4. The core parses the changed files into a candidate document. A parse error emits
   `CoreEvent::ExternalEditRejected { path, error }` and changes nothing.
5. With no unsaved edit, the core swaps the document, increases the version, and emits
   `CoreEvent::DocumentReloaded { version }`.
6. With an unsaved edit, the core does not merge. It emits `CoreEvent::ExternalEditConflict { paths }`.
   The application offers three choices: commit to a new branch, discard, or cancel. The default is
   commit to a new branch (PR 11 Q8). Silent loss is not an option the design offers.

---

## 4. The project bundle

The crate is `duet-project`. It owns the bundle, the content store, the history, and the file watch.
It declares no document (critic 8.2).

### 4.1 Directory layout

```
<name>.duet/
├── .git/                      gix repository; text only
├── .gitattributes             written at creation
├── .gitignore                 written at creation
├── duet.toml                  bundle identity and schema number
├── score/
│   ├── meta.json
│   ├── notes.jsonl
│   └── spanners.jsonl
├── session/
│   ├── session.json           tracks, parts, record modes, transport settings, calibrations
│   ├── takes.jsonl            one take per line
│   ├── regions.jsonl          one region per line
│   └── locations.jsonl        marks, loop, punch
├── mix/
│   ├── strips.json            strips, aux sends, buses
│   └── automation.jsonl       one curve point per line
├── media.manifest             one source per line: hash, channels, rate, frames, bytes
├── media/                     content store, outside the git index
│   ├── <hh>/<hash>.wav
│   ├── incoming/              a take in progress
│   └── dead/                  unreferenced sources, never deleted by the app
├── derived/                   never tracked; a cache in full
│   ├── peaks/<hash>.peaks
│   └── analysis/<hash>.pitch
├── state/                     never tracked; NOT a cache
│   ├── save.commit            the two-phase marker, present only during a save
│   ├── view.json              per-mode view state (section 10.2)
│   ├── duet.lock
│   ├── agent.sock.path
│   └── .tmp/<job>/            one directory per running job that is not a render
└── exports/                   never tracked; user output
    └── .tmp/<job>/            one directory per running render job
```

**`derived/` and `state/` are two different things** (critic N17).

- `derived/` is a cache in full. A user may delete the whole directory, and every file in it
  rebuilds. The bundle README states that.
- `state/` is not a cache. It holds what belongs to this machine and this run: the record of work in
  flight, and the view state. A deletion during a save loses the unsaved edit. A deletion while the
  application runs breaks the writer lock. A deletion of `state/view.json` alone costs the viewport
  and the selection, which the user restores with one scroll.

**`view.json` lives under `state/` because a scroll must not churn a commit** (critic N16).
`ModeView` holds the scroll offset, the zoom step, and the selection, and Appendix A writes that
state on `on_drag_move` and on `on_scroll_wheel`. A tracked `view.json` would put viewport churn in
every user commit and would move the viewport on a checkout, which contradicts property 2 of
section 3.6. History records the project, not the window.

`.gitignore` covers `media/`, `derived/`, `state/`, and `exports/`.

#### Every store carries a bound

Elastic needs a bound on a store, not only on a channel (critic, four unbounded stores).

| Store | Bound | Eviction rule |
|---|---|---|
| `derived/peaks/` (cache) | B59 | The least recently opened file is deleted when the bound is passed. A deleted pyramid rebuilds on demand. |
| `derived/analysis/` (cache) | B60 | The same rule. A pitch track rebuilds from the source. |
| `media/incoming/` | One file per armed track | A file with no live writer is offered for recovery at the next start. The user's answer moves it or deletes it. |
| `media/dead/` | No automatic bound; it holds user audio | `duet gc --purge` is the only remover, and section 4.4 states its rules. `duet status` reports the size. |
| `exports/` | No automatic bound; it holds user output | Nothing in the application deletes a finished render. `duet status` reports the size. |
| `exports/.tmp/` | One directory per running render job | The job deletes its own directory on success, on failure, and on cancel (section 9.6). The next start empties the parent, because no job survives a restart. |
| `state/.tmp/` | One directory per running job that is not a render | The same rule. A job that writes a document, a checkout, or an import owns one. |

### 4.2 What git tracks

**Decision: git tracks text only. Audio bytes live in a content store inside the bundle and outside
the git index** (critic 2.1).

Tracked: `duet.toml`, `score/`, `session/`, `mix/`, `media.manifest`, `.gitattributes`,
`.gitignore`.

Not tracked: `media/`, `derived/`, `state/`, `exports/`.

The reason is size. One take costs B66, and audio does not compress with zlib. Fifty takes give
several gigabytes, and every checkout of an old commit would rewrite gigabytes in the worktree.

Three consequences follow, and the product states each one.

1. **A `git clone` of the bundle carries no audio.** The unit of backup is the bundle directory. The
   create dialog and the export surface say so.
2. **`git clean -xdf` deletes every take.** The application writes a `media/README.txt` at creation
   that states it in one line.
3. **The content store needs its own collector.** Section 4.4 gives the rule.

PR 11 Q3 keeps audio in history. That holds: a source is immutable and written once, so history
growth follows the count of takes, not the count of edits.

### 4.3 How a take is referenced

A source is named by the lowercase hexadecimal BLAKE3 hash of its file bytes. Lowercase hexadecimal
avoids a collision on a case-insensitive APFS volume (critic 2.5).

The test for this is macOS only. macOS creates a case-insensitive volume with
`hdiutil create -fs "HFS+" -size 64m`. Linux needs a loopback image and privileges that the runner
does not hold. **The test carries `#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]` and no `#[ignore]`, so it runs in
the ordinary gate on the macOS runner.** Revision 5 assigned it to `soak.yml`, whose two commands
never reach `duet-project`, so a test that guards a documented data-loss path ran nowhere
(critic S8). The Linux substitute is a pure unit test that asserts every generated name matches
`^[0-9a-f]{64}$`.

`SourceHash` and `AudioContainer` are declared in `duet-session`, because a region names a source.
`duet-project` depends on `duet-session` directly, and section 1.3 carries that edge.

```rust
// in duet-session
/// A content address for one audio source. It is a BLAKE3 digest, printed as
/// 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters, and the PG24 table prints its size.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct SourceHash([u8; 32]);

/// The container a captured source is stored in.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum AudioContainer { Wav, Rf64 }

// in duet-project
/// One line of `media.manifest`.
#[expect(
    missing_copy_implementations,
    reason = "one manifest line is the size the PG24 table prints for `ManifestEntry`, and it \
              grows when the manifest gains a column; VR5 refuses `Copy` past the size bound"
)]
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct ManifestEntry {
    hash: SourceHash,
    channels: NonZeroU8,
    sample_rate: SampleRate,
    frames: u64,
    bytes: u64,
    container: AudioContainer,
}
```

`media.manifest` is tracked text, sorted by hash. A commit therefore pins exactly which audio bytes
it needs. A region in `regions.jsonl` names a `SourceHash`, never a path.

### 4.4 Garbage collection of the content store

PR R-07 says an undo of a record pass removes the take and keeps the audio file. PR R-09 and X-13
say a delete keeps it too. After either one, no manifest names the hash, and the redo has nothing to
restore (critic N4).

**The live set has four sources.**

1. The working `media.manifest` on disk, plus every file in `media/incoming/`.
2. Every commit reachable from any reference: a branch, a tag, the reflog, or a detached `HEAD`.
3. Every `SourceHash` that the undo stack of any open session names.
4. Every `SourceHash` that the redo stack of any open session names.

**`gc` reads the live set through the gateway, never from disk alone.** Sources 3 and 4 live in
`DuetCore` memory, so a disk-only walk cannot see them. `Verb::Gc` is a deferred verb. The core builds sources 1, 3,
and 4 from memory into a snapshot. A job thread then walks the commits and scans `media/`
(section 9.6).

```rust
/// Build the live set. Only the core can call this, because sources 3 and 4
/// are in-memory stacks.
///
/// # Errors
/// Returns `GatewayError::RecordInProgress` during a record pass, and
/// `GatewayError::HistoryUnresolved` while an external `HEAD` change waits
/// for the user.
pub fn live_sources(&self) -> Result<BTreeSet<SourceHash>, GatewayError>;
```

Three refusals protect the user.

- **`gc` refuses while a record pass runs.** A take that is open has no manifest line yet.
- **`gc` refuses while an external `HEAD` change is unresolved.** The live set would be computed
  against a state the user has not accepted.
- **`gc` refuses when the core is not reachable.** A command-line `duet gc` with no open project
  opens the bundle itself, and a `duet gc` that finds a live socket forwards the verb. No code path
  computes a live set without the core.

```
duet gc
```

It moves every file that the live set does not name to `media/dead/`. It never deletes.

```
duet gc --purge <hash> [<hash> ...]
```

`--purge` takes an explicit hash list and never a wildcard. It recomputes the live set from all four
sources and refuses the whole call when any named hash is live, with `ProjectError::HashReachable
{ hash }`. It then deletes only the named files. Ardour takes the same care: `cleanup_sources()`
moves unreferenced media to `dead/` (Ardour 8).

### 4.5 The git history model through gix

`gix` types stay inside `duet-project` behind one trait, because gix is 0.x and breaks often
(critic 2.6).

```rust
/// The history operations the project needs. One implementation uses gix.
pub trait History {
    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `HistoryError::Write` when an object cannot be written.
    fn commit(&mut self, message: &str, files: &[TrackedFile]) -> Result<CommitId, HistoryError>;

    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `HistoryError::MissingRef` when the branch does not exist.
    fn branch(&mut self, name: &BranchName, from: CommitId) -> Result<(), HistoryError>;

    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `HistoryError::Read` when an object cannot be read.
    fn log(&self, start: CommitId, limit: u32) -> Result<Vec<CommitSummary>, HistoryError>;

    /// Read a commit's tracked files into memory. It touches no worktree file.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `HistoryError::Read` when an object cannot be read.
    fn read_tree(&self, commit: CommitId) -> Result<TreeSnapshot, HistoryError>;

    /// The commit that `HEAD` names now.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `HistoryError::Read` when `HEAD` cannot be resolved.
    fn head(&self) -> Result<HeadState, HistoryError>;

    /// The object format this repository uses.
    ///
    /// **The repository configuration is the authority, and an absent key is
    /// an answer.** `extensions.objectFormat` is a repository-format-version-1
    /// extension. This method reads `core.repositoryFormatVersion` first. At
    /// version 0 it returns `HashKind::Sha1` and reads no extension, because a
    /// version-0 repository carries no extension and SHA-1 is the default. At
    /// version 1 it reads `extensions.objectFormat` and maps the value.
    /// Revision 10 read the key alone, so the one shape this build creates
    /// answered with a refusal (critic C-3, W9). `duet.toml` mirrors the value
    /// for a reader and decides nothing, because a user who runs plain `git`
    /// can convert a repository without touching a Duet file (section 4.6).
    ///
    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `HistoryError::Read` when the configuration cannot be read, and
    /// when the repository declares a format version this build does not know.
    fn object_format(&self) -> Result<HashKind, HistoryError>;
}
```

A commit is one user action or one agent verb group. The application writes the tracked files,
hashes them, writes the blobs, builds the tree, and commits. It never runs the `git` binary.

**Every gix call runs on a job thread under B19** (TH3). A call that passes the budget returns
`HistoryError::Timeout`, and the user interface shows the history surface in a failed state with a
retry action. A repository on a stalled network volume cannot hang a verb.

#### Which pointers must be a symbolic reference

| Pointer | Form | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| The project's current line of work | A branch name in `duet.toml` | A rebase or an amend rewrites every commit identifier on the branch. |
| The autosave target | The symbolic reference `refs/duet/autosave` | The same reason, and it must survive a branch switch. |
| A take's origin commit, shown in the take list | Not stored | It is computed from the manifest at read time. |
| A history entry the user pinned | A tag under `refs/tags/duet/<name>` | A tag survives a rewrite of the branch that created it. |
| A commit identifier inside a `Verb` call | A bare identifier | It is a transient argument. The verb fails with `HistoryError::MissingCommit` when the identifier is gone. |

No stored pointer is a bare commit identifier. `duet.toml` holds a branch name, and it mirrors the
object format that `History::object_format` reads. It decides neither.

**The open path refuses an object format this build cannot read.** `ProjectOpen` calls
`object_format` and returns `ProjectError::ObjectFormat` for anything but `HashKind::Sha1`, because
`CommitDigest` reads its length from that answer (section 15.5). **An absent
`extensions.objectFormat` key is never a refusal**: at format version 0 the method answers
`HashKind::Sha1`, which is the one shape section 4.7 creates (critic C-3).

**Checkout of an earlier commit into the live project** never touches the worktree first.

1. Read the target tree into memory with `read_tree`.
2. Parse it into a candidate project state.
3. Look up every `SourceHash` in the candidate `media.manifest` against `media/`.
4. A missing hash is not a failure of the checkout. The region draws as absent and the core emits
   `CoreEvent::MissingSource { hash }`. Ardour draws an absent waveform rather than a stall
   (Ardour 9).
5. On success the core swaps the whole candidate state in one step, writes the files, and moves the
   branch reference.
6. A failure at step 2 changes nothing and emits `CoreEvent::CheckoutRejected { commit, error }`.

### 4.6 The contract for a user who runs plain git

The application watches `.git/HEAD` and `.git/refs` (critic 2.2).

1. On an external `HEAD` move, the application stops the transport first. It then flushes any open
   take to disk and hashes it.
2. It then follows the rule of section 3.9. No unsaved work means reload. Unsaved work means commit
   to a new branch, discard, or cancel, and commit to a new branch is the default (PR 11 Q8).
3. While a record pass runs, the application refuses every history verb that rewrites:
   `HistoryCheckout`, `HistoryBranch`, and any reset. The verb returns
   `GatewayError::RecordInProgress`.
4. A rewrite of history by an external tool while the project is open is unsupported. The release
   notes state it. The application detects an unknown `HEAD` and offers a reload.

### 4.7 Repository configuration written at creation

`gix` runs no clean or smudge filter, no hook, and no Large File Storage. A user's global git
configuration would change what a plain `git` writes, and gix would then read a file that differs
from the one it wrote (critic 2.3).

```
# .gitattributes
* -text
*.json   text eol=lf
*.jsonl  text eol=lf
*.toml   text eol=lf
media.manifest text eol=lf
```

```
# repository-local config
core.autocrlf=false
core.safecrlf=false
```

**Bundle creation writes no `extensions.objectFormat` key, and that is a decision.**
`extensions.objectFormat` is a repository-format-version-1 extension. A repository that carries an
extension key at format version 0 is one that `git` refuses to open at all: `verify_repository_format`
reports a version-0 repository with version-1 extensions and every `git` command inside the bundle
stops. Section 4.6 makes a user who runs plain `git` a supported path and story A-03 makes it a
MUST, so revision 10's block made every bundle this build creates unreadable (critic C-3).
`git init` writes no such key, and only `--object-format=sha256` writes it and raises the version to
1. **SHA-1 is the default, and a version-0 repository states it by omission.** `duet.toml` records
the value as a mirror a reader can see without a git tool, and it decides nothing (section 4.5).

A test writes a bundle with the real `git` binary, runs `git status` inside it, reads it with gix,
and asserts both that `git` opens it and that the bytes match.

### 4.8 The object count stays bounded

gix exposes no repack and no garbage collection (critic 2.4). The design bounds the object count
instead: git holds text only, one commit covers one user action, and no derived data enters the
repository. B69 gives the count after one year, which every supported file system handles.

No repack is planned. If a measurement shows one is needed, it becomes a user-invoked step that
names the `git` binary as an explicit, documented dependency.

### 4.9 Undo against history

**`duet-core` owns the undo stack.** `duet-project` owns neither mechanism.

| Property | Undo | History |
|---|---|---|
| Owner | `DuetCore` | `duet-project` |
| Grain | One command | One user action or verb group |
| Storage | Memory only | The git object store |
| Lifetime | The session | Forever |
| Bound | B63, B64, and B65 | B69 |
| Content | An inverse `EditCommand` list | The full tracked file set |

```rust
/// One undo step. It is a named group of edits with their inverses.
///
/// It holds `EditCommand`, which section 3.5 declares. It never holds a
/// `Verb`, because a `Verb` can be a query or a job and neither is undoable.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct Transaction {
    name: TransactionName,
    commands: Vec<EditCommand>,
    inverse: Vec<EditCommand>,
    cost: InverseCost,
    /// Every source this transaction's inverse would restore. `gc` reads it
    /// as source 3 and source 4 of the live set (section 4.4).
    sources: SmallVec<[SourceHash; 4]>,
}

/// The in-session undo stack, owned by `DuetCore`.
#[derive(Debug, Default)]
pub struct UndoStack { done: VecDeque<Transaction>, undone: VecDeque<Transaction>, total: InverseCost }
```

`InverseCost` is a `duet-score` type (section 15.3). `Applied` carries one, and `duet-core`
depends on `duet-score`, so the cost cannot be declared here (critic S2).

**Three bounds, not one.** A transaction count bounds no memory: the inverse of `RemoveMeasures`
holds one `InsertNote` per removed note. B63, B64, and B65 bound the count, the commands, and the
bytes.

The stack drops the oldest transaction when any bound is passed. It drops whole transactions, never
part of one, so the stack is always a valid replay. **The application tells the user when it drops.**
It emits `CoreEvent::UndoHorizonMoved { dropped, oldest_name }`, and the History surface shows one
line.

A transaction that collects nothing is dropped, so an empty undo entry never appears (Ardour 8).

**A checkout clears the undo stack.** The inverse commands name identifiers that the earlier document
may not hold. The application tells the user before it acts.

### 4.10 Crash safety and atomic save

A single file is written as a temporary file in the same directory, then `fsync` of the file, then
`rename`, then `fsync` of the directory.

A multi-file save is not atomic by rename alone. A two-phase marker makes it crash consistent with
no database.

**The five steps, with every `fsync` named.**

1. Write every temporary file. `fsync` each file.
2. `fsync` every directory that received a temporary file.
3. Write `state/save.commit`, which lists each temporary name and its final name. `fsync` the marker
   file, then `fsync` `state/`.
4. Rename each file. `fsync` every directory that a rename touched.
5. Delete `state/save.commit`. `fsync` `state/`.

#### The crash matrix

| Crash point | State on disk | Recovery at the next start |
|---|---|---|
| During step 1 or step 2, before the marker | Temporary files, no marker | The old state is intact and durable. The start deletes every temporary file whose name matches the save pattern. The unsaved edit is gone. |
| During step 3, marker partly written | A marker that does not parse | The start deletes the marker and every temporary file. The old state stands, and the application tells the user that the last save did not finish. |
| After step 3, during step 4 | A valid marker, some files renamed | The start reads the marker and completes every rename whose temporary file still exists. The result is the new state. |
| After step 4, before step 5 | A valid marker, every file renamed, every directory synced | The start reads the marker, finds no temporary file, and deletes the marker. The result is the new state. |
| After step 5 | No marker | Nothing to do. |

The marker plus the presence of a temporary file decides the answer. Every rename is durable before
the marker goes away. The result is the old state or the new state, never a mixture.

**The marker lives in `state/`, which `.gitignore` covers.** `git clean -xdf` deletes it and the
temporary files together, so the bundle returns to the old state, which is the answer the recovery
gives. The bundle README states that a clean run discards an unfinished save.

**A record pass writes audio to disk as it records** (PR 10.5). The disk writer streams to
`media/incoming/<uuid>.wav` and flushes on every ring drain. On stop it calls `fsync`, hashes the
file, renames it to `media/<hh>/<hash>.wav`, `fsync`s both directories, and appends a manifest line.
A crash mid-take leaves the file in `media/incoming/`. On the next start the application hashes what
is there, admits it as a take, and tells the user. Every written sample survives (Ardour 8).

ADR: `adr/0003-history-model.md`.

---

## 5. The audio engine

The crate is `duet-engine`. It holds the backend trait, the transport machine, the processor chain,
the mixer runtime, the graph runner, and the disk path.

### 5.1 The backend trait

The backend owns the thread and calls one duplex cycle. Nothing else pulls (Ardour 5, critic 5.2).

```rust
/// One audio device backend.
pub trait AudioBackend: Send {
    fn name(&self) -> BackendName;

    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `BackendError::Enumerate` when the platform refuses the query,
    /// and `BackendError::NoServer` when the platform audio server is absent.
    fn devices(&self) -> Result<Vec<DeviceInfo>, BackendError>;

    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `BackendError::Enumerate` when the device is gone.
    fn supported_sample_rates(&self, device: &DeviceId) -> Result<Vec<SampleRate>, BackendError>;

    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `BackendError::Enumerate` when the device is gone.
    fn supported_block_sizes(&self, device: &DeviceId) -> Result<BlockSizeRange, BackendError>;

    /// Open a duplex stream and take ownership of the process body.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `BackendError::Open` when the device refuses the request,
    /// `BackendError::RateUnavailable` when the device offers no supported
    /// rate, and `BackendError::OpenTimeout` past B18.
    fn open(&mut self, request: &StreamRequest, process: Box<dyn AudioProcess>)
        -> Result<StreamInfo, BackendError>;

    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `BackendError::Start` when the stream will not run.
    fn start(&mut self) -> Result<(), BackendError>;

    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `BackendError::Stop` when the stream will not stop.
    fn stop(&mut self) -> Result<(), BackendError>;

    /// The capture and playback latency in force.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `BackendError::NotOpen` before `open` succeeds.
    fn latency(&self) -> Result<LatencyReport, BackendError>;

    /// The device sample counter at the start of the current cycle.
    fn clock(&self) -> SampleClock;
}

/// The real-time body. The backend calls `process` on its own thread.
///
/// **`EngineProcess` is the one implementor, and it is the root of the audio
/// thread** (section 5.6, section 15.10, critic C20-3). `open` moves the
/// boxed value into the backend's own callback state, so the value the audio
/// thread holds for the life of the stream is an `EngineProcess` and
/// `GraphState` is one of its fields. Revision 20 declared no implementor at
/// all, so six heap-owning handles sat above the root of every audio rule.
pub trait AudioProcess: Send {
    /// Run one cycle. The frame count varies between cycles.
    fn process(&mut self, cycle: &mut Cycle<'_>) -> CycleOutcome;
}

/// The buffers and the clock for one cycle.
///
/// Both planes are de-interleaved and channel major: channel `c` of the
/// input starts at `c * frames`. The backend owns the memory and lends it
/// for the length of one call, so the audio thread allocates nothing.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Cycle<'buffers> {
    input: &'buffers [f32],
    output: &'buffers mut [f32],
    channels: ChannelConfig,
    frames: FrameCount,
    start: SampleClock,
}

impl Cycle<'_> {
    /// How many frames this cycle carries. It varies.
    pub fn frames(&self) -> FrameCount;

    /// The device sample counter at the start of this cycle.
    pub fn start(&self) -> SampleClock;

    /// One capture channel, or `None` when the index is out of range.
    pub fn input(&self, channel: ChannelIndex) -> Option<&[f32]>;

    /// One playback channel, or `None` when the index is out of range.
    pub fn output(&mut self, channel: ChannelIndex) -> Option<&mut [f32]>;
}

/// What one cycle produced. Every variant is `Copy` and allocates nothing.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum CycleOutcome { Ran, PlaybackStarved, CaptureOverflow, Faulted(FaultCode) }

/// The latency the backend reports, in frames.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct LatencyReport { capture: u32, playback: u32, block: u32 }
```

`LatencyReport` follows Ardour's two definitions (Ardour 5). Capture latency is the age of data read
from a port. Playback latency is the delay until written data reaches a terminal port.

VR7 of section 3.5 holds the public-field rule for this whole document, and this section states no
rule of its own (DR4).

### 5.2 The block size varies

A device can refuse a fixed buffer size (survey). The engine therefore accepts a variable block size
on every cycle (critic 5.3).

- `open` returns a `StreamInfo` that carries `max_block: FrameCount`.
- Every internal buffer is sized to `max_block` once, at configure time, off the audio thread.
- `process` reads `cycle.frames()` each cycle. No internal buffer takes its size from a constant.
- The dummy backend varies the frame count on purpose, with a fixed seed, over the whole range from
  1 to `max_block`. Every engine test therefore meets the variation.

### 5.3 The dummy backend

`DummyBackend` is the first implementation and the reason headless tests exist (Ardour 5, adopt
item 8).

| Mode | Behaviour | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `RealTime` | A thread sleeps to match the wall clock of each block | Manual headless work |
| `Freewheel` | The cycle runs as fast as the process body allows | Tests and offline export |

It reports a configurable `LatencyReport`, so a latency-alignment test runs with no device.

### 5.4 cpal is the real backend on both platforms

**Decision: the one real backend is cpal 0.18.2, pinned as
`cpal = { version = "0.18.2", default-features = false, features = ["pipewire"] }`** (platform,
verified facts). Default features are empty in 0.18.2, and the `pipewire` feature adds
`pipewire` 0.10.1 with `v0_3_53`. The consumer line links `libpipewire` and `libasound` on Linux and
nothing extra on macOS.

**The host is selected by identifier, never by `default_host()`.** On Linux `default_host()` tries
PipeWire, then PulseAudio, then ALSA (platform, cpal facts). Two of those three are outside the
operator decision, so the backend names the host it wants.

| Platform | Host | When the host is absent |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | `HostId::PipeWire` | `BackendError::NoServer`, which the core maps to `EngineState::NoServer { detail }`. |
| macOS | `HostId::CoreAudio` | `BackendError::NoServer`, which cannot happen on a supported macOS. The same three messages serve it. |

**There is no ALSA host fallback.** cpal's own source documents unreliable period sizes and
continuous xruns on the ALSA host over the pipewire-alsa plugin (platform, cpal facts, issues 1029,
1036, 1250). A fallback would trade a clear failure for a dropout the user cannot diagnose. When no
PipeWire socket exists, the window opens, the status bar shows one line, and the user installs or
starts PipeWire.

Section 12.4 holds the message for each `ServerDetail`, so no other section states one.

**cpal has no duplex stream in 0.18.2** (survey; the duplex interface merged to `develop` after the
release). Input and output are two callbacks with two clocks (critic 5.2).

**Decision: the cpal backend satisfies the one-cycle trait by making the output callback the process
cycle.** The input callback writes into an `rtrb` ring. Before each cycle the backend drains up to
`cycle.frames()` frames from that ring into the capture buffers.

**Decision: version one refuses a record pass across two different devices.** With one device there
is one clock and no drift. With two devices a drift-corrected vocal take is a silent quality loss
the user did not ask for. The user picks one duplex device, or an Aggregate Device on macOS.

#### The PipeWire host, in the terms cpal 0.18.2 gives

| Fact | What the backend does |
|---|---|
| `BufferSize::Fixed(n)` is validated against the server quantum range and set as `node.latency`; an out-of-range value returns `UnsupportedConfig` | The backend requests the configured block. On `UnsupportedConfig` it falls back to `BufferSize::Default`, reads the real block from `StreamInfo`, and emits `EngineFault::BlockSizeAdjusted { requested, actual }`. |
| The host offers one sample rate, the graph rate | `supported_sample_rates` returns that one value. When the project rate differs, `open` returns `BackendError::RateUnavailable { project, device }`. |
| An xrun arrives as `ErrorKind::Xrun` | The error callback pushes `EngineFault::PlaybackStarved` into the B34 `FaultQueue`. **It is a second producer**, which is the whole reason that queue is a `crossbeam_queue::ArrayQueue` and not an `rtrb` ring (section 5.8, TH11). **This push is NOT latched and it cannot be** (critic C21-1): the callback holds one `basedrop::Shared<FaultQueue>` and no `ChainState`, so it has no per-track run to open, and TH11 lets it touch no other value of the engine. A device that xruns repeatedly is contained by B34 itself: the queue refuses the newest record and the drain mints `EngineFault::FaultsDropped`, so the burst reaches one bounded queue and one counter and never the B29 channel of every client. |
| Socket detection without an environment variable landed after 0.18.2 | The backend sets no environment variable and accepts the pinned behaviour. Chunk C4 records the pin in a comment on the host selection function. |

**The rate mismatch has a user answer, not a resample.** Version one does not resample on playback.
The engine moves to `EngineState::RateUnavailable { project, device }`, section 12.4 holds the
message, and `Verb::ProjectConvertRate` is the answer. It is a deferred verb that resamples every
source through `rubato`, which section 9.6 covers.

#### Where `LatencyReport` comes from

**Decision: `LatencyReport` comes from a loopback calibration that the user runs once per device, on
both platforms.** cpal exposes callback timestamps, not a latency query, and a timestamp gives the
callback's own jitter rather than the path through the converter and the analogue stage. The
PipeWire `pw_time.delay` value is not used for the same reason.

```rust
// in duet-session
/// A stable key for one audio device.
///
/// It is a 64-bit digest of the platform device identifier, not the name a
/// user reads, so `Calibration` stays `Copy` and a device rename never loses
/// a measurement. `DeviceLabel` carries the name a user reads (section 12.4).
/// Section 15 declares every placed name, and this one is declared here
/// beside the record that holds it (critic Q1, R1).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct DeviceKey(u64);

/// A measured device calibration, stored in the bundle.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Calibration {
    device: DeviceKey,
    sample_rate: SampleRate,
    block: FrameCount,
    /// The measured time from a written frame to the same frame read back.
    round_trip_frames: u32,
    /// How the value was obtained.
    source: CalibrationSource,
    measured_at: UnixSeconds,
}

/// How a calibration value was obtained.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum CalibrationSource {
    /// The user ran the loopback measurement on this device.
    Measured,
    /// No measurement exists. The value is the stated default.
    Default,
}
```

**The measurement.** The application plays a short chirp, records the input, and finds the offset by
cross-correlation in `duet_dsp::align`. It runs B74 and takes the median, so one bad pass does not
set the value. The result is stored in `session/session.json`, keyed by device, sample rate, and
block size. The measurement covers the whole path, so the input ring offset is inside the number.

**The split into capture and playback, with no underflow.** The round trip is one number, and
`LatencyReport` needs two. `LatencyReport::capture` is a `u32`, and the release profile sets
`overflow-checks = true` with `panic = "abort"`, so a measured round trip below one block would end
the process (critic N3).

```rust
/// Split a measured round trip into a capture part and a playback part.
///
/// # Errors
/// Returns `BackendError::CalibrationInvalid` when the measured round trip
/// is below the playback part, which means the measurement is not a
/// physical round trip.
pub fn split(round_trip: u32, block: u32, output_buffer: u32)
    -> Result<LatencyReport, BackendError>
{
    let playback = block.checked_add(output_buffer)
        .ok_or(BackendError::CalibrationInvalid)?;
    let capture = round_trip.checked_sub(playback)
        .ok_or(BackendError::CalibrationInvalid)?;
    Ok(LatencyReport::new(capture, playback, block))
}

/// The report to use when no calibration exists.
///
/// It reports the observable part and nothing else: one block plus the
/// reported output buffer as playback latency, and zero capture latency.
/// It guesses no round trip, so it cannot be too large.
#[must_use]
pub fn observable_only(block: u32, output_buffer: u32) -> LatencyReport;
```

`unwrap_or(0)` is not allowed here. A zero capture latency is a claim about the device, and a floor
would make the engine assert that claim after a failed subtraction. The `Option` propagates instead.
A `None` discards the calibration, falls back to `CalibrationSource::Default`, and raises
`EngineFault::CalibrationInvalid`. A test feeds a round trip of one frame with a block of 128 and
asserts `BackendError::CalibrationInvalid` and no panic.

**The measurement has a deadline.** The whole run is bounded at B20 and each pass at B21. On expiry
the run aborts, the device keeps `CalibrationSource::Default`, and the backend raises
`EngineFault::CalibrationTimeout`. The user interface closes the progress surface and shows one
line, which the section 12.4 fault table holds for `EngineFault::CalibrationTimeout`
(critic C21I-W4).

**With no calibration the backend applies the observable latency and guesses nothing.** B72 is one
block plus the reported output buffer, which the backend reads from `StreamInfo`. It applies no
default round trip, because the converter and the analogue stage are not observable from software.

**The error is therefore one-signed, and the sign is known.** The true round trip of a consumer
interface is B82, and B72 is below the whole of that range, so an uncalibrated take lands **late**
by B73 and never early. Revision 7 guessed a whole round trip that sat inside the B82 range, so the
take landed early at one end of that range and late at the other, while the sentence that justified
the guess claimed "never late" (critic Q4). A guess that is sometimes early and
sometimes late teaches the user nothing; an offset that is always late by a bounded amount teaches
one direction.

B71 is the tolerance for a **measured** device. B73 is fifty-eight to two hundred and fifty-eight
times that tolerance, which is why `TakeFlag::Uncalibrated` and the `Calibrate` action exist, and why the
Record top bar shows the alert while any armed device is uncalibrated.

**The alignment policy on a default value.** A take recorded with `CalibrationSource::Default` is
committed with `TakeFlag::Uncalibrated`. Three things follow.

1. The take list shows a marker on that take with the tooltip `Recorded without a device calibration`.
2. The Record top bar shows a one-line alert with a `Calibrate` action while any armed device is
   uncalibrated.
3. The region keeps its `AlignChoice`, so the offset is applied. A later calibration does not move
   an existing take, because a take is a fact about what was recorded. The user may nudge the
   region, which is an ordinary undoable region edit.

**The alignment test.** A test in `duet-engine` runs the dummy backend with a configured latency. It
records a synthetic impulse, commits the take, and asserts that the region position is inside B71.

#### The capture shortfall

A cycle whose input ring holds fewer frames than `cycle.frames()` zero fills the difference. The
first draft counted it and told nobody, so silence entered a vocal take in silence.

The cycle adds the zero-filled frames to `ChainState::shortfall`, and the runner pushes one
`EngineFault::CaptureShortfall { track, frames }` when that run closes, with `frames` the whole run
(critic C21-1). It travels the fault queue of section 12.4, whose fault table holds the one user
message for it (critic C21I-W4). The take list marks the affected region.

#### Drift is still measured

The backend measures the relation between the two callbacks over the window B70, even in the
one-device case, so the refusal above is verifiable.

```rust
/// The measured relation between the capture clock and the playback clock.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct DriftReport { frames: i64, window_seconds: u32, parts_per_million: i32 }
```

A magnitude over the B70 threshold raises `EngineFault::ClockDrift { parts_per_million }`, which is the form section 12.4 declares. `DriftReport` derives no `Serialize`, so the tuple form would not build (critic C10). The native backends of
section 11 remove the two-callback shape altogether, and this measurement is the evidence that
decides when to build them.

`rubato` stays a dependency of `duet-export` only. It resamples an export or a whole-project
conversion, never a live take.

### 5.5 The processor chain is a typed fixed skeleton

Ardour rebuilds an invisible processor list by search and splice, guarded by assertions. The research
file rejects that design (Ardour, reject list). Duet encodes the order in the type.

**Topology and state are two types, not one.** A published value is read through a shared reference,
and a processor needs `&mut self` to run.

```rust
/// The immutable shape of one track chain. It is published, never mutated.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct ChainTopology {
    /// The identity of this chain, which is the identity of its strip.
    ///
    /// **Every chain has one, a bus chain included** (critic WARNING on the
    /// bus identity). The mix document addresses a chain by `StripId`,
    /// `MeterSnapshot` indexes by `StripId`, and B86 counts strips, so one
    /// identity serves the whole path and no conversion exists to get wrong.
    strip: StripId,
    /// The track this chain reads and writes, or `None` for a bus.
    ///
    /// **A bus has no track and therefore no disk path**, which is what
    /// section 5.5 means by "a bus is a chain with no disk reader and no disk
    /// writer" and what keeps 16 of the 48 strips out of the ring count
    /// (critic CR on the ring arithmetic).
    track: Option<TrackId>,
    channels: ChannelConfig,
    polarity: bool,
    /// Which processor sits in each slot, and its parameter identifiers.
    pre_fader: ArrayVec<SlotSpec, MAX_SLOTS>,
    post_fader: ArrayVec<SlotSpec, MAX_SLOTS>,
    sends: ArrayVec<SendSpec, MAX_SENDS>,
    meter_tap: MeterTap,
    output: StripTarget,
    /// Computed off the audio thread from every strip's mute and solo flag
    /// (section 7.1). The audio thread reads it and never computes it.
    audible: AudibleState,
}

/// One slot's declaration: what it is, which parameters address it, and
/// which pool buffer it uses. `configure` writes `buffer`; the audio thread
/// only reads it.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct SlotSpec { slot: SlotId, kind: SlotKind, params: ParamIdRange, buffer: Option<PoolSlot> }

/// Which processor a slot holds. Plugins are out of scope, so the set is
/// closed and the dispatch is static.
///
/// **The set covers every tool the product stories name** (critic C19-11).
/// Revision 19 held six kinds and three stories needed eight: PR M-03 names
/// a high-pass in every track tool set, PR MA-02 names a limiter in the
/// master chain, and contract 5.2 draws a limiter stage with its own gain
/// reduction bar. None of the three could be built, because no kind named
/// the processor and `clippy::wildcard_enum_match_arm` is denied, so no
/// chunk could add an arm without editing this enum.
///
/// `PitchCorrect` is absent. PR 8.2 rules pitch correction out of version
/// one, and `clippy::wildcard_enum_match_arm` is denied, so a variant no
/// chunk builds would force a dead arm in every match.
///
/// **`Gain` and `Dither` are absent, and each one has a stated home**
/// (contract 5.2). Gain is `ChainState::trim`, which every chain already
/// carries, so a gain slot would give one value two owners. Dither narrows a
/// render to an integer format and changes no live sample, so it is
/// `DitherKind` on the section 7.4 export spec and never a processor the
/// audio thread runs. `MasterStage` names all five boxes the contract draws
/// and states which of the three homes each one has.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum SlotKind { HighPass, Equalizer, Compressor, Gate, DeEsser, Limiter, Delay, Reverb }

/// The mutable running state of one chain. The audio thread owns it and no
/// other thread ever holds a reference to it while a cycle runs.
///
/// **`configure` builds it, and `basedrop` releases it** (critic CR-16). The
/// audio thread never constructs one and never drops one: a whole
/// `ChainSetHandle` arrives at B105 and the retired array leaves through the
/// collector, so every `DiskReader` and every `DiskWriter` this value owns
/// is allocated and freed on another thread.
///
/// **No other thread ever reads one** (critic CR-17). The live filter
/// history, the meter hold, and the gain ramp this value carries exist in one
/// copy, and that copy is the one the audio thread holds. `configure`
/// therefore builds the state of a chain the change ADDS and it never builds
/// the state of a chain the change KEEPS: a kept chain's state MOVES inside
/// the audio thread, from its position in the old array to its position in
/// the new one, and the move is a `core::mem::replace` and not a copy.
/// Revision 14 said that `configure` copied every kept chain's state across,
/// which Appendix A forbids and which no `Clone` impl of this type allows.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct ChainState {
    /// The identity of this chain, which `ChainTopology::strip` names.
    strip: StripId,
    /// The capture path, or `None` for a bus and for a track that is not
    /// armed. **An `rtrb` end cannot exist without its ring**, so a
    /// non-optional field here would put one ring pair on every one of the
    /// B86 strips and the ring count of section 5.5 would be wrong by the 16
    /// buses (critic CR on the ring arithmetic).
    writer: Option<DiskWriter>,
    /// The playback path, or `None` for a bus.
    reader: Option<DiskReader>,
    trim: GainState,
    pre_fader: ArrayVec<SlotState, MAX_SLOTS>,
    fader: GainState,
    post_fader: ArrayVec<SlotState, MAX_SLOTS>,
    meter: MeterState,
    /// The meter-reset generation this strip last acted on. `GraphState`
    /// holds one `ChainState` per strip, so this field is the per-strip
    /// array of last-seen values that section 7.3 needs. It sits here and
    /// not on `MeterState`, because `MeterState` is a `duet-dsp` type and
    /// `Generation` is a `duet-engine` type (PG20).
    reset_seen: Generation,
    /// The `PlaybackStarved` run of this strip.
    starved: FaultRun,
    /// The `CaptureOverflow` run of this strip.
    overflow: FaultRun,
    /// The `CaptureShortfall` run of this strip.
    ///
    /// **The three fields above are the per-track, per-condition fault
    /// latch** (critic C21-1). Section 12.4 states the arithmetic: at B1's 32
    /// tracks and B7's cycle rate an unlatched per-track fault is up to
    /// twelve thousand records a second, and `ChainState` is the one value
    /// this design holds per strip on the audio thread, so the latch lives
    /// here and nowhere else. Revision 21 stated the remedy in a doc comment
    /// and declared no field for it.
    shortfall: FaultRun,
}

/// One per-condition fault run of one chain.
///
/// `open` is the latch bit and `frames` is the running total of the whole run
/// of cycles, which is the number `EngineFault` carries (critic C21-1).
///
/// **`GraphRunner::run` owns all four transitions.** It opens a run on the
/// first cycle a condition holds, it adds that cycle's frame count on every
/// cycle the run stays open, it pushes NOTHING while a run is open, and it
/// closes the run and pushes ONE `EngineFault` on the first cycle the
/// condition stops. **A run also closes at B136 frames**, so a condition that
/// never stops still reports on a bounded period instead of never; that is
/// the Responsive half of the same rule, and a latch with no cap would trade
/// a flood for a silence.
///
/// It holds two plain scalars, it owns no heap, and it takes no lock, so it
/// is an audio-reachable leaf and not a root of its own (section 5.7, TH1).
/// `configure` builds every field closed, at `open` false and `frames` zero.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct FaultRun { open: bool, frames: u32 }

/// The running state of one slot. One variant per `SlotKind`.
///
/// **Every arm is inline, and the spread is intended.** Revision 11 boxed the
/// equalizer arm to satisfy `variant_size_differences`, which put one
/// allocation and one free inside the cycle: migration rule 2 builds the
/// default state of a new kind and migration rule 3 clears a dropped slot,
/// and both run on the audio thread inside `GraphRunner::run`. TH1 forbids
/// both (critic CR-2). **Audio-owned state never holds a heap type**, which
/// PG26 now reads from the section 5.7 block.
///
/// The enum therefore carries the one `variant_size_differences` refusal of
/// the audio path. The arm spread is bounded by B51, which PG24 prints and
/// PG25 measures, and every migration is a copy of at most B51 bytes inside
/// a budget of B8.
///
/// It derives no `Copy`. `BiquadState` and the five other state types are all
/// `Copy`, so VR5 would demand the derive at B51 bytes; the type refuses it
/// because a slot state is the identity the audio thread owns for the life of
/// the chain, and Appendix B.1 carries both expectations.
#[expect(
    variant_size_differences,
    reason = "audio-owned state stays inline; the arm spread is intended and bounded by B51"
)]
#[expect(
    missing_copy_implementations,
    reason = "one slot state is B51 bytes and it is the identity the audio thread owns for the \
              life of the chain, so a `Copy` derive would hide a copy of that size at every \
              migration site"
)]
#[derive(Debug)]
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
pub enum SlotState {
    /// One biquad section. A high-pass needs no state of its own, so the
    /// arm holds the `duet-dsp` biquad directly and no seventh state type
    /// exists to keep in step with it (PR M-03).
    HighPass(BiquadState),
    Equalizer(EqualizerState),
    Compressor(CompressorState),
    Gate(GateState),
    DeEsser(DeEsserState),
    /// The look-ahead limiter of the master chain. PR MA-02 makes it a MUST
    /// and contract 5.2 draws its gain reduction bar.
    Limiter(LimiterState),
    /// The state holds coefficients and a pool handle, never the buffer.
    Delay(DelayState),
    /// The same shape. PR M-04 makes a reverb bus a MUST.
    Reverb(ReverbState),
}
```

Both slot lists and the send list are an `ArrayVec` at B45 and B46, so no heap allocation happens on
the audio thread. A closed enum gives static dispatch and no `Box<dyn Trait>`.

#### The buffer pool

**Decision: a slot state holds no audio buffer. One `BufferPool` per project holds every long
buffer, and `GraphState` owns it on the audio thread** (critic R5).

```rust
/// A preallocated set of long audio buffers. One pool serves one project.
///
/// It derives `Debug` and nothing else. No published type holds one, so no
/// container is ever forced to derive `Clone` or `PartialEq` over it.
///
/// **Every allocation happens off the audio thread**, at `configure` time.
/// The audio thread receives the whole pool through the B105 handoff queue
/// and never grows it, never shrinks it, and never drops it; `basedrop`
/// defers the free to the collector thread (section 5.5).
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct BufferPool {
    /// One delay line per B47 slot, each one B49 bytes.
    delays: Box<[PoolBuffer]>,
    /// One reverb tail per B48 slot, each one B50 bytes.
    reverbs: Box<[PoolBuffer]>,
    /// One look-ahead line per B120 slot, each one B121 bytes.
    ///
    /// **It is a third class and not a delay slot** (critic C20-N3). A
    /// `LimiterState` takes a `PoolSlot` and revision 20 stated no class for
    /// it, so `configure` had no rule to write and `PoolExhausted { kind }`
    /// keyed on a class no arithmetic counted. A limiter needs a few
    /// milliseconds of look-ahead and a delay slot is B49, which is far above
    /// the need, so the cheaper answer is a class sized for the job.
    limiters: Box<[PoolBuffer]>,
    /// Bit k is set when slot k is free. B47 plus B48 plus B120 sits below
    /// the bit width of a `u64`, so one word covers the whole pool.
    free: u64,
}

/// One long audio buffer of the pool, with the channel count it was sized for.
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct PoolBuffer {
    samples: Box<[f32]>,
    channels: ChannelIndex,
}

/// A handle into the pool. A `SlotSpec` holds one; it never holds a buffer.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct PoolSlot(u16);

// in duet-engine
/// The audio thread's owned pool, behind a hand-written `Debug`.
///
/// `missing_debug_implementations` is denied workspace-wide, and
/// `GraphState` derives `Debug`, so every field of `GraphState` must carry
/// one. **`basedrop` 0.1.3 implements `Debug` for neither `Owned<T>` nor
/// `Shared<T>`**: `src/owned.rs` declares `Deref`, `DerefMut`, `Clone`, and
/// `Drop` and nothing else, and `src/shared.rs` declares `Deref`, `Clone`,
/// and `Drop`. That is the answer revision 14 left for chunk C3 to obtain, it
/// is recorded here, and **no chunk may delete this wrapper**. Its `Debug`
/// prints the pool's class counts and no buffer.
///
/// **The pool is built once per open stream and it is never rebuilt**
/// (critic CR-18). B47, B48, B49, B50, B120, and B121 are each a fixed
/// number, so one
/// pool is B52 bytes whatever the topology is; a topology change writes a
/// `PoolSlot` index into a `SlotSpec` and allocates nothing. Revision 14 put
/// a whole new pool in every handoff, which made two pools live at once for
/// no gain.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
pub struct PoolHandle(Owned<BufferPool>);

impl core::fmt::Debug for PoolHandle {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct("PoolHandle").finish_non_exhaustive()
    }
}

/// A position in the audio thread's chain-state array.
///
/// It is not a `NodeIndex`: a node index addresses the published topological
/// order, and this addresses the state array that `GraphState` owns.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct ChainIndex(u16);

/// Where one position of the new chain-state array gets its state.
///
/// It is `Copy`, it is the size the PG24 table prints for it, and the audio
/// thread reads it once per position of one migration. A tag sits beside the
/// `ChainIndex`, because a `u16` carries no spare bit pattern.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum ChainSource {
    /// `configure` built this position's state off the audio thread.
    Adopt,
    /// The state moves out of this position of the array the audio thread
    /// holds now.
    Keep(ChainIndex),
}

/// One position of the audio thread's chain-state array.
///
/// **It is the plan and the destination at once.** `configure` builds the new
/// array off the audio thread: every ADDED position carries `Adopt` with its
/// state already in `state`, and every KEPT position carries `Keep(index)`
/// with `state` at `None`. The audio thread then writes
/// `new[i].state = old[k].state.take()` for each `Keep`, which MOVES the kept
/// state and leaves `None` behind. No value is copied, nothing is allocated,
/// and nothing is freed (critic CR-17).
///
/// **The plan is a struct and not an enum on purpose.** An enum with one arm
/// holding a `ChainState` and one holding an index carries a spread that
/// `clippy::large_enum_variant` refuses, and the one suppression that would
/// cover it is a lint expectation that the layout may leave unfulfilled. The
/// `Option` here is a standard-library enum, so no lint of this workspace
/// reads it and the design needs no suppression at all.
///
/// A `state` that is still `None` when the cycle runs is a malformed plan.
/// Section 5.6 states what the runner does with one, and it is a named fault
/// and never a panic.
///
/// `reported` is the LATCH of that fault (critic C19-W25). `configure` clears
/// it for every position of every array it builds, and the runner sets it
/// when it pushes one `EngineFault::ChainSlotVacant`, so a vacant position
/// reports once per topology and not once per cycle. An unlatched report is
/// about 375 faults each second at B7, which fills B34, then B29, and then
/// passes B39.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct ChainSlot { source: ChainSource, state: Option<ChainState>, reported: bool }

/// The audio thread's owned chain-state array, behind a hand-written `Debug`.
///
/// **`configure` builds the array off the audio thread**, with a ring already
/// allocated for every chain the change adds and a `ChainSource::Keep` for
/// every chain it keeps, and the audio thread adopts it through the B105
/// handoff. The
/// audio thread never grows the array, never shrinks it, and never frees it:
/// the retired array drops into `basedrop`, which releases it and every
/// `ChainState`, `DiskReader`, and `DiskWriter` still inside it on the engine
/// handoff thread (TH5). Revision 13 named no mechanism for a length change
/// at all (critic CR-16).
///
/// It writes `Debug` by hand for the reason `PoolHandle` states.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
pub struct ChainSetHandle(Owned<Box<[ChainSlot]>>);

impl core::fmt::Debug for ChainSetHandle {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct("ChainSetHandle").finish_non_exhaustive()
    }
}

/// The audio thread's read end of the B105 handoff ring, behind a
/// hand-written `Debug`.
///
/// It exists for the reason `PoolHandle` exists: `GraphState` derives
/// `Debug`, `missing_debug_implementations` is denied, and `basedrop` 0.1.3
/// implements `Debug` for neither of its smart pointers. A bare
/// `Owned<Consumer<GraphHandoff>>` field on `GraphState` therefore does not
/// build, which the roster compile proves.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
pub struct HandoffReader { consumer: Owned<Consumer<GraphHandoff>> }

impl core::fmt::Debug for HandoffReader {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct("HandoffReader").finish_non_exhaustive()
    }
}

/// One owned handoff from the engine handoff thread to the audio thread, at
/// B105.
///
/// **It carries its own generation** (critic CR-20). The audio thread records
/// the generation of the last handoff it adopted, and section 5.6 compares
/// that record with `GraphChain::handoff_generation`, so the array the runner
/// holds can be proved to be the array the published topology names. Revision
/// 14 gated a first-in ring with a latest-value counter and the two could
/// disagree in silence.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct GraphHandoff {
    /// The generation this handoff belongs to.
    generation: Generation,
    /// The new array. It holds no pool: one pool serves the open stream.
    slots: ChainSetHandle,
}

/// The strip order one chain-state array holds, one `StripId` per position,
```
