```rust
/// and the ring pairs that array holds in total.
///
/// The engine handoff thread owns it and it is the only thing that thread
/// needs to know about the audio thread's array. It names an ORDER and a
/// COUNT and never a state, so building a plan from it reads nothing the
/// audio thread holds (critic CR-17). `ChainTopology::strip` is the identity
/// of every chain, a bus chain included, so one `StripId` addresses every
/// position and no conversion exists to get wrong.
///
/// `pairs` is the first term of the B56 formula. **It counts EVERY allocated
/// pair**: the reader pair and the writer pair of every chain that has one, a
/// bus included when a bus has rings, and the device bridge pair. One owner
/// allocates them all, so the count is complete by construction (critic
/// C15-1). `configure` adds the pairs the change would ADD and refuses past
/// B57 before it allocates a byte, which is the whole reason this count is a
/// field and not a derivation (critic CR-18).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct ChainLayout { strips: Box<[StripId]>, pairs: u32 }

/// Everything `configure` reads. The core builds it on the core thread.
///
/// **This type carries the whole request, and it is not the whole input**
/// (critic WARNING on I6). `GraphConfigurator::configure` reads this value,
/// `self.layout`, `self.handoff_retry`, and the free-slot count of
/// `self.handoffs`; its own doc comment names all four. This type carries no
/// global, no engine state, and no value the audio thread owns.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct ConfigureRequest {
    /// One entry per strip of the new graph, in the new order.
    chains: Box<[ChainTopology]>,
    /// The new topological order.
    order: Box<[NodeIndex]>,
    /// The stream the rings are sized for.
    stream: StreamInfo,
    /// The generation this configuration publishes.
    generation: Generation,
}

/// What one `configure` produced.
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Configured {
    /// The topology to publish once the handoff is in the ring.
    topology: GraphChain,
    /// The handoff to push at B105.
    handoff: GraphHandoff,
    /// The layout the audio thread holds once it adopts the handoff.
    layout: ChainLayout,
}

/// What the core asks the engine handoff thread to do, at B109.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum ConfigureCommand {
    /// Configure the graph this request describes.
    ///
    /// **It is boxed**, so this arm and the `Open` arm are both one pointer
    /// wide and the enum carries no `variant_size_differences` spread. The
    /// roster compile proved the unboxed shape trips the lint; this command
    /// crosses a channel off the audio path, so one allocation per topology
    /// change costs nothing that TH1 or B110 bounds.
    Apply(Box<ConfigureRequest>),
    /// Open a stream: build the first `GraphState`, call `AudioBackend::open`
    /// with it, then call `AudioBackend::start`.
    ///
    /// **This is how the thread learns that a stream exists** (critic C15-8).
    /// Revision 15 gave the thread the duty and no input: no field reached an
    /// `AudioBackend`, and no command carried a `StreamRequest`. This arm
    /// carries the request, and the core sends it once the device is chosen.
    /// The thread replaces `handoffs` and `topology` on every open, which is
    /// what a restart needs.
    Open(Box<StreamRequest>),
    /// Stop the stream: call `AudioBackend::stop`, then drop the last
    /// `GraphState` the stream held.
    ///
    /// **This is how a stream closes, and it is the ONE caller of
    /// `AudioBackend::stop`** (critic C19-7). Revision 19 gave the core the
    /// sentence "the core closes the stream" in the shutdown order and in
    /// the `Reset` rule, and the core owns no `AudioBackend`: this thread's
    /// `backend` field is the one owner, `stop` takes `&mut self`, and no
    /// command carried the request. The duty therefore had no caller that
    /// could perform it. The core now sends this arm, and the thread that
    /// opened the stream is the thread that stops it, which is the order
    /// `cpal` needs and which keeps one owner of the device on every path.
    ///
    /// **It answers with `EngineEvent::StreamClosed`**, so the core learns
    /// that the audio thread has stopped and only then sends `Reset`. B116
    /// bounds the wait and section 5.12 states what an expiry does.
    Close,
    /// Drop any pending attempt and forget the layout.
    ///
    /// **The core sends it only after `EngineEvent::StreamClosed` arrives**,
    /// which is the order that makes forgetting the layout safe (critic
    /// WARNING on `Reset`, critic C19-7). A closed stream means the audio
    /// thread has stopped, the last `GraphState` has been dropped, and its
    /// array holds nothing, so an empty layout and an empty array agree. A
    /// project close sends `Close` first. Every engine state that is not
    /// `Running` is reached by a `Close` or by a stream that never opened,
    /// `Faulted` included, so the same order holds on every path (critic
    /// WR-27).
    Reset,
    /// End the loop.
    ///
    /// **It is the one message that stops the engine handoff thread**
    /// (critic C22I-3). The thread runs `Collector::collect`, then
    /// `Collector::try_cleanup`, sends `EngineEvent::HandoffStopped` on the
    /// B138 channel, drops `backend`, and returns. Revision 22 gave step 8 of
    /// section 9.5 rule 8 a wait for that event and gave no command and no
    /// dropped sender that could produce it, so the loop never ended, the
    /// wait always reached expiry, and every quit paid B119 in full.
    ///
    /// **The core sends it after `EngineEvent::StreamClosed` and after
    /// `Reset`**, so the backend is stopped and the layout is forgotten
    /// before the thread that owns both goes away.
    Stop,
}

/// The engine handoff thread's own state. One exists per engine.
///
/// **It is the one writer of the published `GraphChain` and the one producer
/// of the B105 ring** (section 5.7), and it runs `configure`. No allocation
/// of a topology change therefore reaches the GPUI foreground thread, which
/// revision 14 made the site of a 94 MB allocation inside an immediate verb
/// (critic CR-19).
///
/// It writes `Debug` by hand, because `basedrop::Collector` implements none.
pub struct GraphConfigurator {
    /// **The one owner of the audio backend** (critic C16-7).
    ///
    /// `ConfigureCommand::Open` calls `AudioBackend::open` and then
    /// `AudioBackend::start` through this field, and both methods take
    /// `&mut self`, so the value needs one owner and section 5.5 names it
    /// here. **The core constructs it and moves it into this thread at
    /// spawn**, which is the one moment the core touches a backend value;
    /// the thread table forbids the core from touching a device after that.
    /// **This thread drops it**, when its loop ends, and the drop closes the
    /// `cpal` stream on the thread that opened it. Revision 16 gave the
    /// thread the duty and gave no declaration the value.
    backend: Box<dyn AudioBackend>,
    /// The `basedrop` collector. One pass of the loop drains it (TH5).
    collector: Collector,
    /// The B34 fault queue this thread drains once per pass (section 12.4).
    ///
    /// Revision 22 gave section 12.4 step 2 to this thread and declared the
    /// handle on `EngineProcess` alone, so the one consumer of the fault
    /// queue held no end of it (critic C22I-1). The third clone is moved
    /// into the cpal error callback at `ConfigureCommand::Open`, which TH11
    /// governs and which is a closure and not a field.
    faults: Shared<FaultQueue>,
    /// The read end of the configure channel at B109. `recv_timeout` gives
    /// the loop the B108 deadline that the drain needs (section 5.8).
    commands: Receiver<ConfigureCommand>,
    /// The one write end of the B105 handoff ring. One writer exists because
    /// one thread owns this value.
    handoffs: Producer<GraphHandoff>,
    /// The one write end of the published topology (section 5.8). Revision 14
    /// gave it to the core, which is the GPUI foreground thread in the
    /// application (critic CR-19).
    topology: Input<GraphChain>,
    /// The layout the last accepted handoff left on the audio thread.
    layout: ChainLayout,
    /// The topology change this thread has not built yet, or `None`.
    ///
    /// **Latest wins.** A second `ConfigureCommand::Apply` replaces it, so
    /// the audio follows the newest topology and no refusal travels to the
    /// core (critic CR on the unbounded loop).
    pending_request: Option<ConfigureRequest>,
    /// The configuration this thread built and has not pushed, or `None`.
    /// **Every wait runs here**, on this thread, so no wait and no
    /// allocation reaches a thread that paints (critic CR-15, WR-27).
    handoff_retry: Option<Configured>,
    /// Consecutive passes on which the B105 slot was not free, against B95.
    /// The period between passes is B108, so the cap is a time as well as a
    /// count.
    attempts: u8,
    /// The write end of the engine-to-core event channel at B138.
    ///
    /// **It is the carrier of every `EngineEvent` this thread reports**
    /// (critic C22I-1). Revision 22 gave this thread the fault drain of
    /// section 12.4 step 2, the `GraphConfigured` report, the
    /// `ConfigureRefused` report, `StreamClosed` and `HandoffStopped`, and
    /// declared no sender of any kind, so five stated duties had no value
    /// that could perform them. TH13 now holds every such duty against one
    /// row of the carrier table.
    events: EngineLink,
    /// Every event `try_send` refused, at B147.
    ///
    /// **While it is not empty this thread drains no further fault**, so the
    /// backpressure of a slow core reaches the B34 queue, whose own rule
    /// refuses the newest fault and counts it (section 5.8). On a FULL list
    /// the thread performs one blocking send of the oldest event, which is
    /// legal here and never on the audio thread, so no event of this channel
    /// is lost; revision 23 gave this thread one slot, and a refused
    /// `EngineEvent::GraphConfigured` would have stranded a topology change
    /// for the rest of the session with no user message (critic C23I-W5).
    ///
    /// **The terminal send is a BLOCKING send** (critic C23I-W6).
    /// `EngineEvent::HandoffStopped` is the last act of this loop, so a
    /// refused `try_send` would have no next pass and B119 would reach
    /// expiry on a thread that finished its work correctly.
    pending_events: ArrayVec<EngineEvent, MAX_PENDING_EVENTS>,
}

impl core::fmt::Debug for GraphConfigurator {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct("GraphConfigurator").finish_non_exhaustive()
    }
}
```

**The pool is built once and the chain array is handed over per position.** Revision 3 let
`configure` assign a slot off the audio thread while migration returned one on it, which gave one
free list two writers. Revision 4 put the pool inside `ChainTopology`, which is per track and which
derives `Clone` and `Eq` that `BufferPool` does not have. Revision 14 rebuilt the whole pool and the
whole chain-state set on every change, which needed a copy of state that only the audio thread holds
and which made every ring live twice (critic CR-17, CR-18). All three are gone.

#### The five steps of one topology change

Each step names the thread it runs on, and no step runs on a thread the step before it used.

1. **The verb runs on the core thread and returns inside B5.** It validates the change against B86,
   B90, and B57 with arithmetic alone, it changes the session document or the mix document IN
   MEMORY through `Arc::make_mut`, it emits its own `CoreEvent`, and it sends one
   `ConfigureCommand::Apply` on the configure channel at B109. **It serializes nothing and it opens
   no file**: a save is a separate path on a job thread (section 4.10), and the thread table
   forbids blocking input and output on the GPUI foreground thread (critic WARNING on the document
   write).
   **It allocates nothing above B110** (critic CR-19): the largest value it builds is the
   `ConfigureRequest`, which is B86 times the size the PG24 table prints for `ChainTopology` plus
   B86 times the size it prints for `NodeIndex`, and that sum sits under B110 at every project the
   product allows. TH3 carries that bound, so a later verb cannot put a larger allocation on this
   thread without
   breaking a stated rule. `Verb::TrackSetArmed` and `Verb::MixAddBus` therefore both answer at
   once, which `VerbOutcome::Applied` requires and which revision 14 could not do.
2. **`configure` runs on the engine handoff thread** (section 5.7). It reads four things and
   nothing else: the `ConfigureRequest`, `self.layout`, `self.handoff_retry`, and the free-slot
   count of `self.handoffs`.

   **The LOOP does not build while a handoff is un-adopted, and it refuses nothing** (critic CR on
   the peak formula and critic CR on the unbounded loop). Revision 15 first advanced `ChainLayout`
   at push time and let the next command build at once. The audio thread adopts up to one cycle
   later, so in that window the layout named the NEW array while the audio thread still held the
   OLD one, and a second build allocated against a count that omitted the old rings.
   `rtrb::Producer::slots` answers the question exactly (`rtrb-0.4.0/src/lib.rs:364`): the ring is
   capacity one, so a free-slot count of one means the audio thread has POPPED the last handoff,
   and the drain rule applies a handoff in full in the same step it pops it, so popped means
   adopted.

   **A wait is a wait and never a refusal.** An arriving `ConfigureCommand::Apply` goes into
   `GraphConfigurator::pending_request`, latest wins, and the loop builds it on the first pass
   where the slot is free. **No refusal travels to the core on this path**, so no re-send can
   answer one and the refuse-and-resend loop that a returned `HandoffRetryPending` would open does
   not exist. `ConfigError::HandoffRetryPending` stays a declared error of the function, for a
   caller that ignores the rule; the loop never produces one.

   **The wait is capped.** `attempts` counts consecutive passes on which the slot is not free.
   Past B95 the thread reports `EngineFault::HandoffBusy`, drops `pending_request` into
   `basedrop`, and stops building until a `ConfigureCommand::Reset` arrives, which is the bound
   that revision 15 lost when it moved the cap off the push (critic CR on the unbounded loop). The
   period between passes is B108, so the cap is a stated time as well as a stated count. It refuses first and allocates second: `PoolExhausted` past B47, B48, or B120,
   `StripBudgetExceeded` past B86, `ParamBudgetExceeded` past B90, and `RingBudgetExceeded` past
   B57, each one computed from the request before a byte is allocated. It then allocates one ring
   pair for each chain the change ADDS, writes every `PoolSlot` into the matching `SlotSpec` from
   the fixed table, and builds one `Box<[ChainSlot]>` of the new length: `ChainSource::Adopt` with
   the state it just built for each ADDED chain, and `ChainSource::Keep(ChainIndex)` with no state
   for each chain the layout already holds. The whole array goes inside one `basedrop::Owned`. B27 bounds this step and `EngineFault::AllocationSlow` reports an
   overrun; a thread that paints nothing can carry that bound.
3. **The engine handoff thread pushes the `GraphHandoff` at B105 and then publishes the new
   `GraphChain`.** The push happens first, so the audio thread never sees a raised
   `handoff_generation` with no handoff behind it. **The push cannot meet a full ring**, because
   step 2 built nothing until the slot was free and this thread is the one producer, so
   `hand_off` answers `Ok(Some(generation))` on every call the loop makes.
   `ConfigError::PoolHandoffBusy` stays the declared error for a caller that skips the slot test.
   `configure` never waits and no thread that paints is involved at any point (critic CR-15).
4. **The audio thread drains the ring at the top of the cycle and applies every handoff in order**
   (critic CR-20). Section 5.6 states the drain rule and the generation proof. For each `Keep(k)`
   position of the new array it takes the state out of position `k` of the old array with
   `Option::take`, which leaves `None` there. It then swaps the new `ChainSetHandle` into
   `GraphState` and lets the old one drop. **The audio thread never allocates
   and never frees on this path**: a move is a move, and the retired array leaves through
   `basedrop`.
5. **The engine handoff thread reports the outcome, and there are three outcomes.**

   **Outcome one, the push succeeds.** It advances its `ChainLayout`, clears `pending_request` and
   `attempts`, and sends `EngineEvent::GraphConfigured { generation }`.

   **Outcome two, the wait passes B95.** It sends `EngineEvent::Fault` with
   `EngineFault::HandoffBusy` and drops `pending_request` into `basedrop`.

   **Outcome three, step 2 refuses the request on a budget.** `PoolExhausted`,
   `RingBudgetExceeded`, `StripBudgetExceeded`, `ParamBudgetExceeded`, and `Mix` are decided by
   arithmetic before a byte is allocated, so the thread has built nothing and holds nothing. It
   drops `pending_request` into `basedrop`, it clears `attempts`, and it sends
   `EngineEvent::ConfigureRefused(cause)` with the `ConfigError` step 2 raised. **The core then
   clears `pending_configure` and sends nothing**, so a refusal is answered once and never
   re-sent. Section 12.4 holds the CONFIGURE table, which gives each refusal a user message.
   Revision 16 recorded this outcome in its closure appendix and wrote none of it at this site
   (critic C16-4). The core then closes the stream and marks the engine
   `Faulted`, in that order, and only then sends `ConfigureCommand::Reset`; forgetting the layout
   while the audio thread still holds its array would let the next `configure` build a whole new
   set beside a live one, which is the whole-set replacement this design forbids (critic WARNING on
   `Reset`).

**What the user does after a refusal, and whether the change is lost** (concern N-7). Nothing is
lost. The document already changed in step 1 and the user already sees it; only the audio follows
later. A second `Apply` that arrives while one waits replaces
`GraphConfigurator::pending_request`, latest wins, so the audio follows the newest topology and
never a stale one. **`DuetCore::pending_configure` covers one case only**: a full B109 channel, on
which `try_send` fails. It never answers a
`HandoffRetryPending`, because the loop produces none (critic CR on the unbounded loop).

**The re-send has one trigger and one cap, and both are stated here** (critic C16-4).
**The trigger set is `EngineEvent::GraphConfigured` alone.** On that event, and only on that event,
the core makes ONE `try_send` of whatever `pending_configure` holds; a send that succeeds clears the
field and a send that fails leaves it.

**Four events CLEAR the field, and the two new ones close a state that no event could drain**
(critic C20-W1). `EngineEvent::GraphConfigured` clears it on a successful send.
`EngineEvent::ConfigureRefused` clears it and sends nothing. **`EngineFault::HandoffBusy` clears
it**, because the engine handoff thread then stops building until a `ConfigureCommand::Reset`
arrives and no `GraphConfigured` can follow, so a request set inside that window would wait for a
trigger that cannot happen. **`EngineEvent::StreamClosed` clears it**, because a
`ConfigureRequest` carries a `stream: StreamInfo` and a queued request that names a closed stream
would size rings for a device that is gone; the first `GraphConfigured` after a restart would send
it. Revision 20 carried both states, and each one either lost a change in silence or replayed a
request against the wrong device. **The cap is the field itself**: it holds at most one
request, latest wins, so one send is in flight at a time and a re-send produces no event that
triggers another send of the same request. The engine handoff thread drains B109 once per B108, so
the mailbox empties inside one drain period after the channel has room. **On
`EngineEvent::ConfigureRefused` the core clears `pending_configure` and sends nothing**, because a
budget refusal is a fact about the request and a second send of the same request would be refused
again. Revision 16 made both events re-send, which is the unbounded producer the Elastic property
forbids. Past B95 the engine state becomes `Faulted`, and the FAULT table of
the section 12.4 fault table holds the row for `EngineFault::HandoffBusy` (critic C21I-W4).

#### The engine handoff thread, and what it owns

**Decision: one thread owns `configure`, the B105 producer, the `GraphChain` publication, and the
`basedrop` collector.** One thread means one writer of each, which is why no rule here needs a lock.

Its loop runs three things in a fixed order, and it never runs a deferred verb.

1. **It drains the collector.** `Collector::collect` is `while self.collect_one() {}`
   (`basedrop-0.1.3/src/collector.rs:238`). `collect_one` drops one node, and dropping a node that
   holds another `Owned` appends that inner node to the same queue, which the same loop then picks
   up. **One drain therefore releases a whole nest**: a retired `ChainSetHandle`, every
   `ChainState` still inside it, and every `Owned` ring end of every `DiskReader` and `DiskWriter`
   go in one pass.
2. **It serves at most one `ConfigureCommand`**, or one retry of the pending `Configured`.
3. **It parks on a bounded receive of B108**, so the drain runs at least once per B108 while
   nothing arrives. **It drains B109 rather than taking one command**: every waiting
   `ConfigureCommand` is read and the last `Apply` wins, so a burst costs one build and not one
   build each (critic CONCERN on the B109 service rate).

**What survives a stream stop, and what a restart rebuilds** (critic WARNING on the stop and the
restart). A stop destroys everything the audio thread held: the backend drops the callback state,
so `GraphState`, the pool, the chain array, and the B105 consumer all go, and the ring itself dies
with its two ends, an un-adopted handoff inside it included. The engine handoff thread keeps only
its `Collector`, and the core keeps only its documents. A restart therefore builds a new pool, a
new first chain array, and a new B105 pair, and `ConfigureCommand::Reset` before the restart is
what makes the empty layout agree with the empty array.

**The shutdown order, which a leak makes load-bearing** (critic WARNING on the collector).
`basedrop` 0.1.3 states it at `src/collector.rs:160`: a dropped `Collector` LEAKS every allocation
still in its queue and its own structures, and `try_cleanup` is the only clean end. At B55 that is
about 104 MB per project close. The engine therefore shuts down in five steps, and **every step that
touches the device runs on the engine handoff thread, because that thread owns the backend**
(critic C19-7). (1) The core sends `ConfigureCommand::Close` and starts B116 on its own clock, and the engine
handoff thread calls `AudioBackend::stop`, so the audio thread stops. (2) The SAME thread then drops
the last `GraphState`, which queues the pool and the last array; it can do that because `stop` has
returned, which is `cpal`'s own guarantee that the callback will not run again. (3) The core drops every
`basedrop::Handle` clone it holds, which it does when `EngineEvent::StreamClosed` arrives. (4) The
engine handoff thread drains the collector with `Collector::collect`. (5) It calls
`Collector::try_cleanup` and reports a refusal as `EngineFault::HandoffBusy`.

**B116 is a REPORT and never a cancel, and the party that measures it is not the party that
waits** (critic C20-4). `AudioBackend::stop` is a blocking device teardown, and a blocking call on
macOS and on Linux cannot be interrupted without a second thread, which is the rule B117 and B118
already state for a blocking file call. Revision 20 gave B116 an `std::time::Instant` read on the
thread that is inside the call: if `stop` returns, the elapsed time is known and nothing is left to
do, and if `stop` hangs, the next statement never runs. The prescribed expiry action was unsound as
well, because dropping `GraphState` while the callback may still run releases values the callback
reads.

**The core therefore measures it, because the core is waiting for a MESSAGE and not inside a
call.** The core starts B116 when it sends `ConfigureCommand::Close`. If `EngineEvent::StreamClosed`
has not arrived at expiry, the core raises `EngineFault::DeviceStalled`, moves the engine
to `EngineState::Faulted`, and refuses every `ConfigureCommand::Open` until `StreamClosed` arrives.
The engine handoff thread is untouched: it stays inside `stop`, it drops the last `GraphState` only
after `stop` returns, and it sends `StreamClosed` whenever the device finally answers. **A device
that hangs therefore holds ITS OWN stream closed and holds nothing else**, and the user is told
inside B116 rather than left with a window that reports nothing. **B18 is the same shape**: the core
measures the open from `ConfigureCommand::Open`, because no channel receive sits on the handoff
thread's `open` path and the section 5.7 thread table holds no thread named "the engine thread".

**The quit path is bounded too, at B119** (section 9.5). It joins the engine handoff thread, and on
expiry it abandons the thread and exits. `Collector::try_cleanup` then does not run and the
operating system reclaims the bytes, which is why a B55 leak costs nothing at process exit and costs
B55 inside a live session.

**Revision 19 gave step 1 and step 2 to two threads that could not perform them** (critic C19-7).
It said that the core closes the stream, and the core holds no `AudioBackend`; it said that "the
thread that owns the stream" drops `GraphState`, and the value the audio callback holds is dropped
by the backend when the stream closes, on the thread that called `stop`. One thread now owns the
device, the stop, and the drop, which is the same single-owner rule that made the handoff need no
lock.

**A refusal has two causes and the report names both** (critic C16-W4).
`basedrop-0.1.3/src/collector.rs:328-341` returns `Err(self)` when the handle count is non-zero
**or** when the allocation count is non-zero, and the crate's own doc at `collector.rs:304-305`
states the pair. Cause one is a `Handle` that outlived step 3. Cause two is an `Owned` or a
`Shared` that step 4 did not reach, which happens when a value was queued after `collect` began.
The thread therefore runs step 4 a second time before it reports, and it reports
`EngineFault::HandoffBusy` only when the second `try_cleanup` refuses as well. Revision 16 named
cause one alone, which sends a reader to the wrong place during a shutdown fault.

**Who builds a deferred value, and who drops the last one.** `basedrop::Owned::new` and
`basedrop::Shared::new` each take a `&Handle` (`basedrop-0.1.3/src/owned.rs:34`,
`src/shared.rs:41`), and a `Handle` is `Clone`, `Send`, and `Sync`. `GraphConfigurator` owns the one
`Collector` and hands a clone of its `Handle` to every thread that builds a deferred value, which
today is itself and the core (section 5.8, the `basedrop::Shared<T>` row). **The pool and the last
chain array are dropped at stream close**, by the thread that owns the stream and never by the audio
thread, and the drop queues them exactly as a migration does. The longest a retired array can wait is B108 plus B27, because step 2 is the one
   thing that can delay step 1 and B27 bounds it (critic WR-25). Revision 14 put the collector on
   the two job threads that also run an export render, which can hold one for minutes.

**How the pool reaches the audio thread, once** (critic WARNING on the pool path). The engine
handoff thread builds the whole first `GraphState` when the stream opens: the pool, the first
chain array, the B105 consumer inside `HandoffReader`, and the `Arc<ResetGenerations>` clone. It
hands that one value to the backend at **`AudioBackend::open`**, which is the method that takes a
`Box<dyn AudioProcess>`; `start` takes no argument and revision 15 named it (critic C15-8). `open`
moves it into the callback
state. **Nothing about the pool crosses B105**, because B105 carries a `GraphHandoff` and a
`GraphHandoff` holds no pool.

**Why the pool never travels.** `BufferPool` holds B47 delay buffers of B49 bytes, B48 reverb
buffers of B50 bytes, and B120 look-ahead buffers of B121 bytes. All six are fixed numbers, so one
pool is B52 bytes whatever the topology is (critic C21I-3).
A topology change writes a `PoolSlot` index into a `SlotSpec`; it resizes nothing. The pool is
therefore allocated once, when the stream opens, and the audio thread adopts it once beside the
first chain array. `configure` returns `ConfigError::PoolExhausted { kind }` when the new topology
asks for more buffers than B47, B48, **or B120** allows, and the refusal is **three sums over the
fixed table and not two** (critic C21I-3). `PoolSlot` is one `u16` index across all three classes and
`BufferPool::free` is one bit word, so a class the arithmetic does not count is not a missed refusal;
it is an aliased buffer on the audio thread.

**A buffer a new slot takes is cleared, and the clear is a write.** `configure` never assigns a
`PoolSlot` that a kept slot already holds, so only a newly assigned buffer needs clearing. The audio
thread clears it with one `slice::fill` inside the migration step. The largest single clear is B50,
which the cycle budget B8 carries.

#### Why B47 delay buffers, B48 reverb buffers, and B120 look-ahead buffers

The number is a product decision, not a memory decision. A vocal project uses send-based reverb on
two to four buses, which PR M-04 states, and an insert delay on a handful of lead tracks. The limit
exists to keep the mix legible, not to save bytes; the pool costs B52.

**B120 is the limiter class**, and PR MA-02 makes the master limiter a MUST, so at least one exists
in every project. B120 allows one per bus at the B1 part count plus the master, and B121 sizes one
for the B122 look-ahead. `SlotKind::Limiter` is the `kind` a `PoolExhausted` refusal carries for it,
so the enum already names all three classes and `configure` computes three sums rather than two
(critic C20-N3).

`ConfigError::PoolExhausted { kind }` maps to `GatewayError::PoolExhausted { kind }`, and the
CONFIGURE table of section 12.4 holds the one message. **This section writes no user string**
(critic C21I-W5): revision 21 carried a second wording here, which named a count and told the user to
hide a part, while section 12.4 named no number and told the user to remove a track. One string, one
home. The verb is refused before audio flows.

#### The ring buffers, counted per track state

Section 5.8 lists one ring per playback channel, one per capture channel, and one per device input
channel. A stereo armed track therefore needs four.

**Rings are allocated when a track enters the playable set, and released when it leaves.** The
playable set changes when a track is added, removed, hidden, shown, or armed. That is a topology
change, which runs on the engine handoff thread under B27. **A ring is allocated into a `ChainState`
that `configure` builds there, and it is released by the collector on that same thread when the
retired `ChainSetHandle` drops** (TH5). No ring is ever allocated or freed inside
`GraphRunner::run`, and none is allocated on a thread that paints (critic CR-19). **`Play` allocates
nothing**, so no transport action carries an allocation pause. **A migration allocates one ring pair
per ADDED chain and none for a kept chain**, because a kept chain's rings move with its state
(critic CR-18).

| Track state | Rings | Bytes at B53, 96 kHz, `f32`, stereo |
|---|---|---|
| Idle | 0 | 0 |
| Playing | 2 playback | B54 |
| Armed and playing | 2 playback, 2 capture | 2 times B54 |
| The device input bridge, once per device | 2 | B54 |

**The memory number at B1, and the formula B57 enforces.** The rings are one pair per playing
track, one more pair per armed track, and one pair for the device bridge. Each pair costs B54, and
B1 with B83 sets the counts: 32 playing pairs, 8 armed pairs, and 1 device pair is 41 pairs. Each
track also holds two slot lists of B45 states, and each state costs B51. One pool costs B52, once,
for the life of the stream. The steady total is B55.

**A bus contributes no ring, and the TYPE is what makes that true.** B86 is 48 strips and 16 of
them are buses, so a ring pair on every position would make the count 57 and not 41, and the steady
total alone would pass B57. `ChainState::reader` and `ChainState::writer` are therefore each an
`Option`, and a bus position carries `None` in both: an `rtrb` end cannot exist without its ring,
so a non-optional field would BE a ring. `ChainTopology::track` is an `Option<TrackId>` for the
same reason and at the same site.

**B56 is the peak of one migration, and it is a formula and not a guess** (critic CR-18). During a
migration the rings of the old array are all still live, because the retired array waits for the
next collector drain, and the rings of every ADDED chain are live beside them. Nothing else doubles:
one pool serves both arrays, and a kept chain's rings move rather than being rebuilt.

```text
peak = B52 + B54 * (ChainLayout::pairs + added pairs)
```

`ChainLayout::pairs` is the first term, and the definition is what makes it exact: **it counts
every ring pair this configurator has allocated and has not yet ACCOUNTED as released**, so it
carries the retired array that the collector has not drained as well as the array the audio thread
holds (critic WARNING on the retired term). **The count is bookkeeping and never an observation**
(concern N15-6): `Collector::collect` returns nothing, so the loop learns nothing about which node
it freed. The loop keeps the count true with two writes at two stated points: it adds the pairs of a
migration when it builds one, and it subtracts the pairs that migration retired on the first pass
AFTER the drain that follows adoption. That is sound because the audio thread queues its drop inside
the cycle that adopts it, and the loop drains before it builds.

**One owner allocates every pair**, so no ring is outside this count by construction (critic
C15-1). The loop drains before it builds,
so the subtraction is never late. Step 2 builds nothing while a handoff is un-adopted, so no second
build can read the count between those two writes. B107 bounds the added pairs of one MIGRATION. **The first configure of an open stream is not a
migration**: the old set is empty, so the added pairs are the whole set and the peak equals the
steady total, which is B55 (critic CONCERN on the first configure). At B1, B83, and B107 that is 9.0 plus 2.3 times 49,
which is B56. `configure` evaluates the same formula from the `ConfigureRequest` and the
`ChainLayout` before it allocates a byte, and it refuses past B57. Revision 14 rebuilt every ring on
every change, which made the true peak about 1.6 times B57 while B56 named the pool alone.

**`ConfigError::RingBudgetExceeded { requested_bytes }` is the one name for this refusal.**
`configure` returns `ConfigError`, so the variant belongs to that enum; `EngineError` wraps
`ConfigError` with `#[from]` (section 12.1), so a caller that holds an `EngineError` still sees the
cause, and no second variant exists. Revision 6 wrote both names in three places and a reader could
not tell which one `configure` returns (critic N11). **`requested_bytes` is the peak of the formula
above and not the steady total**, so the number the refusal carries is the number the bound
measures. It maps to `GatewayError::RingBudgetExceeded`, and the CONFIGURE table of section 12.4 holds the one
message. **This section writes no user string** (critic C21I-W5). The user interface names the track
count and offers the part filter.

#### How state migrates across a topology change

Two migrations exist, and they are not the same shape. **A change of the chain SET is a per-position
move.** **A change inside a kept chain is an in-place slot migration.** Revision 13 stated the second
and stated nothing for the first (critic CR-16). Revision 14 stated a first that needed a copy of
state only the audio thread holds (critic CR-17).

**Rule 0. The audio thread never resizes the chain array, and no other thread ever reads one
`ChainState`.** A strip the user adds or removes changes the length of `GraphChain::chains`, so the
length of the state array changes too. `configure` therefore builds a new `Box<[ChainSlot]>` of the
new length off the audio thread, and it fills each position in one of two ways.

- A position the change ADDS gets `ChainSource::Adopt` and the `ChainState` that `configure` just
  built, with its rings already allocated and its `PoolSlot` handles already written.
- A position the change KEEPS gets `ChainSource::Keep(ChainIndex)` and no state, where the index is
  that chain's position in the layout the audio thread holds now. `configure` reads that index out
  of `ChainLayout`, which names an order and holds no state.

At the generation check the audio thread walks the new array once. For each `Keep(k)` it writes
`old[k].state.take()` into that position's `state`, which MOVES the kept value and leaves `None` in
the old array. It leaves each `Adopt` position as it stands. It then swaps the new
`ChainSetHandle` into `GraphState` and drops the retired one, which now holds `None` at every kept
position and the retired state at every removed one. **Nothing is copied, nothing is allocated, and
nothing is freed on this thread.** The walk is bounded by B86, so it fits the cycle budget B8.

**Rule 1 is therefore true by construction.** A kept chain's filter history, meter hold, and gain
ramp are the same bytes after the migration, because the bytes moved and were never rebuilt. A user
who adds one aux send to one strip resets nothing on the other 47.

The in-place rules below then run over the chains the new array kept.

1. A slot whose `SlotId` and `SlotKind` are unchanged keeps its state. A filter does not reset when
   the user adds an unrelated send.
2. A slot whose `SlotKind` changed resets to the default state for the new kind. **The reset is a
   write and never an allocation**, because every arm of `SlotState` is inline (section 15.2). A
   slot that needs a long buffer takes a `PoolSlot` handle that `configure` already assigned, and
   the audio thread clears that buffer with one `slice::fill`. A reset is audible, so the user
   interface shows the change as a replacement, not as an edit.
3. A slot that the new topology drops has its state cleared in place. **The clear frees nothing**,
   for the same reason: the arm owns no heap, and the pool handle it returns is an index. TH1,
   PG26, PG26b, and PG26c all hold on this path (critic CR-2).
4. A slot that the new topology adds takes the default state from the array `ChainState` already
   holds. Its `PoolSlot` is the one `configure` wrote into the `SlotSpec`.

Rule 4 is why no allocation is needed inside a kept chain: the slot array is full-size from the
start, the pool is preallocated, and the topology selects a prefix and a handle. Rule 0 is why no
allocation is needed for the array itself: every added position arrives built and every kept
position is a move.

**Parameter values do not travel in the topology.** They travel in `ParamSnapshot` through its own
triple buffer, addressed by `ParamId` (section 5.8). A fader move publishes no topology and resets
no filter.

#### The two configure functions

Revision 14 declared one function that took one chain's topology and gave it the whole graph, the
pool, the chain array, and the B105 push in prose (critic WR-29). Two functions exist, and each one
does what its own signature can do.

```rust
impl GraphConfigurator {
    /// Build everything one topology change needs, on the engine handoff
    /// thread.
    ///
    /// **It reads four things and nothing else**: `request`, `self.layout`,
    /// `self.handoff_retry`, and the free-slot count of `self.handoffs`
    /// (critic WARNING on I6). `self.layout` names an order and a count, so
    /// this function reads no value the audio thread owns and copies no
    /// `ChainState` (critic CR-17). It allocates one ring pair for every
    /// chain the change adds, and none for a chain it keeps.
    ///
    /// **`&mut self` writes one field**: on success it stores the built
    /// `Configured` in `self.handoff_retry` and sets `self.attempts` to
    /// zero, so `hand_off` takes no argument and the retry re-enters through
    /// the same field.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `ConfigError::ChannelMismatch` when a stage cannot accept the
    /// count that the stage before it produces, `ConfigError::PoolExhausted`
    /// past B47, B48, or B120, which are the THREE pool classes and not two
    /// (critic C21I-3), `ConfigError::RingBudgetExceeded` when the migration

    /// `ConfigError::ParamBudgetExceeded` past B90,

    /// `Some` (critic WR-27), and `ConfigError::Mix`, which is the one arm
    /// that carries `MixError::SlotBudgetExceeded`,
    /// `MixError::SendBudgetExceeded` and `MixError::CurveBudgetExceeded`
    /// out of this call (critic N22I-3). Every refusal is computed before any
    /// allocation.
    pub fn configure(&mut self, request: &ConfigureRequest)
        -> Result<Configured, ConfigError>;

    /// Push the pending handoff at B105 and publish its topology, or leave
    /// it in `handoff_retry` for the next attempt.
    ///

    /// `self.handoff_retry`, which `configure` filled, so no caller has to
    /// move a value out of the field and back into it on a refusal (critic
    /// WARNING on the deferred attempt).
    ///

    /// ordinary case on attempts one to B95 minus one is that the ring is
    /// full and the next pass tries again (critic WARNING on the deferred
    /// attempt). `Ok(Some(generation))` means the ring took the handoff and
    /// the topology is published, and `self.attempts` carries the count
    /// against B95. The outcome is an `Option` and not an enum of this
    /// crate, because an enum with one eight-byte arm and one one-byte arm
    /// trips `variant_size_differences`, which the roster compile proved.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `ConfigError::PoolHandoffBusy` on a full ring at the B95
    /// attempt, and `ConfigError::NothingToHandOff` when `handoff_retry` is
    /// `None`, which means no caller built anything (critic C15-6).
    pub fn hand_off(&mut self) -> Result<Option<Generation>, ConfigError>;
}
```

#### The strip count carries a bound and a refusal

`MeterSnapshot` holds a fixed array at B86, and `SessionCommand::BusAdd` accepted a bus with no
limit, so an unbounded producer met a fixed-size consumer and the surplus strip's meter read zero
for the whole session with no fault (critic Q5).

**Two callers refuse, and each one names an error its own crate declares.**
`MixState::validate` and `SessionCommand::BusAdd` return
`MixError::StripBudgetExceeded { requested }`, so a hand-edited `mix/strips.json` is refused at read
time and an added bus is refused at edit time. Both compare against `MAX_STRIPS`, which sits in
`duet-time` and which `duet-session` reaches on its existing edge; revision 12 put the
constant in `duet-dsp`, which `duet-session` does not reach, so neither refusal could be written
(critic CR-12). Section 1.6's shared-limit block names all four enforcers and PG28 proves the
reachability. `configure` returns
`ConfigError::StripBudgetExceeded { requested }`, off the audio thread and before any allocation,
exactly as `PoolExhausted` and `RingBudgetExceeded` do. **`ConfigError` wraps `MixError` through
`From`**, so the engine keeps the cause and `duet-session` names no engine type, which PL1 and rule
4 of section 1.3 both require. Revision 8 gave `MixState::validate` a `ConfigError`, which
`duet-session` cannot name, and `MixError` carried no variant for it, so the read-time refusal did
not exist (critic R11). Both map to `GatewayError::StripBudgetExceeded`, and `fault_text.rs` holds
one message (section 12.4).

**B86 budgets every strip the product builds by itself, and then the refusal is a real user
choice.** Count a project at B1 before the user adds anything: 32 track strips, 8 part buses that
PR M-02 requires one of per part, the reverb bus and the delay bus that PR M-04 requires from the
first draw, the monitor bus, and the master. Revision 8 set the budget at 41 and that project needs
44, so the bundle refused to build itself at the product budget every other number is sized against
(critic R5). B86 is 48: it carries the 44 and leaves room for the three extra reverb buses and the
second delay bus that PR M-04 allows. A user who passes 48 has built sixteen buses, and the refusal
names the limit.

#### The parameter count carries a bound and a refusal

`ParamSnapshot` holds a fixed array at B90, and the audio thread addresses it by `ParamId`. A
parameter at or above B90 therefore has no cell, and a fader ride on it would be a silent loss in
the mix. Revision 9 set B90 at 512, stated a derivation that gives at least 576 at B86, and declared
no refusal at all (critic W1).

**B90 is a budget with a refusal, not a theoretical maximum.** `SlotConfig::params` records a
`ParamIdRange { first, count }` that `configure` assigns when a slot is created, so the budget bounds
the parameters a project holds and not the parameters B45 slots could hold. B96 gives the count per
`SlotKind`, and the B90 row carries the whole arithmetic.

**Two callers refuse, in the shape the strip budget already has.** `MixState::validate` and
`SessionCommand::StripInsertSlot` return `MixError::ParamBudgetExceeded { requested }`, so a
hand-edited `mix/strips.json` is refused at read time and an inserted slot is refused at edit time.
Both compare against `MAX_PARAMS`, which sits in `duet-time` for the reason the strip budget
states; a `duet-session` edge to `duet-engine`, where revision 12 put the constant, is a Cargo cycle
(critic CR-12).
`configure` returns `ConfigError::ParamBudgetExceeded { requested }`, off the audio thread and
before any allocation. `ConfigError` wraps `MixError` through `From`, so `duet-session` names no
engine type. Both map to `GatewayError::ParamBudgetExceeded`, and `fault_text.rs` holds one message
(section 12.4).

**`ParamSnapshot` stays `Copy` at the size the PG24 table prints for it, and VR5 states why.** The core is the writer
and the dropper on that path, so TH9 does not bind it; one write is a memory copy off the audio
thread, and a fader drag pays that copy once per frame at B2.

The mixer is a module of this crate. A bus is a chain with no disk reader and no disk writer. The
master is a bus with a true-peak meter. One node type, one `process` call (Ardour 2, adopt item 11).

### 5.6 The graph runner

```rust
/// A publication counter. The audio thread compares two of these once per
/// cycle and does nothing else with them.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Generation(u64);

/// A pre-computed, immutable topology for the whole graph. It is built off
/// the audio thread and published. It holds no processor state and no pool.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct GraphChain {
    chains: Box<[ChainTopology]>,
    /// Node indexes in topological order.
    order: Box<[NodeIndex]>,
    generation: Generation,
    /// Increases when a new `GraphHandoff` waits in the B105 queue. One
    /// counter gates the pool and the chain-state set together, because
    /// `configure` builds both on every topology change (section 5.5).
    handoff_generation: Generation,
}

/// Every strip's meter-reset generation, shared by the core and the audio
/// thread.
///
/// It derives no `Default`: the standard library implements `Default` for an
/// array up to thirty-two elements and B86 is larger, so the type carries a
/// named constructor instead. The array is the one piece of memory both
/// threads touch, and every access is a relaxed atomic load or a relaxed
/// atomic store, so TH1 holds (section 7.3).
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct ResetGenerations { entries: [AtomicU32; MAX_STRIPS] }

impl ResetGenerations {
    /// Every strip's generation at zero.
    ///
    /// An `AtomicU32` is not `Copy`, so the array repeat carries an inline
    /// `const` block, which is the one form that builds a long array of a
    /// non-`Copy` element with no loop and no panic primitive.
    pub const fn new() -> Self {
        Self { entries: [const { AtomicU32::new(0) }; MAX_STRIPS] }
    }
}

/// `clippy::new_without_default` asks every `new` with no argument for a
/// `Default`. A derived `Default` is impossible past thirty-two elements, so
/// the chunk writes this impl by hand and it calls `new` (critic K-3).
impl Default for ResetGenerations {
    fn default() -> Self { Self::new() }
}

/// The audio thread's own mutable state for the whole graph. It owns the one
/// `BufferPool` of the open stream.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct GraphState {
    /// The chain-state array the audio thread adopted. Its length changes
    /// only by adoption: `configure` builds the new array off this thread and
    /// the retired one leaves through `basedrop` (section 5.5, critic CR-16,
    /// CR-17).
    chains: ChainSetHandle,
    /// The one buffer pool. It is built once when the stream opens and it is
    /// never rebuilt, because every number that sizes it is fixed
    /// (section 5.5, critic CR-18).
    pool: PoolHandle,
    /// Which generation this state was reconciled against.
    generation: Generation,
    /// Which handoff generation this state adopted, taken from the handoff
    /// itself and never from the published topology (critic CR-20).
    handoff_generation: Generation,
    /// The read end of the B105 handoff ring. Step 1 of the drain rule below
    /// is a step of the runner, so the runner's own state holds the end.
    ///
    /// It sits inside a `basedrop::Owned` because the rule is a property of
    /// the TYPE and not of one drop site: PG26 refuses a bare `rtrb` end
    /// inside any audio-owned declaration, so no reader has to trace which
    /// thread drops which value. The `HandoffReader` newtype carries the
    /// `Debug` that `basedrop` does not supply.
    handoffs: HandoffReader,
    /// The shared meter-reset generations. `duet-core` holds the other
    /// handle, and neither side ever writes the other's memory.
    resets: Arc<ResetGenerations>,
}

/// How a chain runs. One implementation exists in version one.
pub trait GraphRunner {
    fn run(&mut self, topology: &GraphChain, state: &mut GraphState, cycle: &mut Cycle<'_>)
        -> CycleOutcome;
}
```

The signature is the fix. The topology is a shared reference, because it is published and immutable.
The state is an exclusive reference, because the audio thread owns it.

**Where each read end lives, and what declares it** (critic C20-3). The three
`triple_buffer::Output` values, the B32 MIDI consumer, the B33 refill producer, and the B34 fault
queue are fields of `EngineProcess`, which section 15.10 declares and which the `audio-owned` block
names. `EngineProcess` is the value `AudioBackend::open` moved into the backend's callback state, so
it is the audio thread's real root and `GraphState` is one of its fields. `EngineProcess::process`
resolves the topology before it calls `GraphRunner::run` and hands it in as a shared reference,
which is why no `Output` appears in `GraphState`. The B105 ring end is different: draining it is
step 1 of the runner's own cycle, so `GraphState` holds it.

**Revision 20 rooted every audio rule one level below the real root.** `AudioBackend::open` took a
`Box<dyn AudioProcess>`, no type implemented the trait, and section 5.6 put six heap-owning handles
in "the backend callback's own state", which is not a declaration. PG26, PG26b, PG26c, PG26e and
PG26f each walk from `EngineProcess` now, and **every handle it holds sits inside a `basedrop`
wrapper**, which is the rule `DiskReader` already states: an `rtrb` end, a `triple_buffer::Output`
and a `crossbeam_queue::ArrayQueue` each own a heap allocation, and a drop of a bare one on this
thread is a free TH1 forbids.

**PG26b stops below a read end, and PG26 and PG26c do not.** A `triple_buffer::Output` hands this
thread a SHARED reference to the published value, and a container needs an exclusive reference to
grow, so no `Vec` below a read end can call the allocator here. `TempoMap` holds two of them and is
published by the core, which is the one shape this stop exists for. The handle still owns a heap
allocation, so it still needs the deferring wrapper, and a lock needs only a shared reference, so
the lock test still descends. The run prints `AUDIO READ ONLY` beside `AUDIO DEFERRED`, and the
section 1.9 external table carries the word "reads" that the rule reads.

#### The drain rule at the top of the cycle

At the top of every cycle the runner does three things in this order.

1. **It drains the B105 ring to empty, and it applies each handoff IN FULL before it pops the
   next.** Applying one handoff is four moves and no more. It resolves every
   `ChainSource::Keep(k)` position of the new array against the array `GraphState` holds at that
   moment, with one `Option::take` each. It swaps the new `ChainSetHandle` into `GraphState`. It
   lets the superseded handle drop into `basedrop`. It records that handoff's own `generation` in
   `GraphState::handoff_generation`.

   **Applying in full before the next pop is what makes an index sound.** A plan's `Keep(k)` names
   a position of the array its own builder last handed over, so a plan applied against a later
   array would name the wrong chain. **The rule is a drain and never a single pop**, so the ring
   can never hold a value the runner has not seen: revision 14 wrote "pops" in the singular at
   three sites, and two `configure` calls between two cycles left one handoff in the ring for ever
   (critic CR-20). A `Keep(k)` whose index is outside the old array, or whose state was already
   taken, leaves `state` at `None`.
2. **It proves the generation it adopted against the generation that is published.** The record
   comes from `GraphHandoff::generation` and never from the published `GraphChain`. A difference
   between the two means the publication and the ring disagree. **That window is real**, and
   revision 15 called it impossible (critic C15-9): step 3 pushes before it publishes, and the
   callback resolves the topology before it drains, so a callback that lands between the two
   instructions adopts handoff N plus 1 against topology N. The runner reports
   `EngineFault::HandoffGenerationSkew { published, adopted }` once per change and runs the array it
   actually holds. The mismatch costs one cycle: a position with no topology entry is not run, and a
   topology entry with no position reports `ChainSlotVacant`. The next cycle reads the published
   value and the two agree. Test 14 of section 10.7 opens the window on purpose.
3. **It compares the topology generation** and runs the in-place slot migration of section 5.5
   inside each chain the array keeps.

**An empty position is a named fault and never a panic, and the report is LATCHED** (critic
C19-W25). `GraphRunner::run` reads each `ChainSlot::state` with `as_mut`, and a `None` makes it
leave that strip silent for the cycle. **It reports `EngineFault::ChainSlotVacant { index }` once
per position per topology**, not once per cycle: `ChainSlot` carries a `reported: bool` that
`configure` clears for every position of every array it builds, and the runner sets it when it
pushes the fault. The condition lasts until the next topology change, so an unlatched report is
about 375 faults each second at B7, which fills the B34 queue, then fills the B29 event channel, and
then passes B39 and degrades the client. A latch costs one bit per slot and turns a flood into one
message.
`clippy::indexing_slicing` and `clippy::panic` are both denied, so the alternative does not exist.
The whole graph keeps running, which is what a failure contained in one strip means.

**What makes a `Keep` index sound is the apply-in-full rule, and nothing else here.** A plan is
always resolved against the array its own builder handed over, because step 1 applies each handoff
completely before it pops the next. The ring capacity does NOT carry that property: `configure`
builds a plan and `hand_off` pushes it, so a full ring stops the push and never the build, and
revision 15 first claimed the reverse (critic WARNING on the soundness sentence). B105 at 1 carries
a different property, which section 5.5 step 2 states: with one slot, a free-slot count of one
proves that the audio thread has adopted the last handoff, which is what lets `configure` refuse to
build against a stale count.

Both paths are bounded by B86, so both fit the cycle budget B8.

**Decision: version one runs the graph on the audio thread in one topological pass.** The order is
computed off the audio thread, so a run is a loop over `order`. The reason is B1: a work-stealing
pool adds thread wake latency and a class of bugs that 32 nodes do not pay for. The trait keeps the
door open, and a parallel runner enters the plan when the single-threaded runner passes half of B7.

A connection change never edits a live graph. The core builds a new `GraphChain` off the audio
thread and publishes it (Ardour 5).

### 5.7 The threading contract

**PG26, PG26b, and PG26c read two blocks here**, and DR7 governs both: each one carries a marker
line with its own minimum row count, and the rules exit 2 when a heading stands with no block under
it, when the marker is absent, or when the parsed set is below the minimum. Revision 12 deleted the block under a
kept heading and the run printed `AUDIO OWNED: 88` and exited 0, because a lazy regular expression
walked on to the next fenced block and parsed 88 source fragments out of it (critic CR-14).

**The rule also refuses a token that is not a placed type name**, so a parse that finds prose fails
closed rather than scanning a set of words.

#### Every audio-owned declaration

Each line names one type whose **value the audio thread constructs, replaces, adopts, moves, or
drops inside `GraphRunner::run`**, plus `GraphState`, which is the root the runner holds. TH1 bans
three things on this thread, and three rules read the three of them.

**PG26 holds the free half.** For every name here, and for every declared type it reaches through a
field, the rule refuses a field that names a heap-owning type: `Box`, `Vec`, `String`, `Arc`, `Rc`,
`BTreeMap`, `BTreeSet`, `HashMap`, `HashSet`, `VecDeque`, `Cow`, `PathBuf`, or any external name
whose section 1.9 row carries the word "heap". Revision 11 put an allocation and a free inside the
cycle by boxing one enum arm (critic CR-2).

**One escape exists, and it is a type and not a sentence.** A field whose outermost head is an
external name whose section 1.9 `Why` cell carries the word "defers" moves the free of everything
below it to the collector thread (TH5), so the heap test is switched off for that subtree and the
field is counted on `AUDIO DEFERRED`. `basedrop::Owned` and `basedrop::Shared` are the two names
that carry it. **A bare `rtrb`, `triple_buffer`, `crossbeam_queue`, `async_channel`, or
`std::thread` handle inside an audio-owned declaration is a failure**, because every one of those
owns a heap allocation that a drop on this thread would free (critic CR-16).

**PG26b holds the allocation half, and the escape does not reach it.** A deferring wrapper answers
the free and it can never answer the allocation: a `Vec` inside an `Owned` still calls the allocator
on every `push`, and `Owned` implements `DerefMut`, which this design already relies on. **A
container that GROWS therefore fails at any depth, a wrapper included**: `Vec`, `String`, `HashMap`,
`HashSet`, `BTreeMap`, `BTreeSet`, `VecDeque`, `Cow`, `PathBuf`, `SmallVec`, and any external name
whose section 1.9 `Why` cell carries the word "grows". A FIXED `Box<[T]>` or `Box<str>` allocates
once, off this thread, so it passes inside a wrapper. Revision 14 accepted `Owned<Vec<u8>>` and a
Critic probe proved it (critic WR-22). **The walk therefore continues through a wrapper** and
suppresses the heap test alone.

**PG26c holds the lock half.** TH1 bans a lock beside an allocation and a free, and PG26 read
neither. **A lock fails at any depth, inside a wrapper and behind an exemption line alike**:
`Mutex`, `RwLock`, `ReentrantLock`, `Condvar`, `Barrier`, `OnceLock`, `LazyLock`, the three guard
types, and any external name whose section 1.9 `Why` cell carries the word "lock". The guard reads
the last path segment, so `parking_lot::Mutex` reds exactly as `std::sync::Mutex` does. Revision 14
let both pass and a Critic probe proved it (critic WR-23). `basedrop::Shared<T>` is the lock-free
shape this design already names, so the correct answer exists at every site.

The run prints `AUDIO DEFERRED` beside `AUDIO EXEMPT`, and `GROW IN AUDIO` and `LOCK IN AUDIO`
beside `HEAP IN AUDIO`, so a reader sees how often each answer applied.

**The completeness rule, stated at the site.** The block is a hand list, because TH1 has no
mechanical guard (section 5.7) and no tool can read a thread affinity out of a declaration. Three
things keep it complete. A type that the audio thread starts to construct, replace, or drop enters
this block **in the same changeset** that puts it on that thread. Chunk C3's verification step
re-reads the block against the body of `GraphRunner::run` and records the comparison. A run whose
parsed set is below the recorded minimum is a failure, so a deletion cannot pass as a clean run.
Revision 12 left `ChainState` and `Transport` outside the set, and a `Vec<u8>` field on either one
passed every guard (critic CR-14).

#### Every audio-owned field the rule exempts

Each line is one `Type.field` path and then the reason token the section it names states. The walk
stops at an exempt field, so nothing below it is read. The run prints `AUDIO EXEMPT`.

**An exemption answers the FREE half of one named field, and it answers neither the allocation half
nor the lock half** (critic CR on the exemption). Revision 15 stated the inverse of its own guard at
this site, and the guard is the thing that runs: PG26c and PG26b both test a field BEFORE the
exemption is read, and PG26 tests it after. A row is therefore a hand decision about one free, and
it can hide no growable container and no lock.

probe put a `Vec<u8>` behind that exemption and the guard exited 0 with `HEAP IN AUDIO: 0`. Both

declaration is legal only inside a `basedrop::Owned` or a `basedrop::Shared`, PG26 reads the

the wrapper**, because PG26b and PG26c have to read what the wrapper carries (critic WR-22, WR-23).
An exemption line cannot switch any of the three rules off.

is `Type.field Head reason`. Revision 15 keyed a row on the path alone, so the row for

there and got a green run with `HEAP IN AUDIO: 0`. PG26 now compares the field's outermost head
with the head the row names, and a field whose head differs falls through to the heap test.

**A `field-path` row proves a referent and not a reason** (concern N-6). The membership kind asks
that the holder be an audio-owned name, that the field be one it declares, and that the head be a
type this document or an external block decides; it cannot read the reason token, and no rule can.
A row here is therefore a hand decision that review holds, which is why the block carries one row
and why PG26b and PG26c read no exemption at all: a growable container and a lock fail behind an
exemption line exactly as they fail in the open.

**One row is left, and it is the one field that no wrapper can express.**

**Each row is a LEAF and not a root.** The heap, grow, and lock rules walk every field of every
root, so a scalar or a fixed array below a root already carries the rule that matters; a marker on
one would add a second assertion with no second reader. The block exists so the closure rule is
CLOSED: every reachable name is a root or is here, and nothing falls between them.

root block states, so a marker on any of them would assert something false. The closure is now
rooted at the value `AudioBackend::open` actually moved into the callback state, so no heap-owning

In the application, the core runs on the GPUI foreground thread inside one entity. In the headless
host it runs on a dedicated thread. Both drive the same `DuetCore` struct with the same input enum.

**The thread rules, TH1 to TH13.** Section 1.7 indexes the range and this sentence states no count, because a count in prose ages and the index is the fact (critic N21I-2, C21-3). Revision 23 adds TH13, the message-carrier rule.

- **TH1.** The audio thread never allocates, never frees, never locks, never blocks, never formats a
  string, never logs, and has no panic path.
- **TH2.** `DuetCore` is the one writer of project state, and it writes on the core thread only.
- **TH3.** No git walk, no file scan, no import parse, no render, **no timed wait**, and **no
  allocation above B110 inside an IMMEDIATE verb** runs on the GPUI foreground thread. **A
  snapshot is not an immediate verb** and B101 is far above B110: `CoreInput::Resynchronize` is
  served on a job thread, which builds the byte form of every document and sends it on the B30
  channel, so the one large allocation of the core has a thread of its own (section 5.8, critic
  WARNING on B101). Each one runs on a job thread or on
  the engine handoff thread, or parks off the foreground thread on the GPUI background executor
  timer and resumes through `cx.update`. Revision 13 put a bounded sleep on that thread and no rule
  of this section saw it (critic CR-15); revision 14 then put a 94 MB ring allocation there inside
  an immediate verb, and an allocation was none of the five things this rule named (critic CR-19).
- **TH4.** The engine disk thread serves the engine only. It moves samples between a ring and a
  take file and it writes peaks. **It allocates no ring and it releases none** (critic C15-1).
  Revision 15 gave the allocation to this thread here and to the engine handoff thread in section
  5.5, so one duty had two owners and `ChainLayout::pairs` counted one of them. **Ring allocation
  has exactly one owner: `GraphConfigurator::configure` on the engine handoff thread**, and the
  collector on that same thread releases every retired ring (TH5).
- **TH5.** The `basedrop` collector runs on the engine handoff thread and drains once per B108.
  **No deferred verb runs on that thread**, so an export render that holds a job thread for minutes
  cannot delay a drain; revision 14 put the collector beside every deferred verb and gave it no
  period at all (critic WR-25). `Collector::collect` is a drain to empty
  (`basedrop-0.1.3/src/collector.rs:238`), so one pass releases a whole nest of `Owned` values when

- **TH6.** No tokio task holds a GPUI entity handle.
- **TH7.** No runtime-bound tokio type crosses into GPUI code. The ban names three kinds: a timer

- **TH8.** Every deferred verb that writes re-validates on the core thread before it commits

- **TH9.** A value the audio thread publishes owns no heap. Every type behind a

- **TH12.** The `duet-quit-save` thread exists for one save and then ends. The core starts it at

claims no more.

1. **A written forbidden-call list** in `crates/duet-engine/src/audio/README.md`, checked at review

2. **A soak test.** It runs the dummy backend in `Freewheel` for B77 with a varying block size, and
