## 10. The GPUI application

The crate is `crates/duet`. It holds presentation only. It computes no domain value.

### 10.1 The mode state machine

```rust
// `Mode` is declared in duet-command (section 1.5). The app re-exports it.
pub use duet_command::Mode;

gpui_kit::actions!(duet, [EnterCompose, EnterRecord, EnterMix, EnterMaster, ClearClip]);
```

`DuetApp` owns the mode. A change is an action, and the handler emits `AppEvent::ModeChanged(Mode)`.

**`ClearClip` is the `Clear clip` command that design contract 4.4 names.** Its handler dispatches
`Verb::MeterReset { strip: None }`, and a click on one strip's meter dispatches the same verb with
that strip. One verb serves both paths, so the menu rule of section 10.2 holds: a menu item with no
verb is not allowed, and revision 8 left the command with no action at all (critic C9).

Every transition is legal except one: the application refuses to leave Record while
`RecordState::Recording` holds. The handler shows a notification and changes nothing.

### 10.2 The entity ownership tree

```
Root (gpui_kit::component::Root)
└── DuetApp
    ├── CoreHost            ├── StartView       ├── MenuHost       ├── ViewStateStore
    ├── AgentBridge         ├── TitleBar        ├── ModeSwitcher   ├── TopBar
    ├── Sidebar             ├── Inspector       ├── StatusBar      ├── HistorySheet
    ├── ComposeView         -> SystemView (per system), PlayheadLayer
    ├── RecordView          -> LaneView (per track), PlayheadLayer
    ├── MixView             -> StripView (per strip), MeterLayer
    ├── MasterView          -> MasterMeterLayer
    └── TransportBar
```

Appendix A names what each entity owns, the one path that mutates it, and its identity source. This
tree states only the parent and the child.

#### One frame driver per work area

**Decision: each work area has exactly one frame-driver entity, and it is a small leaf view.**

| Area | Frame driver | What it paints |
|---|---|---|
| Compose | `PlayheadLayer` | The playhead line only |
| Record | `PlayheadLayer` | The playhead line and the record head |
| Mix | `MeterLayer` | Every strip meter, in one canvas |
| Master | `MasterMeterLayer` | The LUFS meter and the true-peak meter |

Each frame driver requests the animation frame for its own area and reads the slot `CoreHost` filled
at the top of the frame. None of the four owns a publication.

#### Every frame driver has a start condition and a stop condition

Revision 14 gave each driver a stop condition and no start condition, so the loop could end and
nothing could restart it: a user who armed a track and sang with the transport stopped saw a meter
that never moved (critic CR-21). `CoreHost::frame_demand` answers both, and every driver reads the
same answer.

| Driver | Start condition | Stop condition | What restarts it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PlayheadLayer`, Compose and Record | `transport_moves`, which is `Rolling` or `Locating` | `transport_moves` false and the slot equal to `shown` | `Verb::TransportPlay` and `Verb::TransportLocate` each produce a `CoreEvent`, the drain task notifies, and `render` runs |
| `MeterLayer` | `input_live` or `transport_moves` | both false and `meter_decays` false | `MixView` calls `cx.notify` on the layer whenever the armed set changes. It sends no value: `DuetCore` owns the armed set and the layer reads `CoreHost::frame_demand` |
| `MasterMeterLayer` | the same pair | the same pair | `MasterView` calls the same `cx.notify` on its own layer |

**An armed strip OR a monitored track keeps the meter loop alive whatever the transport does**, and
one `input_live` term carries both causes (critic C15-10).
That is the rule design contract 4.4 needs: the peak cap, the fall, and the `CLIP` indicator all exist so a user can set a
record level before the transport rolls. `input_live` reads the armed set that `DuetCore` holds, so
the condition is a fact about the session and never a fact about the meter value. **The field is
`input_live` and never `any_armed`** (critic C22I-W16): the C15-10 merge renamed it in the
declaration and in its closure row and left the old name at two prose sites.

**The decay term ends the loop and the demand terms start it.** A silent meter with no held mark and
no armed strip leaves every term false, so the last frame is the one that paints silence. Nothing
polls while the demand is empty: `CoreHost::poll_frame` re-arms nothing, and no driver requests a
frame.

`MeterLayer` satisfies contract 4.4, which asks for one animation frame for every meter, with one
element that spans the strip row and paints every meter, every peak cap, every `CLIP` text, and
every numeric readout from one `CoreHost::meters` call, which copies the slot the frame order
already filled (section 7.3, critic CR-4, CR-11, WR-5).

#### What an animation frame really costs, from the pinned source

Revision 13 claimed that a sibling leaf avoids a whole-tree relayout. **The pinned framework
contradicts that claim**, so this section states the true behaviour rather than the audit's summary
(critic WR-19). Three facts decide it, and each one is a line of `gpui-pre-0.3.5`, the version
`gpui-kit` 0.6.4 depends on.

1. `Window::request_animation_frame` notifies the **requesting view**: `src/window.rs:2606` is the
   signature, `:2607` reads `let entity = self.current_view();`, and `:2608` schedules
   `self.on_next_frame(move |_, cx| cx.notify(entity))`. Revision 14 wrote the first two of those
   line numbers one line low (concern N-2).
2. A notify marks **every ancestor** dirty, not the view alone: `Window::mark_view_dirty` at
   `src/window.rs:2140` walks `view_path_reversed(view_id)` at `:2146` and inserts each id into
   `dirty_views`.
3. A view **re-renders unless it opts into a cache**: `ViewElement::request_layout` at
   `src/view.rs:314` matches on `self.cached_style`, and with `None` it calls
   `self.view.render(window, cx)` on every frame. `Entity::cached(style)` at `src/view.rs:232` is
   the one public way to set that field, and `ViewElement::cached` at `:271` is crate private on
   purpose, because only an entity-backed view has `Context::notify` to bust the cache.

So a `MeterLayer` frame re-renders `MixView`, `DuetApp`, and the `Root` above it, because all three
are ancestors. **A sibling is not an ancestor**, so the 48 `StripView` entities are the cost this
design must remove, and the framework removes it in one named way.

**Decision: every heavy sibling subtree of a frame driver is an `Entity::cached` child.** `MixView`
builds each strip as `strip.clone().cached(strip_style())`, `RecordView` builds each lane the same
way, and `ComposeView` builds each system the same way. The prepaint path at `src/view.rs:386`
reuses the cached subtree while the bounds, the content mask, and the text style are unchanged and
`dirty_views` does not hold that entity, which is exactly the condition a meter frame leaves true
for a sibling. The style must state a definite size, which `src/view.rs:226` states and which each
of the three has: a strip carries a fixed width, a lane carries its own `LogicalPx` height, and a
system carries its `SizePx`. A `cx.notify` on the child busts that child's own cache, so a strip
whose value changed still repaints.

| Frame driver | Its ancestors, which re-render every frame | Its cached siblings, which do not |
|---|---|---|
| `PlayheadLayer` in Compose | `ComposeView`, `DuetApp`, `Root` | Every `SystemView` |
| `PlayheadLayer` in Record | `RecordView`, `DuetApp`, `Root` | Every `LaneView` |
| `MeterLayer` | `MixView`, `DuetApp`, `Root` | Every `StripView` |
| `MasterMeterLayer` | `MasterView`, `DuetApp`, `Root` | **None**; section 10.2 states what Master pays instead |

**The same mechanism is why the frame order below is correct.** `DuetApp` is an ancestor of every
one of the four frame drivers, so fact 2 marks it dirty on every animation frame and fact 3
re-renders it. `DuetApp::render` therefore runs on every frame a driver requests, before any child
element is built, which is what makes step 1 of the frame order a guarantee and not a hope.
Revision 13 declined to say so and called the order "stated here and not inferred from the
framework"; the order inside `render` is indeed this design's own, and the premise that `render`
runs at all rests on facts 2 and 3 (critic WR-19). **`DuetApp` is never cached**, for the same
reason.

**Master caches nothing, and this is what it pays instead** (critic WR-26). `StageCurve` derives
`IntoElement`, so it is a `RenderOnce` element with no entity and no `EntityId`. `Entity::cached`
takes an `Entity<T>` where `T: Render` (`src/view.rs:232`), and `ViewElement::cached` is crate
private "because only an entity-backed view has `Context::notify` to bust the cache"
(`src/view.rs:266` to `:270`). **The mitigation for Master is therefore a bound and a
precomputation, not a cache**, and revision 14 named a cache that cannot be built.

1. **The count is five and not 48.** `MasterStage::ORDER` holds five arms and contract 5.2 draws
   one box per arm, so a Master animation frame rebuilds five elements where a Mix frame would
   rebuild 48 strips. **The number is a type and no longer a sentence** (critic C19-11): revision 19
   wrote "five stages" here, in the B90 arithmetic, and in the design contract, and no declaration
   agreed with any of the three.
2. **Each build reads samples and evaluates no filter.** `StageCurve::params` is an
   `Arc<[Finite]>` that `MasterView` fills from `MasterView::stages` whenever a parameter changes,
   which is not per frame. A build is one pointer copy and one polyline over stored samples.
3. **A bench measures it.** Chunk K5 owns a `criterion` bench over one Master frame at B1, exactly
   as K4 owns one over a Mix frame, and both report against B4.

**Nothing here is asserted by a test, and a bench measures it.** Chunk K4 owns a `criterion` bench
over one Mix frame at B1, with the cached siblings and without them. It reports both against B4, and
the same run records what one frame leaves for an immediate verb at B5, because both share the GPUI
foreground thread.

`MeterLayer` needs the strip x positions. `MixView` publishes them as a plain `Vec<MeterSlot>`
whenever the strip list or the layout changes, which is not per frame. Design contract 4.4 carries
the matching wording for the canvas and its single animation frame.

#### The frame order: read the publications, then render

**Decision: `CoreHost` owns every `triple_buffer::Output`, and it reads both once per frame before
any child view renders.** Four frame drivers exist, section 5.8 states how many publications exist,
and a publication supplies exactly one read end that is neither `Clone` nor `Copy` (critic CR-11,
C23I-W13). The frame order
resolves it, and it is three steps.

1. **`DuetApp::render` calls `self.core.update(cx, |host, cx| host.poll_frame(window, cx))` as its
   first statement**, before it builds any child element. `Entity::update` takes
   `impl FnOnce(&mut T, &mut Context<T>) -> R`
   (`gpui-pre-0.3.5/src/app/entity_map.rs:476`), so the argument is a two-argument closure;
   revision 13 passed the method itself, which does not build (critic C-6). Chunk K1 writes the
   call and test 12 of section 10.7 rung three asserts it.

   **`render` is not the only caller** (critic CR-21). `CoreHost::poll_frame` re-arms itself with
   `Context::on_next_frame` (`src/app/context.rs:293`) whenever `frame_demand` reports any active
   driver, and that method schedules the closure on `Window::on_next_frame` (`src/window.rs:2586`).
   The poll therefore runs once per frame while any driver is active, whether or not a render of
   `DuetApp` happens to run, and it stops re-arming on the first frame with no demand.

   **The two callers OVERLAP on an active frame, and this sentence states which is which** (critic
   C20-N8). `DuetApp::render` runs on every animation frame, so on a frame with an active driver
   both callers fire and `poll_frame` runs twice. **The re-arm is the GUARANTEE** and the `render`
   call is the BACKSTOP: the re-arm is what makes the meter fall while no render happens, and the
   `render` call is what makes a view read a value no older than the frame it paints. **The second
   call is idempotent by construction**: `MeterReader::poll` takes the milliseconds since its own
   last call, so the B111 hold and the B112 fall are conserved across the two, and the cost is one
   read of every publication the section 5.8 snapshot table carries. Revision 20 stated the two guarantees separately and never said they
   overlap, so a reader could not tell the second call from a defect.
2. **`CoreHost::poll_frame` calls `MeterReader::poll` and `TransportReader::poll`.** Each one reads
   its `Output`, resolves what section 7.3 says it resolves, and stores a `Copy` value in a
   foreground-only slot on the reader itself. Both slots live on the GPUI foreground thread and no
   other thread reads one. **`poll_frame` passes `MeterReader::poll` the milliseconds since its
   last call**, which is the one clock the B111 hold and the B112 fall read. The value comes from
   the frame this call is inside, so the cap ages with the frames the user sees and no entity reads
   a wall clock (section 7.3).
3. **Every view then reads the slot.** `MeterReader::latest` returns a `MeterView` and
   `TransportReader::latest` returns a `TransportView`, each one a copy of a fixed-size `Copy`
   value. A frame driver holds an `Entity<CoreHost>`, which is a handle and not the reader, so any
   number of views may read and no view owns an `Output`.

**A frame driver holds a read-only handle on `CoreHost`, and that is the one exception to the
sibling rule of this section.** It sends `CoreHost` nothing and it calls one method. Every other
sibling relationship stays a subscription, because every other one carries a change the observer
must react to; a meter value changes every frame and a subscription per frame would be an event
storm (critic 4.2).

**What a second reader would cost, stated here.** `triple_buffer` could publish twice, with one
`Input` per consumer, and the audio thread would then write both. That is a second memory copy of
the size the PG24 table prints for `MeterSnapshot` inside B8, once per cycle, to save one method
call on the foreground thread. The frame order costs nothing on the audio thread, so it wins.

#### View state persistence

PR X-08 and PR C-03 make it a MUST. `Mode` and the whole view state are plain data in
`duet-command`, and `crates/duet` maps them onto GPUI values through `ProjectView`.

Revision 5 called one mode's state `ViewState` and implemented `BundleDocument` for it, while
Appendix A assigned the mode, the four sub-states, and the window geometry to `view.json`. No
declared type held those three facts, and `ProjectView`, which did, is an app type that
`duet-project` cannot reach (critic S2). Revision 6 splits the type in two and adds the document.

```rust
// in duet-command
/// The four product modes. It carries `Ord` because `ViewState` keys a
/// `BTreeMap` by it (VR1).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum Mode { Compose, Record, Mix, Master }

/// A length in logical pixels. It is a number, not a GPUI type, so it
/// crosses the transport and lands in a text file.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct LogicalPx(Finite);

impl LogicalPx {
    /// Build a length at compile time, for the constants of section 1.6.
    pub const fn new(value: Finite) -> Self;

    /// The stored length.
    #[must_use]
    pub const fn get(self) -> Finite;

    /// The length as an `f32`, which is what `gpui_kit::Pixels` holds.
    ///
    /// **It is total and it returns no `Result`.** `main_window_options`
    /// returns a `WindowOptions` and not a `Result`, and `unwrap_used` and
    /// `expect_used` are both denied, so a fallible conversion would force a
    /// literal fallback that DR3 forbids. The body is
    /// `duet_time::convert::finite_to_f32_saturating`, which is the one
    /// narrowing site this path uses; Appendix B.1 carries its row
    /// (critic W-6).
    #[must_use]
    pub fn to_f32(self) -> f32;
}

/// One zoom step. Compose and Record read it as a staff-space scale; Mix
/// and Master read it as a samples-per-pixel step.
///
/// It counts from zero upward, and B99 is the step a mode opens at. It
/// carries the VR1 comparison set, because it is one part of the Compose and
/// Record path-cache key (section 10.5).
///
/// **A step is bounded and the bound is B137** (critic C21-W18). B137 is the
/// staff-space map, `ZOOM_STAFF_SPACE` holds it, and a step at or above its
/// length addresses nothing. `state/view.json` persists a `ZoomStep` and a
/// hand edit of a canonical file is a product path this design already
/// recognises, so `from_step` refuses an out-of-range value and the
/// deserialization path calls it. ADR 0002 decision 4b and section 2.6a put a
/// guarded constructor on the deserialization path of `Finite` for exactly
/// this reason, and revision 21 gave this type a total `new` and twenty
/// unguarded sites.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct ZoomStep(u8);

impl ZoomStep {
    /// Build a step at compile time, for the constants of section 1.6.
    ///
    /// **It is `const` and total, and it is reachable only from section
    /// 1.6.** A `const fn` cannot return a `Result` a constant could read, so
    /// the compile-time form clamps to the last index of `ZOOM_STAFF_SPACE`
    /// and the run-time form refuses (critic C21-W18). Only `FIRST_OPEN_ZOOM`
    /// calls it, and B99 is inside the range, so the clamp fires nowhere in
    /// this plan and exists so that a future constant cannot be silently
    /// wrong.
    pub const fn new(step: u8) -> Self;

    /// Build a step from a value this process did not write.
    ///
    /// It returns `None` for a step at or above the length of
    /// `ZOOM_STAFF_SPACE`. `ViewDocument::from_bytes` calls it for every
    /// persisted step, and a `None` makes the view loader fall back to
    /// `FIRST_OPEN_ZOOM` and emit `CoreEvent::ViewStateReset`, which is what
    /// ADR 0005 decision 16c requires of a bad view document: it falls back
    /// and it never blocks the project (critic C21-W18).
    #[must_use]
    pub fn from_step(step: u8) -> Option<Self>;

    /// The staff space this step sets, in logical pixels (B137).
    ///
    /// It is the one map from a zoom step to a staff size, and
    /// `LayoutOptions::pixels_per_staff_space` takes its value from it, so
    /// the wrapped timeline needs no zoom mapping of its own and chunks A1
    /// and K2 invent none (critic C21-W19).
    #[must_use]
    pub fn staff_space(self) -> Finite;

    /// The samples-per-pixel scale this step gives a linear timeline.
    #[must_use]
    pub fn scalar(self) -> ZoomScalar;
}

/// The samples-per-pixel scale of a linear timeline.
///
/// Mix and Master key the path cache by it, because a linear timeline has no
/// system and a `SystemId` in that key would be a constant that wastes a slot
/// per region (ADR 0006 decision 8). **It is derived from a `ZoomStep` and is
/// never persisted**, so `state/view.json` still holds one zoom value per
/// mode and the two cannot disagree. Revision 9 named it in Appendix A and in
/// ADR 0006 and declared it nowhere (critic W14).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct ZoomScalar(NonZeroU32);

/// A scroll position, in logical pixels from the top of the content.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct ScrollOffset(LogicalPx);

impl ScrollOffset {
    /// Build an offset at compile time, for the constants of section 1.6.
    pub const fn new(value: LogicalPx) -> Self;
}

/// Which tracks a mode shows. PR R-03 makes the choice a MUST.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum TrackFilter { All, Part(PartId), Tracks(Vec<TrackId>) }

/// The window position and size, in logical pixels.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct WindowGeometry { x: LogicalPx, y: LogicalPx, width: LogicalPx, height: LogicalPx }

/// What one mode's work area remembers.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct ModeView {
    sidebar_width: LogicalPx,
    inspector_width: LogicalPx,
    /// The Mix work area holds a second, vertical split (contract 1.6).
    mix_vertical_split: Finite,
    zoom: ZoomStep,
    scroll: ScrollOffset,
    selection: Selection,
    shown_tracks: TrackFilter,
}

/// Everything about the project's presentation that survives a restart.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct ViewState {
    /// The mode the project reopens in.
    mode: Mode,
    /// One entry per mode the user has visited.
    per_mode: BTreeMap<Mode, ModeView>,
    window: WindowGeometry,
}

/// The `view.json` document. It is the one type that `BundleDocument`
/// carries for the view, and `duet-project` serializes it.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct ViewDocument { schema: SchemaVersion, view: ViewState }
```

Every field type is in `duet-command` or lower (VR3). `Selection` is a `duet-score` type, and
`Finite` is a `duet-time` type. No framework type appears, so the assertion of section 3.5 and PG7
both hold.

**`Verb::ViewSet` carries the whole `ViewState`, and `Verb::ViewGet` returns the whole
`ViewState`.** Revision 5's `ViewGet { mode }` returned one mode and left the window geometry with
no read path, so a restart could not restore the window. `ViewStateRequest` is deleted, because the
state is now one value and needs no envelope.

**`duet-project` persists `ViewDocument` as `state/view.json`**, an untracked text file
(section 4.1). `ViewDocument` implements `BundleDocument`, and **`duet-project` writes every
bundle file**, including this one; `duet-core` calls the save path and writes nothing itself
(critic Q20). **A scroll therefore never enters a commit and a checkout never moves the viewport**,
which is what property 2 of section 3.6 promises (critic N16). `SessionCommand` carries no
view-state variant (section 3.4).

**A `state/view.json` this build cannot read never blocks a project.** `ProjectOpen` reads the file,
and a `CommandError::Schema` or a `CommandError::Parse` from it is not a failed open. The core logs
the warning, opens the project with `ViewState::first_open()`, and emits
`CoreEvent::ViewStateReset { reason }`; the status bar shows one line. The first `Verb::ViewSet`
then overwrites the file. Every other document refuses the open, because losing a score is not
recoverable and losing a viewport is (critic Q22).

```rust
impl ViewState {
    /// The view state a project opens with when it has none on disk.
    ///
    /// It is a named constructor and not a `Default` impl. `Selection` and
    /// `TrackFilter` are enums with no default arm, and four zeros would be
    /// a window of zero size at the screen origin. Revision 8 named
    /// `ViewState::default`, which no derive could build and whose value
    /// would have been wrong (critic R7).
    #[must_use]
    pub fn first_open() -> ViewState;
}

impl ModeView {
    /// One mode's first-open layout.
    ///
    /// It exists because `ModeView` can derive no `Default` either, for the
    /// same two reasons, and because `ViewState::first_open` must fill the
    /// map rather than leave it empty (critic W4).
    #[must_use]
    pub fn first_open(mode: Mode) -> ModeView;
}
```

**The first-open value, field by field.** `ViewState::first_open` sets three fields and nothing
else. The mode is `Mode::Compose`, because a project opens on the page. The window is
`FIRST_OPEN_WIDTH` wide and `FIRST_OPEN_HEIGHT` high at `FIRST_OPEN_ORIGIN` on both axes. **`per_mode`
holds one entry per `Mode`**, each one `ModeView::first_open(mode)`; revision 9 left the map empty
and then named two `ModeView` fields in this paragraph, so a mode the user had not visited had no
layout at all (critic W4).

`ModeView::first_open` sets all seven fields, and every value is a section 1.6 constant or a named
empty value. Revision 12 carried an eighth, `body_split`, which divided nothing; contract 1.6 gives
the sidebar, the work area, and the inspector their own widths and names the Mix vertical split
separately (critic concern 6).

| Field | First-open value |
|---|---|
| `sidebar_width` | `FIRST_OPEN_SIDEBAR` (B94) |
| `inspector_width` | `FIRST_OPEN_INSPECTOR` (B97) |
| `mix_vertical_split` | `FIRST_OPEN_MIX_SPLIT` (B98) |
| `zoom` | `FIRST_OPEN_ZOOM` (B99) |
| `scroll` | `FIRST_OPEN_SCROLL`, the top of the content |
| `selection` | `Selection::Notes(Vec::new())`, an empty selection |
| `shown_tracks` | `TrackFilter::All` |

Every one of those names is a `pub const` of section 1.6, so DR3 holds and no literal appears here.
`Finite::from_finite_const` builds each float at compile time and asserts that it is finite
(section 2.6a).

```rust
// in crates/duet
/// The app-side view of the persisted state. It holds GPUI values and it
/// never crosses the transport.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub(crate) struct ProjectView { state: ViewState }

impl ProjectView {
    /// Read the state back from the core, through `Verb::ViewGet`.
    pub(crate) fn load(state: ViewState) -> Self;

    /// Clamp every stored length against the current window, then apply.
    ///
    /// Contract 1.6 requires the clamp. A width wider than the window, from
    /// a larger display, would otherwise hide the work area.
    #[must_use]
    pub(crate) fn clamped(&self, window: Bounds<Pixels>) -> Self;

    /// The value `Verb::ViewSet` carries back to the core.
    #[must_use]
    pub(crate) fn to_state(&self) -> ViewState;
}
```

`ViewStateStore` calls `clamped` on restore, so a project saved on a large display opens usable on a
small one. Chunk K6 writes the store, chunk K1 writes the round-trip test, and chunk F1 writes the
persistence (section 13.2).

**`ViewStateStore` applies the contract 1.1 breakpoint rules before any stored width, and it does
so on a first open as well as on a restore.** A clamp is not a breakpoint: contract 1.1 replaces the
sidebar with a 48-pixel icon rail in the narrow band and moves the inspector into a `Sheet`, which
no clamp of a stored number can express. The order is one rule. First the window width selects the
band. Then the band decides the sidebar form and whether the inspector is a panel or a sheet. Then
`clamped` bounds every remaining stored length against the window. Revision 10 opened at the
contract's minimum, which put the first frame in the narrow band while B94 and B97 named a
240-pixel sidebar and a 300-pixel inspector that the band refuses; at 1024 pixels the Mix work area
was 484 pixels, which is below the contract 1.6 minimum of 560 (critic W-5). B91 and B92 are the
contract's **default** now, and B102, B103, and B104 carry the minimum and the hard floor.

**One required test, in section 10.7 rung three.** It opens the window at each of the three
breakpoint widths, and it asserts the sidebar form, the inspector form, and that the work area is
at or above the contract 1.6 minimum in every mode.

#### The four surfaces a work area shows instead of its content

Contract section 8 specifies a load state, an empty state, an error state, and a no-device state for
each of the four modes. PR X-09, X-10, X-11, and X-12 make all four a MUST, and revision 5 gave
none of them a file or a chunk (critic S12).

**Decision: one type serves all four modes, and one shell file holds it.** A work area renders its
content only in `Ready`; every other variant renders the matching surface with the same spacing and
the same copy rules.

```rust
// in crates/duet
/// What a work area shows instead of its content.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub(crate) enum WorkAreaState {
    /// A job is running. `what` names it, and the progress comes from
    /// `CoreEvent::JobProgress` (PR X-09).
    Loading { what: SharedString, done: u32, total: u32 },
    /// The project holds nothing this mode can show (PR X-11).
    Empty,
    /// A verb was refused or a document failed to parse (PR X-12).
    Error { message: SharedString },
    /// The engine is in any `EngineState` other than `Running`.
    NoDevice { state: EngineState },
    Ready,
}
```

`crates/duet/src/shell/states.rs` holds it, chunk K1 writes it, and `ComposeView`, `RecordView`,
`MixView`, and `MasterView` each render it above their own content.

#### The start surface and the menus

- **`StartView`** shows the two templates of PR 11 Q5, "Solo voice" and "SATB", a recent project
  list, and an Open action. **It opens no file** (section 1.3 rule 6). It calls `Verb::RecentList`,
  `Verb::RecentAdd`, `Verb::ProjectCreate`, and `Verb::ProjectOpen`, and paints the `RecentEntry`
  values the core hands back. `duet-project` owns `RecentList` and reads the user configuration
  directory, because it is the crate that does file work. Chunk K6 writes the view, chunk F1 writes
  the template files, and chunk F2 writes `recent.rs`.
- **`MenuHost`** builds the macOS menu bar with `App::set_menus`, which the audit records at
  `gpui-pre-0.3.5` with the example `examples/set_menus.rs` (audit 9). On Linux it builds the
  in-window `AppMenuBar` that the same audit names. Both are driven by one list of
  `(MenuPath, Action)` pairs, so every menu item dispatches an action that maps to a `Verb`. A verb
  with no menu item is allowed; a menu item with no verb is not. Chunk K1 writes it.

Only `DuetApp` sends `CoreHost` a command, and a sibling view never reads another sibling's fields;
it subscribes to `DuetApp`. The four frame drivers read one `CoreHost` slot each, which the
frame-order rule above states and bounds. Appendix A gives the full ownership table.

### 10.3 The custom elements

The audit records two gaps. No timeline, waveform, knob, or level meter component exists, and no
toolbar component exists (audit 5, audit 9, PR 10.2, PR 10.3).

**Decision: the list is the contract's eleven rows plus `StageCurve`.** Eleven of the twelve rows
are GPUI elements and `SystemXMap` is not, which its own row states. **No thirteenth row exists**:
`ModeToolbar` is a trait and not an element (section 15.16), and revision 10 declared it with
`IntoElement` under `src/shell/`, which made the element list smaller than the element set
(critic K-11).

Contract 5.2 requires each of five
master stages to paint its own curve. Contract 4.2 and 1.10 require the same curve inside a mixer
strip's insert slot. Revision 4 had no element, no file, and no chunk for either surface, so PR M-03
and PR MA-02 had no user interface (critic R15). The design contract carries the `StageCurve`
appendix with the file, the chunk, the stories, and the visual rules, so the twelfth row is
settled and nothing is outstanding.

| Element | Purpose | File | Chunk |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SystemXMap` | Pure map from a beat position to an x offset. Not a GPUI element | `crates/duet-engrave/src/map.rs` | A1 |
| `StaffSystem` | Paints one system: lines, glyphs, stems, beams, ties | `crates/duet/src/element/staff_system.rs` | K2 |
| `WaveformLane` | Paints one audio lane from cached peak paths | `crates/duet/src/element/waveform_lane.rs` | K3 |
| `PlayheadLayer` | Paints the playhead only, in its own small view | `crates/duet/src/element/playhead_layer.rs` | K3 |
| `PunchRange` | The punch band and its two drag handles | `crates/duet/src/element/punch_range.rs` | K3 |
| `LevelMeter` | One meter bar, stateless, painted from the reading and the resolved over mark its parent hands it. `MeterLayer` paints the mixer strip row and every numeric readout | `crates/duet/src/element/level_meter.rs` | K4 |
| `Fader` | Channel fader with a dB taper and detents | `crates/duet/src/element/fader.rs` | K4 |
| `Knob` | Radial control with an arc and a pointer line | `crates/duet/src/element/knob.rs` | K4 |
| `AutomationLane` | Polyline and handles over a linear time axis | `crates/duet/src/element/automation_lane.rs` | K4 |
| `StageCurve` | One processor's response curve: an equalizer response, a compressor transfer curve with a live dot, a limiter gain-reduction bar | `crates/duet/src/element/stage_curve.rs` | K4 |
| `LufsMeter` | Momentary, short term, integrated, target, tolerance | `crates/duet/src/element/lufs_meter.rs` | K5 |
| `Toolbar` | The top bar container with the overflow rule | `crates/duet/src/element/toolbar.rs` | K1 |

`SystemXMap` is the one item that is not a GPUI element. It lives in `duet-engrave`, because it is a
pure function and a test must reach it without a window.

**Where three design-contract names land** (concern N-9). Each one is a framework component that
this design composes and never declares, so no row of section 1.5 carries it and this paragraph is
its home.

1. **`DropdownMenu`.** Contract 1.5 gives the top bar an overflow menu and contract 4.1 gives the
   transport one. **`DropdownMenu` is a TRAIT and not a widget**
   (`gpui-component-0.6.4/src/menu/dropdown_menu.rs:12`), and the same file implements it for
   `Button` at line 34. A view therefore builds no `DropdownMenu`: it calls
   `Button::dropdown_menu`, which the trait supplies, and fills the `PopupMenu` the closure
   receives. The path is `gpui_kit::component::menu::DropdownMenu`, because
   `gpui-component-0.6.4/src/lib.rs:56` declares `pub mod menu;` with no glob re-export
   (critic C16-6). `TopBar` builds both menus that way, with one item per
   `ToolbarControl` past `ToolbarGroups::visible`. The menu holds no state of its own, so no
   declaration names it.
2. **`ResizableState`.** Contract 1.6 gives the body an `h_resizable` with a persisted
   `ResizableState`. `ViewStateStore` owns the persisted numbers as `ProjectView` fields at B94,
   B97, and B98, and it hands them to the resizable panel on each render; a drag writes them back
   through `Verb::ViewSet`. The framework value is therefore rebuilt from the document and never
   stored beside it, which is why one owner exists (Appendix A).
3. **The two `StageCurve` sizes.** The design-contract appendix gives the element 96 logical pixels
   in a strip inspector and 160 in the master chain. Both are layout constants of one element in
   one file, which DR3 leaves to the design contract exactly as it leaves every other spacing
   number there; no Rust block of this document carries either one.

**Eleven more contract names are the same class** (concern N15-18). `ToggleGroup`, `NumberInput`,
`Spinner`, `SidebarHeader`, `SidebarGroup`, `resizable_panel`, `v_resizable`, `flex_1()`,
`min_w_0()`, `canvas()`, and `Window::paint_glyph` are framework components and framework calls that
this design composes and never declares, exactly as the three above are. Two need a sentence of
their own.

1. **`v_resizable`.** Contract 1.6 gives Mix a vertical split. `MixView` builds it from
   `v_resizable` with a `resizable_panel` per half, and `ProjectView` persists the fraction at B98;
   a drag writes it back through `Verb::ViewSet`, which is the `ResizableState` rule above applied
   to the second axis.
2. **`Window::paint_glyph`.** `StaffSystem` paints every Bravura glyph with it, from the
   `GlyphPlacement` list section 10.5 declares. It is the one call that turns an engrave result into
   ink, and no type of this plan wraps it.

**The contract writes a token id in dotted form and this document writes it in snake case.** The
two are one name: contract `duet.meter.peak_cap` is the `meter_peak_cap` field of `DuetTokens`. A
Rust field cannot carry a dot, and a contract row reads better with one.

`crates/duet/src/element.rs` holds one `mod` line per file above. **Chunk K1 writes `element.rs`
with all eleven `mod` lines, creates all eleven element files as stubs, and fills `toolbar.rs`**
(SM2). K2, K3, K4, and K5 each modify a stub and create no file, so the crate compiles at the end of
every phase. K6 writes no element file at all.

The linear timeline of Mix and Master is drawn by `AutomationLane` plus a ruler that `MixView`
composes from `h_flex` and quads. It is not a thirteenth element.

**`Toolbar` lands in chunk K1, not K6.** Four later chunks add a per-mode group set to the top bar,
and every one of them builds on the container and its overflow rule. Revision 9 put the container
four phases after the first chunk that needs it (critic W5).

#### Virtualization

**`gpui_kit::component::VirtualList` is the scroll surface of the wrapped view, and the work-area view owns
it.** `ComposeView` owns one in Compose and `RecordView` owns one in Record. Revision 9 cited a
paragraph in this section that did not exist, in Appendix C and in ADR 0006 decision 9, and the type
appeared only in the framework block of section 1.3 (critic W13).

Four facts settle it.

1. **The item is one system.** The item count is the length of the `Vec<SystemPlacement>` that the
   last engrave result produced, and `SystemView` renders one item.
2. **The width model is `SizePx`.** Each item reports its own width and height from
   `SystemPlacement::size`, which the layout output already carries. The audit records that
   `VirtualList` needs a width model the kit does not supply, and this is it.
3. **The identity is `SystemId`**, never the list index, which rule 2 of Appendix A requires and
   test 5 of section 10.7 asserts.
4. **The chunks are K2 and K3.** K2 writes the Compose list inside
   `crates/duet/src/compose/view.rs` and K3 writes the Record list inside
   `crates/duet/src/record/view.rs`, both of which those chunks already own (section 13.2). Test 4
   of section 10.7 asserts that the correct systems render at a given scroll offset, and SM7 binds
   it to those two chunks.

**Mix and Master use no virtual list.** The linear timeline draws one `AutomationLane` and one ruler
over the visible span, and the strip row is bounded by B86, so the whole row fits one pass.

### 10.4 Axis-aligned rectangles are quads, not paths

`Window::painted_quads()` returns the quads of the last frame. No equivalent exists for paths or
glyphs (audit 12).

**Decision: every axis-aligned rectangle is a quad.** Staff lines, ledger lines, bar lines, stems,
and lane backgrounds are quads. Paths carry slurs, ties, hairpins, beams, and stage curves. Glyphs
carry note heads, clefs, accidentals, rests, and dynamic marks.

Two gains follow. Those rectangles become assertable in a test. The batch also splits less often:
the audit warns that `BatchIterator::next` splits when the draw order alternates between primitive
kinds (audit 1, critic 9.2). The fixed order per system is quads, then paths, then glyphs.

### 10.5 How the engraver output reaches the element

`duet-engrave` is pure and produces absolute positions in pixels. The element adds only the element
bounds origin and performs no other arithmetic (critic 9.1).

```rust
/// What the paint element receives. Every position is absolute within the
/// system, in pixels, at the scale the engrave step was given.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct SystemPlacement {
    id: SystemId,
    tick_range: (Ticks, Ticks),
    size: SizePx,
    /// Axis-aligned rectangles.
    quads: Vec<QuadPlacement>,
    /// Slurs, ties, hairpins, and beams.
    paths: Vec<PathPlacement>,
    /// SMuFL symbols.
    glyphs: Vec<GlyphPlacement>,
    /// One rectangle per note, for hit testing.
    hits: Vec<NoteHit>,
    /// The monotone map from ticks to x for this system.
    map: SystemXMap,
}

/// Lay out a score.
///
/// # Errors
/// Returns `EngraveError::Metrics` when the font metadata lacks a glyph, and
/// `EngraveError::Overflow` when a system cannot fit the page width.
pub fn engrave(score: &Score, map: &TempoMap, options: &LayoutOptions, metrics: &FontMetrics)
    -> Result<Vec<SystemPlacement>, EngraveError>;

/// A monotone, strictly increasing, piecewise-linear map from a beat
/// position to an x offset inside one system.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
pub struct SystemXMap { knots: Vec<Knot> }

/// One knot. `x` is in pixels at the scale the engrave step was given.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
pub struct Knot { at: Ticks, x: f32 }

impl SystemXMap {
    /// The x offset of a beat position, by linear interpolation.
    pub fn x_for_beat(&self, at: Ticks) -> f32;

    /// The beat position at an x offset. The inverse exists because the map
    /// is strictly increasing.
    pub fn beat_for_x(&self, x: f32) -> Ticks;
}
```

`LayoutOptions` carries the scale in pixels per staff space, so a zoom change reruns `engrave`. That
is correct: a zoom in a wrapped view changes the staff size, which moves every line break
(critic 7.4).

Contract 3.1 names `SystemXMap` with `x_for_beat` and `beat_for_x`, and it states
`beat_for_x(x) -> Ticks`. This specification and ADR 0006 decision 2 say the same. The three
documents agree, and no signature item is open (critic S13).

The engrave step runs on `cx.background_spawn`, keyed by `Score::revision()`. The result lands
through `cx.update`, and a result whose revision no longer matches is dropped, per the coding guide
rule on stale work.

`FontMetrics` comes from our own SMuFL metadata reader in `duet-engrave`, which chunk A1 writes. The
audit records that no metadata reader exists in the kit, and contract 2.2 makes the reader a Duet
deliverable. The `smufl` crate is not a dependency. The Bravura font ships with the application, and
its SIL Open Font License text goes in the NOTICE file.

**The `Arc` costs one clone of the vertex vector per painted path per frame, and the site states
it** (concern N16-3). `gpui-pre-0.3.5/src/window.rs:4457` declares
`pub fn paint_path(&mut self, mut path: Path<Pixels>, ...)`, which takes the path BY VALUE, so a
cache that hands out a shared handle must clone the value at the paint site. **The saving is the
tessellation and not the allocation.** `PathBuilder::build` walks every segment and produces the
vertex list; a clone copies a vector that is already built. The `Arc` is there so the cache can hand
the same value to two frames and to two views without a second build, and B61 bounds the bytes it
holds. A design that removed the clone would have to hand ownership out of the cache, which turns
every hit into a miss.

**Who calls `PathBuilder::build()`, and what holds its result** (critic C15-2). The engrave result
carries a `Vec<PathPlacement>`, which is a point list and the INPUT of the cache. The GPUI
background path-build task turns one placement into one `Path<Pixels>` with `PathBuilder::build()`
and hands it back through `cx.update`, which is the one write path Appendix A names. `PathCache`
then holds that tessellated value, and `WaveformLane` paints it. **Nothing tessellates inside
`render`**, which is the whole reason ADR 0006 decision 6 adopted the cache and the reason design
contract 3.3 asks for it. Revision 15 cached the point list, which removed none of that cost.

**A miss paints nothing rather than tessellating on the frame path.** A `LaneView` that finds no
entry draws the lane background and requests the build, and the next frame paints the wave. B4
bounds a whole visible frame, and a tessellation inside that budget is the cost this design refuses
to pay.

**The paint segment and the path cache are app types.**

```rust
// in crates/duet
/// One painted piece of one region inside one system. Derived data.
///
/// It holds a beat span and a reference to the system's map. It holds no x
/// range and no frame range, so it encodes no scale of its own.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub(crate) struct TakeSegment {
    region: RegionId,
    system: SystemId,
    /// The beat span this segment covers, clipped to the system.
    beats: (Ticks, Ticks),
    /// The map that turns a beat position into an x offset.
    map: Arc<SystemXMap>,
}

/// The tessellated path cache. One owner per mode, bounded by B61.
///
/// **It holds the value `PathBuilder::build()` returns** (critic C15-2).
///
/// `order` is the least-recently-used queue: the front is the next key the
/// cache evicts when either half of B61 would be passed.
#[derive(Debug)]
pub(crate) struct PathCache {
    /// The TESSELLATED value, which is what ADR 0006 decision 6 adopted the
    /// cache for and what B61 bounds (critic C15-2).
    ///
    /// Revision 15 held an `Arc<PathPlacement>`, which is a point list that
    /// the engrave result already carries, so the cache removed none of the
    /// `PathBuilder::build()` cost the ADR named and saved one memory read of
    /// a value already in memory. **A `PathPlacement` is the cache INPUT and
    /// never its value.**
    paths: BTreeMap<PathKey, Arc<Path<Pixels>>>,
    order: VecDeque<PathKey>,
    bytes: u64,
}

/// One path-cache key. Section 10.5 gives the two timeline shapes.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
pub(crate) enum PathKey {
    /// The wrapped shape of Record.
    Wrapped { source: SourceHash, region: RegionId, system: SystemId, zoom: ZoomStep },
    /// The linear shape of Mix and Master.
    Linear { source: SourceHash, region: RegionId, zoom: ZoomScalar },
}
```

`TakeSegment` holds a `duet-session` identifier and a `duet-engrave` map. `duet-engrave` carries no
`duet-session` edge, so `crates/duet` is the lowest crate that reaches both (PL2). ADR 0006 states
the rest.

**Two path-cache keys exist, one per timeline shape, and every document states both.** Revision 9
stated one key and counted three documents that agreed, while Appendix A and ADR 0006 already
carried a second key over a type this document declared nowhere (critic W14).

| Timeline | Key | Owner | Where it is stated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wrapped, in Record | `(SourceHash, RegionId, SystemId, ZoomStep)` | `RecordView`. **Compose holds no cache**, because `ComposeView` owns no `LaneView` and paints no waveform (critic K-13) | This section, Appendix A, ADR 0006 decision 6, design contract 3.3 |
| Linear, in Mix | `(SourceHash, RegionId, ZoomScalar)` | `MixView` | This section, Appendix A, ADR 0006 decision 8 |
| Linear, in Master | the same key | `MasterView`, in its own `cache` field with its own `build` task | This section, Appendix A, ADR 0006 decision 8 |

**Mix and Master each own a cache, and neither reads the other's** (critic C16-15, C17-3).
Revision 17 gave the linear key one owner, `MixView`, while design contract section 5 gives Master
its own linear timeline. `MixView` and `MasterView` are two children of `DuetApp` with no edge
between them, and a GPUI child reaches a sibling only through its parent, so the second view had no
path to the value it was told to paint. **Two caches, not one shared handle**: a shared handle would
need a third owner and a notification path between two views that never render in the same frame,
because the mode machine shows one work area at a time. **B61 bounds each cache on its own**, and
the mode machine makes the worst case one live cache and one idle cache rather than two live ones.
Chunk K5 fills the Master cache and chunk K3 fills the Record cache; `PathCache` itself is K3's
file, and K5 modifies no file of K3.

**`SystemId` is in the wrapped key and absent from the linear one.** A region that runs past one
system appears on several systems, each appearance has its own path, and a two-part key would return
the first system's shape for every lane (critic N9). A linear timeline has no system, so a
`SystemId` there would be a constant that wastes a slot per region.

**`ZoomScalar` is derived, never persisted.** `state/view.json` holds one `ZoomStep` per mode
(section 3.6), and `ZoomStep::scalar` produces the linear scale, so the two values cannot disagree.
Both keys are bounded together by B61, and B62 is the working set the cache must hold at B1 before
it evicts anything, so B61 is larger than B62 by construction.

### 10.6 The duration selector and the held-key tracker

The audit records the gap: no API reports the set of held letter keys, and only modifiers have a
live query (audit 4).

PR 11 Q1 sets six letters: `w` whole, `h` half, `q` quarter, `e` eighth, `s` sixteenth, `t`
thirty-second. Contract 2.7 group 1 also binds `1` to `6` to the same six durations, as a sticky
selection.

**Two inputs, one output.** A number key sets a sticky duration. A held letter overrides it for as
long as the key is down.

```rust
/// Which duration letters are held now, in the ORDER they went down, over
/// the six letters of PR 11 Q1.
///
/// **It is a stack and not a bitset** (critic C19-W17). The product criterion
/// is "the key that went down last wins", and a bitset records membership and
/// not order, so revision 19 declared a type that could not answer its own
/// MUST and wrote "the shortest held letter wins" beside it. A key-down
/// pushes, a key-up removes that one letter wherever it sits, and
/// `release_all` empties the stack. Six letters exist, so the inline capacity
/// is six and the type allocates nothing.
///
/// **The name is the design contract's own.** Contract line 413 names one
/// `HeldDuration` field on the staff view, revision 13 declared the same
/// thing as `DurationKeySet`, and PL3 gives one name to one type, so the
/// architecture takes the contract's name (critic WR-20).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub(crate) struct HeldDuration(ArrayVec<NoteValue, 6>);

/// The duration the next click inserts.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub(crate) struct DurationSelector {
    /// Set by a number key `1` to `6`, and by the top bar toggle group.
    sticky: NoteValue,
    /// Which duration letters are held now.
    held: HeldDuration,
}

impl DurationSelector {
    /// The duration a click inserts now. A held letter wins over the sticky
    /// value, and **the letter that went down LAST wins** over one held
    /// before it, which is the product criterion (PR 11 Q1, critic C19-W17).
    pub(crate) fn pending(&self) -> NoteValue;

    /// Whether a letter is held, so the view can show the override state.
    pub(crate) fn is_overridden(&self) -> bool;

    /// Clear every held letter. Focus loss and window deactivation call it.
    pub(crate) fn release_all(&mut self);
}
```

`ComposeView` holds a `FocusHandle`, tracks `on_key_down` and `on_key_up`, and calls `release_all` on
`on_focus_out` and on a window deactivation. A key-up that lands outside the window is never
delivered, so the clear rule is the defect this design prevents (PR 10.1).

The pending duration is visible in two places while a key is held. The top bar flashes the matching
toggle, and a preview note head follows the pointer (PR 10.1, story C-09, contract 2.7 group 1).

### 10.7 The test strategy

Path output and glyph output are not assertable. The audit states it plainly: there is no
`painted_paths()` and no `painted_glyphs()` (audit 12).

**Rung one: the pure crates hold the assertions.** `duet-engrave` is tested with `cargo test` on
`SystemPlacement` values. The golden corpus B79 lives in `crates/duet-engrave/tests/golden/`, and a
comparator checks every field with a stated tolerance.

**Rung two: the element is tested for plumbing only.** A `#[gpui_kit::test]` renders `StaffSystem`
with a fixed `SystemPlacement` and asserts three things. The first is the requested layout size. The
second is the painted quad set, through `Window::painted_quads()`. The third is that a click at a
point resolves to the correct `NoteId`.
Every one of the eleven GPUI elements of section 10.3 carries the same three-part test.
`SystemXMap` is the twelfth row of that table and it is not an element, so it takes the pure-crate
test of rung one instead (critic K-11).

**Rung three: fourteen behaviours that no pure crate reaches** (critic 9.3). **Items 1 to 13 are
user-interface behaviours**, each one a required UI integration test that a chunk of line K writes.
**Item 14 is an engine behaviour and chunk C3 writes it**: it pushes a handoff and runs an audio
cycle, and no view takes part, so it lives beside the other `duet-engine` tests of that chunk. The
count word and the item count disagreed until this revision, and the chunk authors found it while
they placed the items across the K chunks.

1. The held-key state machine for all six duration keys.
2. The lost key-up case: the window deactivates while `w` is held, and the pending duration returns
   to the quarter note.
3. Hit testing: a click resolves to the correct pitch and the correct time through
   `SystemXMap::beat_for_x`.
4. Virtualization: the correct systems render at a given scroll offset.
5. Element identity: a stable, domain-derived `ElementId` per note and per region, never a list
   index.
6. Subscription retention: the view stores its `Subscription` and the event still arrives after a
   re-render. **The theme observer is one of the subscriptions this test covers** (critic WR-28):
   the test resolves `DuetTokens`, changes `cx.theme().mode`, runs one frame, and asserts that
   `cx.global::<DuetTokens>()` answers the dark value. Appendix A rule 3 makes a dropped
   subscription a defect, and this is the assertion that catches the one on `CoreHost`.
7. One frame driver: exactly one entity per work area requests an animation frame. The test counts
   the requests over ten frames.
8. Layout persistence: a split drag, a mode switch, a return, and the split is where the user left
   it (PR X-08).
9. **The clip latch lights and then clears, in that order.** The test asserts both directions,
   because a test with one oracle direction passes an inverted rule and revision 11's did
   (critic CR-1). It publishes a snapshot whose `over` bit and `latched` entry name strip `i`, runs
   one frame, and asserts that `CLIP` paints on strip `i` and on no other. It then dispatches
   `ClearClip`, runs ten frames against the same stale snapshot with `EngineState` in a state where
   no audio cycle runs, and asserts that `CLIP` paints nowhere. It then publishes a snapshot whose
   `latched` entry carries the new reset generation and asserts that `CLIP` paints again. The
   per-strip compare of section 7.3 is the mechanism.
10. **The breakpoint decides the shell.** The test opens the window at each of the three contract
    1.1 breakpoint widths and asserts the sidebar form, the inspector form, and that the work area
    is at or above the contract 1.6 minimum in every mode (critic W-5).
11. **One owner per meter.** The test renders a strip row and asserts that `MeterLayer` paints every
    live bar and every held over mark, and that `LevelMeter` paints the bar and the resolved mark a
    caller hands it and holds neither value (critic W-7, WR-5).
12. **The frame order: read the publications, then render.** The test publishes one of EVERY
    audio-written publication the section 5.8 snapshot table carries, which is a `MeterSnapshot`, a
    `TransportSnapshot` and a `SlotMeterSnapshot`, runs one frame, and asserts that `MeterLayer`,
    `MasterMeterLayer`, both `PlayheadLayer` values and one `StageCurve` reading through
    `CoreHost::slot_measure` all painted the values of that same frame. It then publishes a second
    set, runs one more frame, and asserts the same thing again. The oracle is that every view reads
    through `CoreHost` and no view owns a read end; revision 12 gave the one `MeterReader` to two
    views and the one `TransportReader` to two more (critic CR-11), and revision 23 published two
    of the three, so a frame order that read the third one frame late would have passed (critic
    C23I-W13).

13. **A frame driver starts as well as stops.** The test arms one track with the transport
    stopped, publishes a rising `MeterSnapshot` on each of ten frames, and asserts that
    `MeterLayer` paints a different value on each one. It then disarms the track, runs frames until
    the meter reads silence with no held mark, and asserts that the driver requests no further
    animation frame. **A third half covers the monitor path** (critic C15-10): the test sets one
    track to `MonitorMode::Always` with no strip armed and the transport stopped, publishes a rising
    snapshot, and asserts the same liveness, then sets `MonitorMode::Off` and asserts the loop
    ends. The oracle is `CoreHost::frame_demand`: the first half proves the start
    condition and the second half proves the stop condition. Revision 14 had the stop half and no
    start half, so an armed input meter froze (critic CR-21).

14. **The generation skew window is real, and this test opens it.** Chunk C3 writes it, in
    `crates/duet-engine/src/chain/graph.rs`. The test pushes a handoff at
    generation N plus 1, runs one audio cycle with the published `GraphChain` still at N, and
    asserts one `EngineFault::HandoffGenerationSkew { published, adopted }` and no panic. It then
    publishes N plus 1, runs a second cycle, and asserts no second fault and a graph that runs every
    strip. The oracle is that push-before-publish leaves a one-cycle window and that the window
    costs one cycle and one fault; revision 15 called the state unreachable (critic C15-9).

**Not a gate: the visual regression suite.** `render_to_image` and `capture_screenshot` exist on
macOS only, and those tests are `#[ignore]` by default (audit 12). The Definition of Done runs on
macOS and Linux, so the visual suite is a developer tool and never part of `scripts/dod.sh`.

**The frame budget is a bench, not an assertion.** No hook asserts a frame cost. `duet-engrave`
carries a `criterion` bench over the layout pass and over the peak path build, against B3 and B4.

ADR: `adr/0006-wrapped-timeline.md` covers the layout contract that sections 10.4 and 10.5 rely on.

## 11. Platform bifurcation

The operator set the targets: Ubuntu 26.04 with PipeWire on Linux, and macOS 26 on Apple hardware.
No PulseAudio or JACK client code exists, no deprecated interface is called, and there is no legacy
support of any kind (platform, operator decisions).

### 11.1 Which crates are platform specific

| Crate | Platform code | Fallback |
|---|---|---|
| `duet-midi` | `platform_macos.rs` over `coremidi`; `platform_linux.rs` over `pipewire`. Both implement `MidiPresence` only | `MidirPresence` with a poll at B22. `MidirStream` is the byte path on both platforms and carries no `cfg` |
| `duet-project` | The runtime socket directory, and the process liveness check of section 3.8 | `std::env::temp_dir()`; a liveness check that returns "unknown" and forces the retry path |

A native duplex backend on each platform is later work and is outside this plan (section 1.3). When
it starts, it is a new crate under `crates/` with the same `cfg` shape as the two rows above.

Every other crate is platform neutral. `duet-engine` carries no `cfg`, because cpal covers both
hosts behind one API. The host **selection** differs by platform and is data, not a `cfg`: section
5.4 gives the table.

### 11.2 The `cfg(target_os)` rule

`pipewire` does not build on macOS, and `coremidi` does not build on Linux. A plain dependency on
either would stop the workspace from building on both platforms.

**The declaration lives in `crates/duet-midi/Cargo.toml`, not in a consumer manifest.**

```toml
[dependencies]
duet-time = { workspace = true }
duet-command = { workspace = true }
midir = { workspace = true }
rtrb = { workspace = true }
crossbeam-queue = { workspace = true }
thiserror = { workspace = true }
tracing = { workspace = true }

[target.'cfg(target_os = "macos")'.dependencies]
coremidi = { workspace = true }

[target.'cfg(target_os = "linux")'.dependencies]
pipewire = { workspace = true }
```

`[workspace.dependencies]` in the root manifest pins both versions. A pin is not a dependency, so
the pin is harmless on either platform. The `pipewire` pin is 0.10.1, which is the version cpal
0.18.2 already brings through its `pipewire` feature, so the tree holds one version (section 8.1).

The rules, in full:

1. A `cfg(target_os)` branch appears in exactly one place per crate: the `mod` lines in the crate
   root. Each branch names `platform_macos.rs` or `platform_linux.rs`. **The same `cfg` guards the
   module and its dependency.**
2. Both modules implement the same trait from the crate root. No caller sees a `cfg`.
3. Every platform module states its fallback behaviour when the facility is missing.
4. A whole-platform crate is declared under `[target.'cfg(target_os = "macos")'.dependencies]` in
   the consumer manifest, by the same rule. This plan builds none.
5. No `cfg(target_os)` appears inside a function body. The branch is at the module boundary.
6. **The workspace builds on macOS and on Linux with no feature flag.** No platform capability is
   behind a Cargo feature, because a feature is a build choice and a platform is not.

### 11.3 The Linux display target

**Decision: Wayland is the Linux display target. XWayland is not a target.** The Ubuntu 26.04
desktop session runs only on Wayland, and X11 applications run through XWayland (platform, Ubuntu
facts).

**The `x11` feature cannot be disabled by a consumer, and this specification says so plainly.**
`gpui-kit` 0.6.4 depends on `gpui-pre` 0.3.5 with default features, and `gpui-pre`'s default set is
`font-kit`, `wayland`, `x11`, and `windows-manifest`. `gpui-kit` exposes no passthrough feature for
`x11`, so `default-features = false` on `gpui-kit` would remove its own `component` and `assets`
features and nothing else. The pin therefore stays as it is, the binary links both back ends, and
the release notes state that Duet is tested on Wayland and untested on X11. A future `gpui-kit`
release that exposes the feature turns this into a one-line manifest change.

### 11.4 The macOS minimum

**Decision: macOS 26.0 is the minimum, and two files state it.** The two files write `26.0`, because a deployment target is a dotted version; every prose sentence of this plan writes `macOS 26`, and the two forms name one release (concern N15-16).

| File | Key | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `crates/duet/packaging/macos/Info.plist` | `LSMinimumSystemVersion` | `26.0` |
| `.cargo/config.toml` | `[env] MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` | `26.0` |

`Info.plist` today carries no `LSMinimumSystemVersion`, so an older macOS would launch the bundle and
fail at a symbol. Chunk M0 adds both, and M0 is dispatched to the Orchestrator because
`.cargo/config.toml` is a policy file (SM4).

### 11.5 Build prerequisites

cpal links `libasound` on Linux whether or not the ALSA host is used, and the PipeWire host links
`libpipewire` (platform, cpal facts). Both development packages are therefore a build prerequisite,
not a run-time one.

| Platform | Packages | Who will install them |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | `libpipewire-0.3-dev`, `libasound2-dev`, `pkg-config` | Chunk M0 adds them to `scripts/bootstrap.sh` and to the Linux CI job |
| macOS | None beyond the Xcode command line tools | Nothing to add |

**The column is in the FUTURE tense on purpose** (critic C20-W6). `scripts/bootstrap.sh` installs
four cargo tools today and no system package of any kind, and revision 20 wrote "Installed by
`scripts/bootstrap.sh`" in the present tense. `scripts/bootstrap.sh` is a policy file, so chunk M0
owns both edits (SM4).

### 11.6 How the gate exercises both platforms

**The gate runs on `ubuntu-26.04` and on `macos-26`** (platform, runner facts). Both runners exist,
and `macos-26` is also `macos-latest`. Neither runner has a PipeWire daemon, and neither one needs
one.

Three rules keep the gate free of hardware.

1. The dummy backend serves every engine test and every export test.
2. A `MidiPresence` double and a `MidiStream` double serve every MIDI test. The first emits
   synthetic hot-plug events; the second records what the bind opened.
3. A test that needs a real device carries `#[ignore]` and a name that states the device it needs.
   The gate never runs it.

One platform-conditional test per platform module runs on its own runner and needs no device. It
opens the platform transport, asserts that `ports()` returns without an error, and closes it. An
empty port list is a pass.

**A second job, `audio-smoke`, proves the real backend once per run.** It runs on `ubuntu-26.04`
only, because a macOS runner offers no virtual audio device.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/audio-smoke.yml, written by chunk M8
# 1. apt-get install pipewire libpipewire-0.3-dev libasound2-dev pkg-config
# 2. start a user pipewire process; wait for its socket under B85 and fail on expiry
# 3. cargo nextest run -p duet-engine --run-ignored ignored-only \
#      -E 'test(pipewire_smoke)' --no-tests=fail
```

The test opens one PipeWire stream through the real backend, runs one cycle, asserts
`CycleOutcome::Ran`, and closes the stream. It is `#[ignore]` by default, so the gate never runs it
and a developer with no daemon is never blocked. A failure of `audio-smoke` blocks a merge by review,
not by the hook, because `scripts/dod.sh` is the only gate surface (CLAUDE.md).
