## 12. Error handling

### 12.1 One typed enum per failure surface

Each crate declares one error enum per bounded failure surface, named `<Surface>Error` and derived
with `thiserror`. Each variant names one failure mode. `#[from]` bridges a lower crate's error so
that `?` composes and the causal chain survives.

**`?` composes down the graph and never across it.** A `From` impl needs one local type, so
`#[from]` works exactly where the wrapping enum's crate also declares the wrapped enum or depends on
its crate. It does **not** work from a crate above `duet-command` into `GatewayError`: `EngineError`
and `GatewayError` are both foreign to `duet-core`, so the orphan rule refuses the impl. Each of the
four upper crates converts its own error into `UpstreamFailure` at its own boundary, which the
orphan rule allows because the source type is local there, and **every call site in `duet-core`
writes `map_err` and never `?`** (section 15.5, critic K-14).

**Section 1.5 is the one list of error enums.** Revision 4 kept a second list in this section, and
the two disagreed in both directions (critic R17). This section states the rule and lists nothing.

Three crates declare more than one enum, and each split is a real surface boundary.

| Crate | Enums | Why the split |
|---|---|---|
| `duet-session` | `SessionError`, `MixError` | The mix document has its own validation, and a routing cycle is not a track failure. |
| `duet-engine` | `BackendError`, `ConfigError`, `TransportError`, `EngineError` | A device failure, a configuration refusal, a transport refusal, and a run-time engine failure reach four different surfaces. `EngineError` wraps five causes with `#[from]`: `BackendError`, `ConfigError`, `TransportError`, `MediaError`, and `DspError`. The crate carries an edge to both lower crates, so both arms are correct; revision 9 wrote "the other three" (critic C4). |
| `duet-project` | `ProjectError`, `HistoryError` | The history sits behind one trait, and `ProjectError` wraps `HistoryError` with `#[from]`. |

`duet-command` declares two: `CommandError`, which carries the document variants `Serialize`,
`Parse`, and `Schema` that `BundleDocument` returns, and `GatewayError`, which is the refusal every
client reads. **`GatewayError` names no crate above `duet-command`.** Four of its arms used to wrap
`EngineError`, `ProjectError`, `InterchangeError`, and `ExportError`, and all four crates depend on
`duet-command`, so each arm was a Cargo cycle (critic S2). One arm, `Upstream(UpstreamFailure)`,
carries a plain-data mirror instead, and each upper crate converts its own error into it with
`From` at its own boundary (section 15.5). `anyhow` appears only in
`tools/xtask` (CLAUDE.md).

### 12.2 No `#[non_exhaustive]` on an internal error enum

`clippy::wildcard_enum_match_arm` is denied. `#[non_exhaustive]` forces a wildcard arm in every other
crate of the workspace, so the two rules contradict each other.

**Decision: no internal error enum carries `#[non_exhaustive]`.** The workspace is closed, no
external consumer exists, and forward compatibility across a version boundary is not a goal.
`wildcard_enum_match_arm` is the rule that catches real mistakes, so it wins. This contradicts the
general advice in the `rust-expertise` skill, and the reason above is why.

### 12.3 No panic path

`unwrap_used`, `expect_used`, `panic`, `todo`, `unimplemented`, `unreachable`, and
`indexing_slicing` are denied, and five house forms replace them.

1. `.get(index)` with a `let ... else`, or one of the five audio forms of section 5.11.
2. `div_euclid`, `div_ceil`, or `checked_div`, with a `NonZero` divisor where one exists.
3. `duet-time::convert` for every numeric narrowing (section 2.3).
4. `std::process::ExitCode` with a locked output handle in every binary.
5. **`assert!` inside a `const fn` whose only caller is a `const` item.** In a `const` item the
   assertion is evaluated at compile time, so a value the assertion refuses fails the build and no
   binary carries the panic. `clippy::panic` does not fire, because the root macro is `assert`, and
   `clippy::missing_assert_message` is denied, so the assertion carries its message.

**Form 5 carries one condition and one documentation rule.** The condition is that a `const` item
is the only caller; a `const fn` is an ordinary function at run time, and `[profile.release]` sets
`panic = "abort"`, so one run-time call with a refused value would end the process. The
documentation rule is that the function carries a `# Panics` section, because
`clippy::missing_panics_doc` is in `pedantic` and the workspace denies it; revision 10 declared
`Finite::from_finite_const` with an assertion, named no house form, and carried no `# Panics`
section, so the function did not build (critic W-9). **Three sites take form 5**, and each one needs no Appendix B.1 row, because none carries a
suppression: `Finite::from_finite_const` (section 2.6a), `duet-time::units::non_zero`, and
`duet-time::units::non_zero_u32` (section 1.6). Revision 23 named one site and gave the two `NonZero`
helpers a fallback arm that shipped a wrong constant instead; ADR 0008 records the repair.

### 12.4 How an engine fault reaches the user interface as a message

The audio thread must not signal the user interface, because that would mean a lock or an
allocation.

1. **A producer pushes a `Copy` record into the one `FaultQueue`**, which holds a
   `crossbeam_queue::ArrayQueue<EngineFault>` at B34 and an `AtomicU32` drop counter beside it.
   Section 5.8 decides the primitive, and this step follows that decision rather than restating it:
   **two threads produce**, the audio callback and the cpal error callback (TH11), so the primitive
   is the multi-producer one. `ArrayQueue::push` refuses the newest record on a full queue and the
   producer increments the counter with one relaxed fetch-and-add, which allocates nothing and locks
   nothing. **Keeping the oldest is the decision**: the first fault of a burst names the cause and
   every later one repeats it. `EngineProcess::faults` and `GraphConfigurator::faults` are the two
   declared handles, and the third clone moves into the cpal error callback when
   `ConfigureCommand::Open` builds the stream (TH11, TH13).
2. **The engine HANDOFF thread drains the queue**, once per pass of its own loop, which parks on a
   bounded receive of B108 (section 5.5, TH5). It sends one `EngineEvent::Fault` per record on the
   B138 channel, through `GraphConfigurator::events`, and it swaps the drop counter to zero and mints
   `EngineFault::FaultsDropped { count }` when the swap returns a value above zero. **Revision 19
   put the drain on the disk thread** (critic C19-10), which is the one
   thread in this design that waits on a file: a `TakeWriter` append on a network volume can hold
   that cycle for seconds, and every fault the stall caused waited behind the stall, `DeviceLost`
   included. The fault path must be the fastest path in the engine, not the slowest. The engine
   handoff thread touches no file, has a bounded period, and already raises `AllocationSlow` and
   `HandoffBusy`, so it is the one thread whose loop cannot be delayed by the failure it reports.
   **Revision 20 left section 5.8 routing this queue to the disk thread over `rtrb`** while this
   step named `ArrayQueue`, so one boundary carried two declarations and C19-10 was closed at three
   sites and open at the one table that decides (critic C20-5).
3. `duet-core` receives it on `DuetCore::engine_events`, records it on the engine state, and emits
   `CoreEvent::EngineFault` to every client on that client's own `ClientLink::events` (section 5.8).
   **Revision 22 declared neither end of that boundary** (critic C22I-1): the engine held no sender,
   the core held no receiver, and no `CoreInput` arm carried an `EngineEvent`, so the fault path was
   complete up to the engine handoff thread and stopped there.
4. `DuetApp` drains the core event channel in a `cx.spawn` task and maps the fault to a message.
5. A fault that makes the engine unusable, such as `DeviceLost`, moves the engine to
   `EngineState::Faulted { fault }`. The user interface shows a persistent bar with a reconnect
   action. **The view is never torn down.** The failure is a value in view state, which is the
   Resilient rule.

**Where a fault appears, in one rule.** Contract 1.9 says the status bar is the single place where
Duet reports a device problem, and no mode repeats a device banner except Record. Revision 4 pushed
every fault through `WindowExt::push_notification`, which would raise a toast the contract forbids
(critic R19).

| Fault class | Surface |
|---|---|
| Every device and engine fault | The status bar fault line. In Record, the Record top bar repeats it as a banner, which contract 1.9 allows. |
| A fault that marks a take | The take list marker, plus the `TakeFlags` of section 6.4 |
| `DeviceLost` and `CoreEvent::LockLost` only | A modal surface, because the user cannot continue without an answer |

`WindowExt::push_notification` is used for nothing else. That method is at
`gpui-component-0.6.4/src/window_ext.rs:65`, and `Root::push_notification` at
`gpui-component-0.6.4/src/root.rs:425` is the implementation.

```rust
/// Which fault one cycle raised. The audio thread writes a code and never a
/// message, so it formats nothing and allocates nothing (TH1). `EngineFault`
/// carries the payload, off the audio thread.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum FaultCode { Starved, Overflow, Shortfall, Misconfigured, DeviceGone }

/// A fault the audio thread reports. Every variant is `Copy`.
///
/// **Every per-track fault of this enum is LATCHED per track and per
/// condition** (critic C21I-W6, C21-1). `PlaybackStarved`, `CaptureOverflow`
/// and `CaptureShortfall` are the three faults an ordinary loaded machine
/// raises, and each one is per track and per cycle. At B1's 32 tracks and
/// B7's cycle rate an unlatched report is up to twelve thousand records a
/// second; B34 and its drop counter absorb that burst, and the engine handoff
/// thread would then send up to 64 `EngineEvent::Fault` values per B108 drain
/// into the B29 channel of every client, which is about 1300 events a second
/// against a frame rate of 60. Revision 21 performed this arithmetic for
/// `ChainSlotVacant`, which cannot happen in normal use, and not for the three
/// that a user meets.
///
/// **The latch is one `FaultRun` per condition on `ChainState`**, which
/// section 5.5 declares. `GraphRunner::run` pushes one fault per run, on the
/// cycle the run closes, and the `frames` payload of that fault is the count
/// of the whole run of cycles and not of one cycle. A run closes when the
/// condition stops and at B136 frames, so one device failure is one message
/// and a permanent failure is one message per B136 frames.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum EngineFault {
    /// `frames` is the whole run that `ChainState::starved` accumulated.
    PlaybackStarved { track: TrackId, frames: u32 },
    /// `frames` is the whole run that `ChainState::overflow` accumulated.
    CaptureOverflow { track: TrackId, frames: u32 },
    /// The input ring held fewer frames than the cycle asked for, so that
    /// part of the take is silent (section 5.4). `frames` is the whole run
    /// that `ChainState::shortfall` accumulated.
    CaptureShortfall { track: TrackId, frames: u32 },
    /// The requested block size was outside the server quantum range
    /// (section 5.4).
    BlockSizeAdjusted { requested: u32, actual: u32 },
    /// A `duet_media::TakeWriter` append or its flush passed B118 on the
    /// disk thread, so the capture pass ended early (section 5.10).
    ///
    /// The take keeps every sample the writer had already flushed and it
    /// carries `TakeFlag::HadOverrun`, because the frames the ring then
    /// refuses are the same hole (critic C19-10).
    CaptureStalled { track: TrackId },
    /// Ring allocation for a playable-set change passed B27, on the engine
    /// handoff thread.
    AllocationSlow { milliseconds: u32 },
    /// The B105 ring stayed full for B95 attempts, so the engine handoff
    /// thread gave up on one configuration (section 5.5).
    HandoffBusy { generation: u64 },
    /// The generation the runner adopted from the B105 ring and the
    /// generation the published `GraphChain` names disagree. Each number is a
    /// plain `u64`, because `Generation` is a `duet-engine` type and this
    /// enum lives in `duet-command` (PG20).
    ///
    /// **The window is real and it is two instructions wide** (critic C15-9).
    /// Step 3 pushes the handoff and then publishes the topology, so between
    /// those two the audio callback can resolve the topology at generation N
    /// and then drain and adopt handoff N plus 1. The cost is one cycle and
    /// one fault, so the failure stays inside one cycle, and test 14 of
    /// section 10.7 opens the window on purpose (section 5.6, critic CR-20).
    HandoffGenerationSkew { published: u64, adopted: u64 },
    /// A position of the chain-state array still holds `None` after a
    /// migration, so one strip has no state this cycle. The strip is silent
    /// and the graph keeps running (section 5.6).
    ChainSlotVacant { index: u16 },
    CalibrationInvalid,
    CalibrationTimeout,
    DeviceLost,
    ClockDrift { parts_per_million: i32 },
    ChainMisconfigured { strip: StripId },
    /// The fault queue was full, so this many faults were not reported.
    ///
    /// The engine handoff thread mints it when its drain swaps the
    /// `FaultQueue` drop counter to zero and reads a value above zero
    /// (section 5.8, section 12.4).
    FaultsDropped { count: u32 },
    /// `EngineEvent::StreamClosed` did not arrive inside B116 after the core
    /// sent `ConfigureCommand::Close`, so the device has not returned from
    /// `AudioBackend::stop`.
    ///
    /// **B116 is a report and not a cancel** (critic C20-4). The core raises
    /// this from its own clock, because the engine handoff thread is inside a
    /// blocking call and can measure nothing. The engine moves to
    /// `EngineState::Faulted` and refuses every open until `StreamClosed`
    /// arrives (section 5.5, section 5.12).
    ///
    /// **It carries no payload**, because `EngineFault` is `Copy` and TH9
    /// binds this enum; the device the user chose is on `EngineState` and the
    /// message reads it from there.
    DeviceStalled,
}

/// What the engine can be, as the user interface shows it.
///
/// Revision 5 gave three different failures one payload-free `NoDevice`
/// variant, so the status bar could not name the cause (critic S7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum EngineState {
    /// The platform audio server did not answer. `detail` names what was
    /// missing, and section 5.4 gives the Linux case.
    NoServer { detail: ServerDetail },
    /// The device open passed B18. `device` is the label the user chose.
    OpenTimeout { device: DeviceLabel },
    /// The server answered and offered no device at all.
    NoDevice,
    RateUnavailable { project: SampleRate, device: SampleRate },
    Running,
    Faulted { fault: EngineFault },
}

/// Why no audio server answered.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum ServerDetail { SocketMissing, LibraryMissing, ConnectionRefused }

/// A device name the user reads. It is not `DeviceId`, which is a
/// `duet-engine` type that `duet-command` carries no edge to (PL1).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct DeviceLabel(Box<str>);
```

**`fault_text.rs` holds FOUR tables, and each one is keyed on one enum.** Revision 5 named a row
for `NoServer`, which belonged to no enum it listed (critic S7). Revision 19 wrote "three tables"
here and "FOUR tables" three lines below, and chunk K1 reads this file top to bottom, so the wrong
count was the first one it met; DR1 forbids that shape (critic C19-W12).

**The fourth is the one
`EngineEvent::ConfigureRefused` needs.** `ConfigureRefused` carries a `ConfigError`, which reaches
the client, and `ConfigError` holds two arms `GatewayError` does not: `PoolHandoffBusy` and
`HandoffRetryPending`, with `NothingToHandOff` beside them. Revision 16 put those rows in the
refusal table, which keys on `GatewayError`, so chunk K1 would have written a match with no arm to
put them in (critic C16-13).

| Table | Key | Rows |
|---|---|---|
| The fault table | `EngineFault` | One row per variant |
| The refusal table | `GatewayError` | One row per variant, including `PoolExhausted`, `RingBudgetExceeded`, `StripBudgetExceeded`, `ParamBudgetExceeded`, `BusRoleReserved`, and one row per `(FailureSurface, FailureCode)` pair of `Upstream` |
| The CONFIGURE table | `ConfigError` | One row per variant. `EngineEvent::ConfigureRefused` carries the value, section 5.5 outcome three sends it, and the four budget arms share the wording of the refusal table's own rows |
| The engine state table | `EngineState` | One row per variant |

The three engine-state rows that revision 5 collapsed now read apart.

| State | Message |
|---|---|
| `NoServer { SocketMissing }` | `Duet found no PipeWire audio server. Start PipeWire, then choose a device in the status bar.` |
| `NoServer { LibraryMissing }` | `This build cannot reach the audio libraries. Install libpipewire and libasound, then restart Duet.` |
| `NoServer { ConnectionRefused }` | `The audio server refused the connection. Check that your user session owns it.` |
| `OpenTimeout { device }` | `<device> did not open in time. Choose another device, or unplug and reconnect it.` |
| `NoDevice` | `The audio server offered no device. Connect an interface, then choose it in the status bar.` |
| `RateUnavailable { project, device }` | `This project is at <p> Hz and the audio server runs at <d> Hz. Change the server rate, or convert the project.` |

## 13. The proposed plan graph

The unit of write scope is a directory or a named file. Two chunks may run together only when their
write scopes do not overlap.

Every chunk table carries a **Completion** column: one command that fails before the chunk and
passes after it, on macOS and on Linux.

### 13.0 The rules that bind every chunk

The gate runs on every commit, so a chunk that cannot commit is not a chunk. These rules are written
against the gate.

**SM0: every chunk verifies before it writes.** Every chunk body opens with the same sentence:
*verify the current state of the files in the write scope; report a discrepancy and stop, instead of
proceeding*. The repository already holds `crates/duet`, `tools/plan-db`, and `tools/xtask`.

**SM1: the manifest seam.** The `M<phase>` chunk of a phase does exactly four things.

1. It pins every third-party dependency and every dev-dependency the phase needs in the root
   `[workspace.dependencies]`, **and every one the phases after it need until the next manifest
   chunk**. **A pin is not a dependency**, so `cargo machete` reports nothing, and a pin made early
   costs nothing. The rule is stated because phases 5, 6, and 9 to 14 have no manifest chunk and
   three of their line chunks add a dependency; revision 16 left the rule implicit and closed one
   instance by hand (concern N16-6). **The edit is confined to `[workspace.dependencies]`**: SM4
   puts `[workspace.lints]` outside every engineer's reach.
2. It creates each new crate skeleton with **no `[dependencies]` section at all**. The skeleton is
   the `*.workspace = true` package fields, a `description`, `[lints] workspace = true`, and a
   `src/lib.rs` that holds the `//!` crate documentation and `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.
3. It writes the repository files its phase needs that are not crate source, which section 13.1
   names per phase.
4. **It adds the root `[workspace.dependencies]` entry of every skeleton it creates**, in the form
   `duet-<crate> = { path = "crates/duet-<crate>" }`. A member crate reaches an internal crate with
   `duet-<crate> = { workspace = true }`, and that entry resolves only when the root table already
   carries the path entry. SM4 puts the root manifest outside every line chunk's reach, so the chunk
   that creates the skeleton is the one chunk that can add it. Revision 23 gave the internal entries
   to no chunk at all, so every first chunk of a line had to read a root entry that nothing wrote,
   and the chunk authors of five lines each reported the same hole.

**The chunk that uses a dependency adds the `{ workspace = true }` entry to its own member manifest,
in the same commit as the code that uses it.** The rule covers a third-party pin and an internal
crate alike, and rule 4 above is what makes the internal half resolve. `cargo machete` therefore
passes at every commit.

**A phase has a manifest chunk only when it adds a crate skeleton, a pin, or a repository file.**
Phases 5, 6, and 9 to 14 add none of the three, so none has one. The manifest chunks are therefore
M0, M1, M2, M3, M4, M7, and M8, and the gap in the numbering is a fact, not an omission.

**The `M` class holds two kinds of chunk, and the number tells them apart.** An `M` chunk is a
chunk in no LINE, so SM6 does not bind it and PG40 reads no crate ownership for it. A **phase
manifest** takes the number of its own phase and does the four things above; `M0` to `M8` are
those. A **repair chunk** takes a number at or above 90 and lands a repair that the Architect
mandates after a line chunk has closed; SM9 states when one exists and what it may write. The two
ranges never overlap, so no reader takes `M90` for the manifest of a phase, and this plan states no
phase above 15.

**SM1 runs EVERY `M` chunk of a phase before EVERY line chunk of that phase, and the phase table
states the order** (critic C1-9). The rule already held the phase manifest apart that way, because
a line chunk builds inside a skeleton the manifest creates. A repair chunk needs the same order for
a second reason: **it changes behaviour that a line chunk of the same phase CONSUMES**, and the
write scopes are disjoint, so PG31 and `check-plan-graph` are blind to that edge. Chunk M91 changes
the value that `unit_to_i24` and `unit_to_i32` return; chunks D1 and T2 consume `duet-time` in
phase 1. A D1 branch that built against the pre-repair conversion would be green on its own and
wrong after the merge.

**A section 13.4 link was REFUSED for this, and the reason is SM8 itself.** Section 13.4 holds a
cross-line order, SM8 makes every link forward, and PG31 refuses a link whose predecessor shares a
phase with its successor. A link `M91 before D1` would therefore push D1 and T2 into phase 2 and
cascade the whole phase table, for an edge SM1 already orders. The cheaper mechanism is the one
that exists.

**The order inside one phase is the order the section 13.3 row prints, left to right.** For phase 1
that is **M1, then M91, then M90, then every line chunk of the phase**. M91 precedes M90 because
M90 adds rule CG9, which compares the Appendix B.1 reason cells with the `reason =` strings of
`crates/duet-time/src/convert.rs`, and M91 is the chunk that repairs those strings. A run of M90
before M91 would be red on its own gate.

**SM2: the module seam.** `clippy::mod_module_files` is denied, so a module directory needs a
sibling file.

**The first chunk of a line creates every module file the whole line will ever need, at every depth,
as a stub, and names each one in its write scope.** A stub holds the `//!` module documentation and
nothing else, so it compiles under the full lint set. Every later chunk in the line **modifies** a
stub and creates no file. **A directory is not a write scope under this rule**, because a stub needs
a name.

**SM2 covers `src/` only.** An integration test file under `tests/` is its own crate root and needs
no `mod` line anywhere, so the chunk that writes the test creates the file and names it in its own
write scope. Two chunks of one line may therefore each create a `tests/` file, which SM6 keeps in
two phases.

**SM3: the Completion command.** Every chunk carries one command that fails before the chunk and
passes after it. A command that is green on the current tree is not a completion check.

1. **Every filtered `cargo nextest` command carries `--no-tests=fail`**, so a filter that matches
   nothing is a failure and not a pass. The rule binds section 14 and both workflow files as well as
   this section; revision 5 stated it here and broke it at four sites (critic S8).
2. **A filter must not match a test an earlier chunk wrote.** `+` is a union in a nextest filterset,
   so `test(job)` also matches `job_runner`, which chunk I1 writes. Each filter below names a term
   no earlier chunk of its line produces (critic S20).
3. **A chunk whose work is platform-specific names a per-platform command and says which runner it
   runs on**; every other command runs on macOS and on Linux.
4. **`--locked` is correct only in a chunk that commits `Cargo.lock`**, which SM5 governs.

**SM4: a policy file is never in a line chunk's write scope, and its chunk goes to the
Orchestrator.** `scripts/dod.sh`, `scripts/bootstrap.sh`, `deny.toml`, `.cargo/config.toml`, the
three workflow files, `.claude/skills/gpui-kit/SKILL.md`, `clippy.toml`, **and the `[workspace.lints]` table of the
root `Cargo.toml`** are policy files. `M0`, `M7`, and `M8` carry a policy FILE, and all three are
dispatched to the Orchestrator rather than to an engineer, because CLAUDE.md makes a gate edit an
adjudication.

**The root `Cargo.toml` is one file with two owners, and the split is by table** (critic C16-W12).
Every manifest chunk writes `[workspace.dependencies]` and no manifest chunk writes
`[workspace.lints]`. Section 13.1 names `Cargo.toml` as a PATH in each manifest cell, because
section 13.0 makes a named file the unit of write scope and "root pins" is a subject. **An edit to
`[workspace.lints]`, to `clippy.toml`, or to the `deny.toml` ignore list made to get past the gate
is a defect that escalates, never a resolution**, which is CLAUDE.md's own rule. Revision 16 gave
three chunks an unbounded edit on the file that holds the lint policy.

**SM5: the lock-file rule.** A new member crate adds a `[[package]]` entry to `Cargo.lock`, and a
new member dependency adds an edge to it. `scripts/dod.sh` runs clippy with `--locked`, which fails
when the lock file is stale.

1. **`Cargo.lock` is in the write scope of every `M<phase>` chunk.**
2. **`Cargo.lock` is in the write scope of every chunk that writes a member manifest**, which means
   every chunk that adds a dependency, a dev-dependency, or a `[[bench]]` target. Section 13.2 names
   both files in the Writes column of each one.
3. **The chunk runs `cargo build --workspace` before it commits**, so the lock it commits matches
   the manifests it wrote.
4. **A merge conflict on `Cargo.lock` is resolved with
   `git checkout --ours Cargo.lock && cargo build --workspace`.** Every version is pinned in the
   root manifest, so the result is identical whichever side wins. This rule is stated once, here.

**SM6: a line is an ordered chain.** A **line** owns exactly one crate, and its chunks run one per
phase: **two chunks of one line never run in the same phase.**

The reason is the member manifest. SM1 makes the chunk that uses a dependency write its own member
`Cargo.toml`, and SM5 makes the same chunk write `Cargo.lock`. Revision 5 ran C2 beside C3, N2
beside N3, G2 beside G3, and F2 beside F3, and each pair wrote one member manifest in one phase
(critic S3). SM5 rule 4 resolves a lock conflict and says nothing about a manifest, and a manifest
conflict loses one side's dependency entries.

Two consequences are stated, not hidden.

- **Every member manifest has one writer per phase, by construction.** Only chunks of one line write
  that crate's manifest, and SM6 puts them in different phases. The `M<phase>` chunk is the one
  other writer, and SM1 runs it alone before every line chunk of its phase.
- **The plan is longer and narrower than revision 5's.** Sixteen phases replace ten, and the widest
  parallel count falls from eleven to seven, at phase 4. The last phase holds no chunk at all and
  the two before it hold one each, because the application line has six chunks and no cross-line
  dependency after phase 11. **Every number in this bullet comes from the phase table**, and PG34
  holds the tail of that table; revision 17 added the sixteenth phase and left this paragraph
  stating thirteen phases and a widest count of eight (critic C17-W10). The alternative rule,
  "two chunks of one line never write the manifest in one phase", would keep the shorter plan and
  would need a per-chunk manifest audit that no machine performs. A rule a machine can check by
  reading the phase table is worth three phases.

#### Every chunk line and the crate it owns

PG31 and PG31b read this block. SM6 says a LINE is an ordered chain of chunks over one crate, and a
chunk id alone does not state its line: `T1` to `T4` are four lines of one chunk each, and `M0` to
`M8` are manifest chunks and no line at all. Revision 17 derived the line from the first letter of
the id and skipped `M` and `T` inside the machine, with no line of this document stating the
exemption (critic C17-W9). The map is data now, so the rule carries no hidden set.

#### Every same-phase crate edge that does not bind

PG31b reads this block. It pairs the line chunks of each phase, asks the section 1.3 edge list
whether one crate depends on the other, and refuses a pair that is neither a 13.4 link nor a row
here. SM8 states when an edge BINDS: when the consumer chunk adds the `{ workspace = true }` entry
for that crate, or names a type the producer chunk in the same phase declares. Every row below is a
pair where neither holds, with the reason.

**Why the block exists rather than a silence.** C16-12 was three chunk pairs sharing a phase across
a crate edge with no link row for any of them, and PG31 reads rows, so a new pair in that state
stayed invisible (critic C17-W9). PG31b reads no row: it derives the pair set from the phase table,
the line map, and the 1.3 edges. Twenty-four pairs exist in this plan and every one is reviewed
here. A twenty-fifth pair is a red run until somebody states why its edge does not bind.

**`T1` to `T4` are four lines and not one**, so two of them may share a phase when no link binds
them, and SM6 is satisfied by construction. **A manifest chunk is in no line**: SM1 runs it alone
before every line chunk of its phase, and exactly one PHASE MANIFEST exists per phase, so two of
those can never share one. A repair chunk of SM9 is in no line either, and two `M` chunks of one
phase are held apart by the write-scope rule that PG31 and `check-plan-graph` already apply to
every pair of one phase. Those are the two exemptions, and this paragraph is the site that states
them.

**SM8: every link is forward, and a crate edge inside one phase is a defect.** Section 13.4 holds
one row for every cross-line order, section 13.3 holds the phase of every chunk, and **PG31 reads
both and fails when a link's predecessor is in the same phase as its successor or in a later one.**

**The rule covers a SAME-PHASE edge and nothing else** (critic N21-9). Section 13.4 carries one
row for every edge that binds between two chunks in ONE phase; an edge whose two chunks sit in
different phases is already ordered by the phase table and needs no row, and all 27 such edges of
section 1.3 are order-correct today. Revision 21 wrote that section 13.4 carries one row for every
edge that binds, which under the wide reading left 27 edges with no row and no rule able to say why
that was correct.

The rule exists because the phase table is the parallelism plan: a phase ASSERTS that its chunks
have no ordering between them. Revision 16 put three pairs in one phase across an edge section 1.3
states, and carried no link row for any of them: `T2` and `T3` over `duet-session -> duet-score`,
`T4` and `X1` over `duet-interchange -> duet-command`, and `J1` and `K1` over `duet -> duet-agent`
(critic C16-12). Under SM1 the consumer of each pair must add a `{ workspace = true }` entry for a
crate its partner is building in the same phase, and it must name types that partner has not
written yet.

**When a 1.3 crate edge binds inside a phase, and when it does not.** The edge binds when the
consumer chunk adds the `{ workspace = true }` entry for that crate, or names a type the producer
chunk in the same phase declares. It does not bind when the consumer chunk added its entry in an
earlier phase and names only types an earlier chunk of the producer line already wrote: `E1` and
`D2` share a phase over `duet-analysis -> duet-dsp`, and `E1` names `SampleSource` and `Pyramid`,
which `D1` wrote one phase earlier. **Section 13.4 carries one row for every edge that binds**, so
the table is the record and PG31 is the check.

**SM7: no command selects a test that no chunk writes.** Every test name that a Completion command
or a workflow command names in a filter, and every integration target a command names with
`--test`, is written by exactly one chunk. That chunk lands in a phase at or before the phase of
the chunk that owns the command.

The rule binds three places. A **Completion** command satisfies it by construction: SM3 makes the
command fail before the chunk and pass after it, so the chunk that carries the command writes the
test. A **section 14 rung-two** command and a **workflow** command satisfy it only by a table, and
section 14 holds that table: one row per selected test, with the filter name, the file, the chunk
that writes it, and the command that selects it. **PG16 checks the table**, and it fails on a name
section 14 selects with no row, and on a row whose chunk id appears in no phase.

Revision 6 broke the rule at four sites. Two rung-two commands and both `soak.yml` commands selected
`soak`, `proptest_large`, and `crates/duet-engine/tests/alignment.rs`, and no Writes column carried
any of the three (critic N3). `--no-tests=fail` made each one a red job rather than a vacuous green,
which is louder and no better.

**SM9: the Architect owns every path under `roadmap/`, and a chunk that finds its own brief wrong
STOPS.** Chunk M0 found that no chunk of this plan names a path under `roadmap/` in its
`write_scope`, and it widened its own scope to land a repair (M0X-W4, R3-N3). A chunk that widens
its own `write_scope` makes `check-plan-graph` circular: the guard reads the front matter, so a
chunk that edits the front matter proves only what the chunk decided. The rule has five parts.

1. **The Architect is the one writer under `roadmap/`.** `roadmap/duet-v1/architecture.md`, every
   `roadmap/duet-v1/*.md` chunk file, `roadmap/duet-v1/design-contract.md`,
   `roadmap/duet-v1/product-requirements.md`, `roadmap/duet-v1/adr/`, and
   `roadmap/duet-v1/tools/` are the Architect's. `roadmap/duet-v1/reviews/` is append-only and the
   Critic is its writer; rule CL1c of section 1.5 depends on that, and the Architect never rewrites
   a stored review.
2. **`roadmap/duet-v1/plan-graph.md` is GENERATED, and it is the one exception.**
   `cargo xtask check-plan-graph roadmap/duet-v1 --write-manifest` writes it from the chunk front
   matter. A chunk that changes the generator regenerates the file in the same commit and names the
   path in its own `write_scope`. That is a refresh of a build artifact and never an edit to a
   brief, so it does not make the guard circular: the front matter the guard reads is unchanged.
   **Chunk M90 owns the `MANIFEST_NOTE` repair**, because the generated text still credits
   `tools/plan_graph_check.py`, which is the Python prototype and no longer the generator (R3-N3).
3. **An engineer that finds its own brief wrong STOPS and reports.** It never widens its
   `write_scope`, it never edits its own chunk file, and it never edits `architecture.md`. It
   writes one plan-store row and it returns the key upward. The row is the FIXED key
   `escalation:<chunk id>-<n>`, written with
   `.claude/plan-coordination/db.sh put roadmap/duet-v1 escalation:<chunk id>-<n> '<json>'`, and
   the JSON carries `kind` (`architect_decision` or `gate_policy`), `source` (the chunk id and the
   report or section that found it), `title` (one line), `detail` (what the brief states, what the
   code states, and what the chunk cannot do), `tier` (`CRITICAL`, `HIGH`, `MEDIUM` or `LOW`),
   `acknowledged_ts` (`null`), `verdict` (`null`), and `opened_ts` (an ISO 8601 time in UTC). The
   nine rows of 2026-09-22 are the worked examples. **A chunk that stops on an escalation is a
   completed chunk when every other step of its brief passed**; the escalation is the deliverable
   for the step it could not take.
4. **A repair chunk carries a document edit only when a `tools/xtask` register change makes the two
   atomic.** The `DATA_BLOCKS` register of `tools/xtask/src/check_placement.rs` states the floor of
   every `<!-- GUARD BLOCK ... -->` block, PG27 refuses a marker that differs from the register,
   and PG27b refuses a block that holds more rows than its floor. A row added to a registered block
   therefore needs the document and the register in ONE commit, which the Architect alone cannot
   make. In that one case the Architect writes the exact replacement text into the repair chunk's
   body and the chunk applies it; the Architect still authors every word, and the chunk is the
   carrier. A repair chunk that carries no register change names no path under `roadmap/`.
5. **An escalation row has a CLOSE state, and an open row BLOCKS a dependent chunk** (critic C1-7).
   The `acknowledged_ts` and `verdict` fields of part 3 had no writer and no time, so the channel
   carried a message that nobody ever answered. **The Architect writes both fields on the same row,
   in the act that resolves the escalation**, with
   `.claude/plan-coordination/db.sh put roadmap/duet-v1 escalation:<chunk id>-<n> '<json>'` over the
   whole row: `acknowledged_ts` takes the time the Architect read the row, and `verdict` takes one
   of `RESOLVED`, `DEFERRED` or `REFUSED` plus one sentence that names the section, the ADR, or the
   repair chunk that carries the answer. **A row whose `verdict` is `null` is OPEN, and a chunk that
   depends on an open row does not dispatch.** The Orchestrator reads
   `.claude/plan-coordination/db.sh scan roadmap/duet-v1 escalation:` before it dispatches a phase,
   and a `DEFERRED` verdict names the plan-store item that holds the deferral. A completed chunk
   beside an open row is the state this rule refuses: it lets a fresh Orchestrator read the plan as
   finished while its principal deliverable is undone.

**Why the rule is written this way.** The alternative is a chunk that owns its own brief, and that
is the shape M0 reported: the document a guard reads and the party the guard judges become one
hand. The escalation row sits in the plan store, which is outside every engineer's write scope and
outside the repository, so a stopped chunk leaves evidence the Architect cannot quietly retype.
That is the same property rule CL1c already relies on.

**Three chunks of line K own `crates/duet/Cargo.toml`, `crates/duet/benches/`, and `Cargo.lock`,
one per phase.** K1 adds the internal `{ workspace = true }` entries in phase 9, K4 adds the Mix
frame-cost bench in phase 12, and K5 adds the Master frame-cost bench in phase 13. SM6 keeps the
three in three phases, so the manifest has one writer per phase and the seam is serial. **Revision
16 gave K5 the Master bench in its goal and none of the three paths in its Writes column**, so the
chunk was told to write a file outside its own scope (critic C16-W10).

**Chunk I3 owns a bench, so it owns the manifest and the directory.** Section 5.12 lists the
`Arc::make_mut` clone as a measured path against B5, and revision 5 gave I3 neither
`crates/duet-core/Cargo.toml`, nor `benches/`, nor `Cargo.lock` (critic S4). SM6 puts I3 in phase 9
and I4 in phase 10, so the `duet-core` manifest has one writer per phase.

**The note-entry drain is split across a crate boundary, and the split is the framework rule**
(critic C16-W9). Section 1.3 lets only `crates/duet` and `duet-agent` name a framework type, and
`duet-core` carries no `gpui-kit` edge. Revision 16 gave chunk I3 "the note-entry drain in
`Window::on_next_frame`", which puts a GPUI type inside `duet-core`. The registration is a
`crates/duet` act and the drain is a `duet-core` act.

- **I1, phase 7, writes `DuetCore::drain_note_entries`**, which takes no framework type and returns
  the entries it drained. It is available to every later chunk in `duet-core`.
- **I3, phase 9, writes `midi_entry.rs`**, which maps one `NoteEntry` to one score command. It names
  no framework type either.
- **K1, phase 9, registers the call.** `CoreHost::poll_frame` already runs once per frame through
  `Context::on_next_frame` (section 10.2), so the drain is one more statement inside a method K1
  owns. K1 calls the phase-7 method, so `I1 before K1` is the link that covers it and no new link
  enters section 13.4.

**Verb dispatch lands in two stages.** I1 delivers every arm whose dependency is in an earlier
phase. I4 delivers the three arms that need `H3` and `F2`. I1 returns
`GatewayError::NotYetImplemented` for exactly those three, and a test asserts the count is three.

**I4 does NOT delete the variant, and the reason is a write scope** (critic C16-10). Line 1.5 places
`GatewayError` in `duet-command`, and `T4` is the one chunk that writes `duet-command`, seven phases
earlier. A deletion would make I4 edit a file outside its own line and outside its own write scope,
which is the contract that lets phases run in parallel. I4 therefore leaves the arm declared and
adds `no_verb_is_unimplemented`, which drives every `Verb` arm and asserts that none answers
`NotYetImplemented`. The arm stays as the declared shape of a verb the plan has not built, and the
test is the guard that no verb uses it.

**I4 adds `crates/duet-core/Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock` to its write scope**, because the
`MasterMeasure` arm calls the measure job and the `ExportAudio` arm calls the encode stage, both in
`duet-export`. SM1 makes the chunk that uses a dependency add the `{ workspace = true }` entry in
the same commit, and SM5 rule 2 then also requires the lock. SM6 keeps I4 alone in its phase for
that manifest.

**The headless product path is TWO tests, and the phase numbers are the reason** (critic C16-9).
`end_to_end` is `Plain`, so `scripts/dod.sh` runs it at every commit from phase 8 onward. The export
half needs `I4` in phase 10, `H3` in phase 9, and `H4` in phase 10, so a single test would fail
every commit of phases 8 and 9, and CLAUDE.md forbids `--no-verify`. The plan would then hold an
interval in which no engineer can commit.

`end_to_end` therefore asserts what phase 8 delivers and nothing more: `ProjectCreate` with the SATB
template, `TrackAdd`, `TrackSetInput`, `TrackSetArmed`, a MIDI file import, eight recorded bars from

with a byte compare of the score, `Status` with the take count, and a `ViewSet` and `ViewGet` round
trip. `export_end_to_end` asserts the rest, and J3 in phase 11 is the one chunk that writes it.
**Neither test is `#[ignore]`**, because each one runs green in every phase from the one that writes
it. SM2 allows both files, because an integration test under `tests/` is its own crate root and
needs no `mod` line.

**`TopBar` calls one `ModeToolbar` per mode through a registry, and each mode owns its own file.**
`ModeToolbar` is a trait (section 15.16). K1 writes `top_bar.rs`, the `Toolbar` element that carries
the overflow rule of contract 1.5, the `BTreeMap<Mode, Box<dyn ModeToolbar>>` registry, and the four
implementations `ComposeToolbar`, `RecordToolbar`, `MixToolbar`, and `MasterToolbar`, one per file
under `src/shell/`. **Each of the four compiles and runs at the end of phase 7**: `group_count`
returns zero and `render` returns an empty `Toolbar`. K2, K3, K4, and K5 each **replace one `render`
body and one `group_count` body** in its own file, and **none of them edits `top_bar.rs`**, which
sits in K1's write scope and in no other.

**SM2 gains one stated exception, and this is the site that states it.** A seam implementation is
not a stub: K1 writes the whole `impl ModeToolbar for ...` block with a body that returns an empty
value. SM2 forbids a stub with an item, because a stub is a file a later chunk fills; a seam
implementation is a file a later chunk **replaces**, and it is reachable from the call graph on the
day it lands.

Three defects close here. Revision 9 sent four chunks to one file that no chunk gave them, so each
one stopped under SM0, and it put the `Toolbar` container in K6, four phases after K2 built on it
(critic R9, W5). Revision 10 made each of the four a documentation-only stub, which `TopBar` could
not call and which `dead_code` refuses (critic W-2).

#### Every MUST story and the chunks that build it

Product requirements section 8 holds 64 MUST rows. Revision 5 carried 18 of them under a heading
that claimed completeness, and five MUST stories appeared nowhere in this document (critic S12).
Every row below names the chunk that holds the model, the chunk that holds the runtime or the verb,
and the chunk that holds the view. A dash means the story needs none of that kind.

**Three claims, and each one is true by construction.**

0. **No link of section 13.4 runs backward or sideways.** SM8 states the rule and PG31 reads this
   table and that one. Revision 16 put three pairs in one phase across a crate edge section 1.3
   states and carried no link row for any of them, so the phase table asserted a parallelism the
   build could not deliver (critic C16-12). `T2 before T3`, `T4 before X1`, and `J1 before K1` are
   now rows of 13.4, and the phase numbers above follow the whole link set. **The plan is two
   phases longer than revision 16's and its widest phase falls from eight to seven**; that is the
   honest cost of an order the document already stated.

1. **No two line chunks in one phase share any write scope.** SM6 puts the chunks of one line in
   different phases, and two lines own two crates, so no file is shared. `Cargo.lock` is the one
   exception, and SM5 rule 4 resolves it deterministically. Revision 5 made the same claim while
   four pairs of phase-4 chunks each wrote one member manifest (critic S3).
2. **Every member manifest has one writer per phase.** It follows from claim 1, plus SM1, which runs
   the `M<phase>` chunk alone before every line chunk of its phase. **Two files an `M` chunk creates
   are later edited by a line chunk**: the `src/lib.rs` of a new crate, to which the line chunk adds
   `mod` lines, and that crate's own `Cargo.toml`, to which the chunk that first uses a dependency
   adds the `{ workspace = true }` entry (SM1). Revision 11 named the first and omitted the second,
   which is thirty pairs (critic 16). **The two are not in two phases, and revision 13 said they
were** (critic C-11). Every manifest chunk shares its phase with the line chunks that edit the
skeletons it creates: M0 with T1, M1 with T2 and D1, M2 with T3, A1, and E1, M3 with T4 and N1,
M4 with C1, F1, G1, and X1, M7 with H1 and I1, and M8 with J1. The mechanism is the serial order SM1 states **inside** one phase: the `M<phase>`
chunk runs alone and completes before any line chunk of that phase starts, so one writer holds each
file at a time and neither pair is a collision.

**Phase 15 has a width of zero, and that is not an omission.** Rung three of section 14 is a
judgement the operator signs; it names no chunk, it writes no file, and it carries no Completion
command, so a width of one would count work that no agent performs (critic C7).

**The cost of SM6 is a narrow tail.** Phases 12 to 14 hold one chunk each,
because the application line has six chunks and no cross-line dependency after phase 11. Section
13.0 states why the rule is worth that cost.

**Per-phase `Cargo.lock` writer counts, phases 0 to 15: 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 6, 4, 4, 4, 3, 1, 0, 1, 1,
0, 0** (concern N16-5, critic C19-6). SM5 rule 4 resolves a conflict deterministically, because
every version is pinned in the root manifest. The counts are printed so the size of the overlap is
visible rather than implied.

**The sequence is DERIVED and never typed, and PG35 is the derivation.** Revision 19 wrote a
hand-counted sequence and it was wrong at seven of the sixteen phases, which is the defect class
DR3 exists to remove: a number this document chooses has one home, and a number this document
MEASURES has a machine. A lock-file writer is a fact of the chunk tables alone, so PG35 reads the
section 13.1 manifest table, the trunk table, and every section 13.2 line table, counts the chunks
of each phase whose `Writes` cell names `Cargo.lock`, and fails on a sequence that differs. The
sequence therefore falls under DR3 exemption 4, a recorded count of this document that changes
whenever this document changes, and no reader has to add the rows by hand to check it.

**The rule's own limit, stated here**: it counts a chunk that DECLARES the file in its own write
scope. A chunk that writes a member manifest and omits `Cargo.lock` from the cell is a defect SM5
names and this rule cannot see, because the cell is the only evidence the document carries.

## 14. The measurable completion outcome for version one

Three rungs. Two carry a command. One carries a name and a signature.

### Rung one: the repository gate

```
bash scripts/dod.sh
```

It passes when every one of these holds. **A line that names a state the repository does not hold
yet is written in the FUTURE tense and names the chunk that builds it** (critic C20-W6). Revision
20 wrote four such lines in the present tense, inside the one section whose job is to state what
"done" means, so a reader could not tell a fact from a plan.

- Every crate is a workspace member and declares `[lints] workspace = true` and a `description`.
  **Chunk M0 will add `cargo xtask check-manifests` to `scripts/dod.sh`**, which reads every member
  manifest and asserts both. **Neither half is covered today, and `clippy::cargo` cannot cover the
  `description` half at all** (critic C20-W7): `cargo_common_metadata` skips a package whose
  `publish` field is set, `Cargo.toml:22` sets `publish = false`, and every member inherits it. The
  evidence is in the tree rather than in the lint's documentation: the same lint demands `readme`,
  `keywords` and `categories`, no member manifest sets one of the three, and the clippy gate is
  green on `main`. A lint that would deny three missing fields and denies none is a lint that is not
  running. The plan creates fifteen crates, and a crate that omits the `[lints]` line sits silently
  outside the whole lint policy, which is CLAUDE.md's own wording. A rung that reports a state no
  step measured is the same class as a probe that records a line no run produced (critic C16-W16,
  C17-W3).
- `cargo fmt --all --check` is clean.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` is clean.
- `cargo doc` is clean at `-D warnings`.
- `cargo nextest run --workspace --locked` and `cargo test --doc` are green.
- `typos` is clean. **It cannot fail the gate today**: `scripts/dod.sh` runs
  `typos --exclude 'crates/duet/assets/fonts/*' || printf ...`, so a finding prints and the script
  continues. **Chunk M90 removes the fallback and the flag, and writes the configuration that makes
  the plain call green**, and until it does this line is a developer signal and not a pass
  condition (critic C20-W6, escalation M0-1). **The repair is a configuration file and no prose
  edit at all.** Revision 24 stated a total that a run refuted, and revision 25 stated a second
  total that a second run refuted (critic C1-3). **The cause is structural, so this bullet states
  NO total.** A plain `typos` total stated inside a checked file cannot be stable, because the
  sentence that states the partition writes the very tokens it counts into this file and into two
  more. Each written token is one more finding, so a third re-measurement gives a fourth wrong
  number. The bullet states instead the CLASSES, the RULE that answers each class, and the one
  number a reader can reproduce.

  **FIVE classes COVER every finding, and the class set is EXHAUSTIVE.** The decision rests on
  that property alone. The classes are NOT disjoint, and they do not need to be: a finding inside an
  excluded path can also match a word class, and either rule answers it. No rule reads disjointness.
  Each class carries its own rule.

  1. **Third-party SMuFL data.** Every finding inside
     `crates/duet/assets/fonts/bravura_metadata.json`. This repository copies that file and never
     authors it. **Rule: a path exclusion.**
  2. **Append-only records.** Every finding under `roadmap/duet-v1/reviews/` and
     `roadmap/duet-v1/research/`. Rule CL1c of section 1.5 rests on a review file that nobody
     rewrites. **Rule: a second path exclusion.**
  3. **The generated protocol word.** The word `Criticals` in each of its three cases.
     `tools/xtask/src/check_closure.rs` GENERATES the count sentence that holds it, and rule CL1b
     of section 1.5 makes that sentence a protocol string. No identifier holds the word.
     **Rule: three word entries, one per case.**
  4. **The SMuFL glyph-name identifiers.** The three whole glyph names `ArticAccent`,
     `ArticStaccato` and `note32ndUp`. Design contract section 4.3 states the third one.
     **Rule: three identifier entries** (critic C1-12). `[default.extend-identifiers]` is the
     narrow tool: it allows each whole name and allows nothing else. A word entry for the bare
     prefix of the first two would hide a real misspelling of the word "arctic" anywhere in this
     repository for ever, and the class-one exclusion already answers every hit of that prefix
     inside the font file.
  5. **The domain term.** The word `tuplets`, which section 2.4 states. **Rule: one word entry.**

  **A sixth named set is a SUBSET of class two and not a class of its own.** Five findings under
  the two excluded directories are genuine prose typos, and this plan KNOWINGLY accepts them. Two

**What a GATE is, stated once.** A gate is a surface that refuses a COMMIT. `scripts/dod.sh` is the
only one, which is CLAUDE.md's own rule, and the versioned hooks `.githooks/pre-commit` and
`.githooks/pre-push` exec it. A workflow job refuses no commit; it reports a red check that a
reviewer acts on. The distinction matters because chunk T1 read it the other way: nine commits
passed the local hook and the `plan-lint` job then refused on `check-placement` rule VR1, which cost
a full push and a continuous-integration round trip (escalation T1-5, critic 3-N7).

**The three CHEAP plan guards run inside `scripts/dod.sh`, and the step is PATH CONDITIONAL.** Chunk
M90 adds it. The step runs `cargo xtask check-placement roadmap/duet-v1/architecture.md`, then
`cargo xtask check-plan-graph roadmap/duet-v1`, then
`cargo xtask check-plan-graph roadmap/duet-v1 --check-manifest`. **It runs only when the change
under test names a path that opens `roadmap/`.** When no clause of the denominator below names one,
the step PRINTS `plan guards: skipped (no change under roadmap/)` and the gate continues; a skip
that prints is not a silent skip.

**The denominator has THREE clauses, and the third one is why the step is reachable at all** (critic
C1-2). Revision 24 defined it as the staged diff plus the working-tree diff against `HEAD`, and both
of those are EMPTY on the two surfaces that matter most. `.githooks/pre-push` runs
`scripts/dod.sh` over a clean tree, so a two-clause step always skipped at every push. `git commit
--amend` has the same shape: the amended commit carries a `roadmap/` change while the diff against
`HEAD` names none, because `HEAD` is the commit being replaced. A step that can never do anything
but skip is a step that reports success it did not earn. The three clauses are:

1. the staged diff, `git diff --cached --name-only`;
2. the working-tree diff against `HEAD`, `git diff --name-only HEAD`;
3. **the commits this branch holds and its upstream does not**, `git diff --name-only @{upstream}..HEAD`, and `git diff --name-only $(git merge-base origin/main HEAD)..HEAD` when the branch has no upstream.

Clause 3 covers the push, because `HEAD` at a push is the tip the push carries. It covers the amend,
because `HEAD` at a pre-commit run for an amend is the commit the amend replaces and clause 3
includes it. **When neither `@{upstream}` nor `origin/main` resolves, the step RUNS.** A step that
cannot compute its denominator does not skip; that is the fail-closed answer the guard family
applies everywhere else, and the three commands cost about one second between them.

**Two residual limits, stated rather than hidden.** A force update that moves the remote ref
BACKWARD leaves clause 3 empty while the push still rewrites history; the `plan-lint` job of
`.github/workflows/ci.yml` reads the whole document on every pull request that touches `roadmap/` or
`tools/xtask/`, and that job is the cover for it. A long-lived branch that has already pushed a
`roadmap/` change carries that change outside clause 3 on the next push; the earlier run covered it,
and the job covers the merge. **So a skipped local step hides nothing from the merge, and it no
longer hides everything from the push.**

**The SAME denominator turns rule CG9 on, and `scripts/dod.sh` computes it ONCE and reads it twice**
(critic C2-1). The `converts` step of the gate runs `cargo xtask check-conversions` on every
commit with no path condition, and rule CG9 of section 2.3 reads `architecture.md`. An unconditional
CG9 would therefore create the exact coupling the paragraph below refuses. **The step passes
`--appendix roadmap/duet-v1/architecture.md` only when the union of the three clauses names a path
that opens `roadmap/` OR names `crates/duet-time/src/convert.rs`**, and it passes no argument
otherwise; the guard then prints `REASON TEXTS:    skipped (no --appendix)` and rules CG1 to CG8 run
unchanged. **Both halves of the binding sit in the condition on purpose**: a `roadmap/`-only
condition would skip CG9 on a commit that edits `convert.rs`, and that commit is exactly a commit
that can break the binding. The `plan-lint` job passes the argument always. Section 2.3 part 6
states the rule, what it covers, what it does not, and the party that clears a red CG9.

**Chunk M90 lands the step, and the Orchestrator dispatches phase 1 in the order section 13.3
prints**: M1, then M91, then M90, then every line chunk of the phase. `scripts/dod.sh` is a policy
file under SM4, so CLAUDE.md makes the edit an adjudication and no engineer may make it. Every chunk
that edits a plan document meets the late signal until M90 lands, and every line chunk of phase 1
gets the early one. **M91 runs before M90** because M90 adds rule CG9, which compares the Appendix
B.1 reason cells with the `reason =` strings of `crates/duet-time/src/convert.rs`, and M91 is the
chunk that repairs those strings. **Both repair chunks run before every line chunk of the phase**,
because M91 changes the value that `unit_to_i24` and `unit_to_i32` RETURN and chunks D1 and T2
consume `duet-time` in the same phase. The write scopes are disjoint, so PG31 and `check-plan-graph`
are blind to that edge; rule SM1 of section 13.0 is the mechanism, and it now covers a repair chunk
(critic C1-9). ADR 0010 records the decision and the repairs beside it.

**The condition exists because the coupling it removes is real** (critic S11). An unconditional gate
line would make every commit in this repository depend on one roadmap markdown file. An edit that
adds a type without a section 1.5 row would block every engineer. A moved or archived document would
fail every commit for a reason unrelated to it. The path condition keeps the cost on the party that
creates it: an engineer who edits no plan document pays nothing, and an author who edits one gets
the finding in one second instead of one round trip.

**`cargo xtask check-roster` stays out of the gate, and the reason is its cost.** It reads the same
document, it builds a scratch workspace outside the repository, and it needs a toolchain: one
measured run reached 4.0 GB of build output and several minutes. It runs in the `plan-lint` job of
`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, which chunk M0 wrote and chunk M90 amends.

**`cargo xtask check-closure` is a REVIEW-TIME command and it runs in no job.** Rule CL1c of section
1.5 takes its second source from the plan store under `~/.claude/plan-dbs/`, which is outside the
repository and outside every write scope by design. A hosted runner carries no such store. Chunk M0
measured both states: against an empty store the guard prints
`STORE: unreachable   STORE COPIES: 0   CLOSURE BAD: 1` and exits 1, and against the operator store
it prints `STORE: matches   STORE COPIES: 1` and exits 0. **Three repairs were considered and two
were refused.** A restore step would need a secret and an artifact, and no chunk can own either. A
copy of the store inside the repository would put the second source back inside the Architect's
write scope, which is the one property CL1c exists to deny, so the guard would prove nothing. A rule
that passes when the store is absent is the vacuous green that CL1b and rule C22I-W4 already
condemn in this document's own words. **The guard therefore runs where the store lives**: the
Architect runs it before a plan revision, and the Engineering Critic re-runs it over the same store
when it verifies the closure. Section 1.5 rule CL1c states the same fact, and chunk M0 removed the
nine job lines that promised the other one (escalation M0-2).

**Every run of it is RECORDED in the plan store, and rule CL1d of section 1.5 binds a closure
section to its run** (critic C1-10). Revision 24 moved the guard out of every job and left its
verdict as a claim in prose, which is the state CL1b condemns two paragraphs above. The party that
runs the guard appends one row per run:

```
.claude/plan-coordination/db.sh append roadmap/duet-v1 closure-run "<body>"
```

The command mints the key `<simpleflake>-closure-run` and prints it. **The body opens with three
fixed lines and then holds the whole stdout of the run**: `COMMAND: ` and the full command line,
`EXIT: ` and the exit code, `TREE: ` and the output of `git rev-parse HEAD`.

**A PREFIX scan cannot enumerate this family, and the command that CAN is named here** (critic
C2-2). `append` mints `<simpleflake>-closure-run`, so the flake is the prefix and the suffix sits at
the END of the key; `scan` matches a key prefix, so `db.sh scan roadmap/duet-v1 closure-run` prints
nothing however many rows exist. The working enumeration reads the key list and filters on the
suffix:

```
.claude/plan-coordination/db.sh keys roadmap/duet-v1 | grep -- '-closure-run"'
```

`keys` prints one JSON record per key with the byte size and no value, so the call costs the key
list alone. **An auditor uses that command and never the prefix scan.** A reader who already holds
the key from a closure section reads the row with `db.sh get`, which is what the guard itself does.

**The store is append-only and it sits outside the repository**, so the row is a second source
for the VERDICT in the same way that the stored review is a second source for the review text, which
is the one property CL1c exists to hold.

### Rung two: named behaviour, machine checked

Five commands. Each one proves a claim this specification makes.

**1. The headless product path.**

```
cargo nextest run -p duet-agent --test end_to_end --no-tests=fail
cargo nextest run -p duet-agent --test export_end_to_end --no-tests=fail
```

**Two tests, and section 13.2 states why.** `end_to_end` is everything the product path delivers
before the export arms exist, and `export_end_to_end` is the export half. The paragraph below
describes the pair.

One test drives the whole product through gateway verbs, with no window and no hardware. It calls
`ProjectCreate` with the SATB template. It calls `TrackAdd`, `TrackSetInput`, and `TrackSetArmed`.
It imports a MIDI file. It records eight bars on a Soprano track from the dummy backend with a
synthetic input. It commits, branches, edits a note, and commits again. It checks out the first
commit and asserts the score bytes equal the bytes of the first save. It calls `Status` and asserts
the take count. It calls `MasterMeasure` and asserts progress and completion. It calls `ViewSet` and then `ViewGet` and asserts that the mode, the four
sub-states, and the window geometry all survive. It exports a 48 kHz 24-bit WAV with the Streaming
preset. It asserts the integrated loudness inside B76 of the B75 target, and a true peak
at or below the B75 ceiling.

This test is the proof that the core runs headless and that the verb list is complete.

**2. The real-time contract.**

```
cargo nextest run -p duet-engine --run-ignored ignored-only -E 'test(soak)' --no-tests=fail
```

Section 5.7 states what it asserts.

**3. Take alignment.**

```
cargo nextest run -p duet-engine --test alignment --no-tests=fail
```

Section 5.4 states the three cases. The first is a measured calibration. The second is the B72
default with its `TakeFlag::Uncalibrated`. The third is a round trip of one frame, which must return
`BackendError::CalibrationInvalid` with no panic.

**4. Notation correctness.**

```
cargo nextest run -p duet-engrave --no-tests=fail
```

The golden corpus B79, compared placement by placement (section 10.7).

**The determinism property is a SECOND command, because it belongs to a second crate** (critic
C16-W11). Section 3.6 gives deterministic output to the `duet-score` canonical writer, and
`-p duet-engrave` cannot run a `duet-score` test.

```
cargo nextest run -p duet-score --test canonical_determinism --no-tests=fail
```

`canonical_determinism` asserts that two writes of one score give equal bytes. Chunk T2 writes it in
`crates/duet-score/tests/canonical_determinism.rs`, and the selected-test table below carries its
row. Revision 16 claimed the property inside the engrave command and no chunk wrote a test for it.

**5. The time kernel and the two guards.**

```
cargo nextest run -p duet-time --no-tests=fail
cargo xtask check-conversions
cargo xtask check-placement roadmap/duet-v1/architecture.md
cargo xtask check-roster roadmap/duet-v1/architecture.md "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/duet-roster" .
```

**`check-roster` takes three arguments and it refuses a scratch directory inside the repository**
(section 1.9). The three are the document, a scratch directory, and the repository root; a workflow
job writes `"$RUNNER_TEMP/roster"` for the second and a developer writes a path under the system
temporary directory. Revision 13 wrote one argument in both rows, and the runner checkout is the
repository, so a defaulted scratch directory would have been refused (critic C-8).

Section 2.3 lists the four kernel tests and the `check-conversions` contract. Section 1.5 gives the
`check-placement` contract, and rung one states why that guard runs in `ci.yml` rather than in the
gate. `roadmap/duet-v1/tools/placement_check.py` and `roadmap/duet-v1/tools/conversion_check.py` are
the two prototypes that chunk M0 ports to `tools/xtask/src/check_placement.rs` and
`tools/xtask/src/check_conversions.rs`.

**The guard probes are part of rung two, and section 1.9 is the one place that counts them.** Each
probe is one test in `tools/xtask`, one per rule (DR5), and section 1.9's own table is the count.
**Chunk M0 ports the recorded TEXT of every cell as well as its exit code**, because PG29 checks the

Revision 11 wrote three counts here by hand and every one was a revision behind (critic WR-9); DR3's

red before the guard exists and green after it. Section 1.5 states the placement rules, section 2.3

The performance budget of B1 is a bench, not a gate:

```
cargo bench -p duet-engrave
cargo bench -p duet
```

The first reports the layout cost at B1 against B4. The second reports the cost of one Mix frame at
B1, with the cached sibling strips of section 10.2 and without them, against B4, and it records what
one frame leaves for an immediate verb at B5 (critic WR-19). A regression is reviewed, not blocked,
because a bench is not stable enough to gate a merge.

### Rung three: the human-review gate

**The freeze rule, stated once** (critic C20-N7). A review reads a FROZEN copy of
`roadmap/duet-v1/`, and the copy carries no `__pycache__` directory. A Python run writes bytecode
there, so a frozen tree that holds one changes while a reviewer checks it and cannot be compared
byte for byte across reviewers; stale bytecode in a frozen tree is also evidence that the tools were
last run against a different source. Every documented command sets `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, and
chunk M0 adds the `.gitignore` rule.

**Name: the Duet v1 product review.**

The operator runs it on macOS 26 and on Ubuntu 26.04 under Wayland, against the checklist below.
**The seven judgements are stated here and in no other file.** Revision 8 named
`roadmap/duet-v1/acceptance.md`, which no chunk writes and which does not exist, while the content
sat in this section already (critic C8). The operator copies this list into a signed record of their
own choosing. The gate passes when the operator signs it. No agent marks it passed.

The checklist holds seven judgements that no command encodes.

1. **Compose.** A MIDI keyboard connects with no dialog and enters notes. A click adds a quarter
   note. Each of `w`, `h`, `q`, `e`, `s`, and `t` changes the pending duration, the pending duration
   is visible, and a focus loss clears it. The context menu edits a note. The top bar shows the
   current key, meter, duration, and dynamic as values.
2. **The page reads as music.** A singer can sight-read the engraved page: spacing, beams, ties,
   slurs, and lyrics.
3. **Record.** The audio lane sits under the correct staff, and the wrap follows the system break at
   every staff size.
4. **Smoothness.** The operator sees no dropped frame during a scroll, during playback, or during a
   mode change.
5. **Mix and Master.** The tool set finishes a vocal project end to end, and every insert stage
   shows its own curve.
6. **History.** A checkout of an earlier commit restores the score and the audio, and the
   application never loses unsaved work in silence.
7. **The agent.** A terminal agent reads the composition, edits a note, imports a MIDI file, and
   commits, with and without a window open.

---

## 15. The complete type roster

Section 1.5 places every type. **This section declares every one of them that no earlier section
declares**, so the two sets are identical and PG4b proves it on every run.

**There is no suffix template any more.** Revision 8 carried ID1, which gave a name that ends in
`Id`, `Name`, or `Text` a shape by inference. `CommitId` names a git object, ID1 told the chunk to
write a `u64`, and the guard read the same suffix and certified the answer (critic R1). A rule that
**decides** a shape is more dangerous than a rule that declines to decide one, because only the
second kind has a counter. Every name now carries its own declaration, and the guard asks every
field of every `Copy` derive.

Each block below is the declaration of record for its crate. A chunk writes exactly these shapes,
and a chunk that needs a different one reports the discrepancy instead of inventing it (SM0).

**A block states the shape, not the documentation.** `missing_docs` is a rustc lint at `deny` and
`clippy::missing_docs_in_private_items` is denied too, so **every type, every field, and every
variant a chunk writes carries its own `///` line**. The blocks below carry a doc comment where the
shape needs a reason and carry none where it does not; a chunk adds the rest, and CLAUDE.md states
the rule. The PG25 roster compile relaxes those two lints and names that as the first line of its
stated profile, because a roster is a shape and not a crate (critic K-1).

**Most blocks state no function body, and a few state one.** An accessor below is usually a
signature: a chunk writes the body, adds `const` where `clippy::missing_const_for_fn` asks for it,
and adds `#[must_use]` where VR6 asks for it; section 2 declares about forty accessors and every one
of them takes that treatment (critic K-2). **This document spells out some of them in
full**, the PG25 roster compile builds every one of those, and the run prints both counts:
`ROSTER IMPL BLOCKS` is every `impl` block the document holds and `ROSTER IMPLS` is the number that
carry a body in every item. Revision 12 stated three different numbers in three places and two were
false (critic WR-14). Those blocks are why the profile
relaxes the four per-impl lints: substitution 1 removes the doc comment that carries the
`#[must_use]` attribute and the `# Panics` section, so each lint fires on a body the roster does
compile. Revision 11 gave the relaxation a reason the compiler contradicts (critic WR-3).

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default)]
pub struct TempoMapEdit { tempos: Vec<TempoPoint>, meters: Vec<MeterPoint> }

///

/// wrap it and both reach the transport inside `GatewayError` (section 15.5).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Error, Serialize, Deserialize)]

    Overflow,
    NotRepresentable,
    NotFinite,

### 15.2 `duet-dsp`

```rust
/// A readable block source of samples. `duet-media` implements it.
pub trait SampleSource: Send {
    /// The frame count of the whole source.
    fn frames(&self) -> u64;

    /// Read one block into `out`, and return how many frames it wrote.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    /// Returns `DspError::SourceRead` when the source cannot answer.
    fn read(&mut self, at: u64, out: &mut [f32]) -> Result<usize, DspError>;
}

/// ONE level of a peak pyramid over one source, held in memory for the lane
/// to paint.
///
/// **It is one level and one span, never the whole file** (critic C20-W4).
/// `Pyramid::load_level` reads the header, seeks to the level the zoom step
/// names, and reads the span the lane draws. B124 bounds the result, so the
/// draw path's residency does not grow with the length of the take. Revision
/// 20 declared the whole file as one `Vec` with no budget row.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct Pyramid { header: PyramidHeader, level: u8, from_bin: u64, bins: Box<[PeakBin]> }

/// The running state of one gain stage.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct GainState { current: Finite, target: Finite, step: Finite }

/// The running state of one meter tap.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct MeterState { reading: MeterReading, over: OverMark, decay: Finite }

/// The running state of one equalizer, as four biquad sections.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct EqualizerState { sections: [BiquadState; 4] }

/// One biquad section: its coefficients and its two delay samples.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct BiquadState { b0: Finite, b1: Finite, b2: Finite, a1: Finite, a2: Finite, z1: Finite, z2: Finite }

/// The running state of one compressor.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct CompressorState { envelope: Finite, gain: Finite, threshold: Finite, ratio: Finite, attack: Finite, release: Finite }

/// The running state of one gate.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct GateState { envelope: Finite, open: bool, threshold: Finite, hold_frames: FrameCount }

/// The running state of one de-esser.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct DeEsserState { detector: BiquadState, envelope: Finite, threshold: Finite }

/// The running state of one true-peak limiter.
///
/// **It is the LIVE limiter of the master chain** (contract 5.2, PR MA-02).
/// The same kernel runs offline in the section 7.4 render, so one
/// implementation serves the monitor and the file and the user hears what
/// the export writes. It holds a pool handle for its look-ahead delay and
/// never a buffer, exactly as `DelayState` does, so the audio thread
/// allocates nothing when the master chain changes. **The handle names a
/// slot of the `BufferPool::limiters` class**, which is B120 slots of B121
/// bytes; a delay slot would be B49 and far above the need (section 5.5,
/// critic C20-N3).
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct LimiterState { buffer: Option<PoolSlot>, write_head: u32, envelope: Finite, ceiling: Finite, release: Finite }

/// The running state of one delay line. It holds a pool handle, never a buffer.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct DelayState { buffer: Option<PoolSlot>, write_head: u32, delay_frames: u32, feedback: Finite, mix: Finite }

/// The running state of one reverb. It holds a pool handle, never a buffer.
/// **Audio-owned** (section 5.7).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct ReverbState { buffer: Option<PoolSlot>, write_head: u32, decay: Finite, damping: Finite, mix: Finite }

/// Every way a signal block refuses.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Error)]
pub enum DspError { SourceRead, BlockTooLong, PoolSlotMissing, PyramidFormat }
```

**`PoolSlot` and `BufferPool` are declared in section 5.5, and two chunks write them.**
`LimiterState`, `DelayState`, and `ReverbState` each hold an `Option<PoolSlot>`, and section 13.2
gives `LimiterState` to chunk D2 in phase 2. The index type therefore lands one phase earlier: chunk
D1 declares `PoolSlot` in `crates/duet-dsp/src/buffer.rs` in phase 1, and chunk D3 builds
`BufferPool`, its three classes, and its free word in `crates/duet-dsp/src/pool.rs` in phase 3.

/// One rest.

    id: VoiceId,

/// A reference to one element of the score, whatever its kind.

/// element reference (critic W16).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum ElementRef { Note(NoteId), Spanner(SpannerId), Mark(MarkId) }

/// The revision counter of one score. It increases on every applied command.
///
/// It derives `Eq`, which VR1 makes the compiler's demand over a `u64`. It
/// derives no order and no `Hash`. The engrave task compares the revision of
